REDUCTION OF CAPITAL AND BUY-BACK OF SECURITIES

8.1

CAPITAL REDUCTION

Share capital of a company gives it strength. Large share capital base means the company is on sound footing. Hence, there are very few restrictions on increase in share capital, but many restrictions on reduction of capital.

Company can reduce share capital, any capital redemption reserve account and any share premium account in any manner subject to provisions of law [Regulation 38 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

In particular, the company can reduce capital by following means, by passing special resolution and on confirmation by NCLT - section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 100(1) of the 1956 Act].

Section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016.

Extinguishment or reduction in liability - Company can extinguish or reduce the liability of members for unpaid capital e.g. if Rs 7.50 are paid in respect of share of Rs 10, the share will be treated as fully paid up for Rs 7.50. Thus, shareholder need not pay the balance amount [section 66(1)(a) of Companies Act, 2013].

Cancel lost capital - Capital which has been lost or is not represented by available assets can be cancelled. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares [section 66(1)(b)(i) of Companies Act, 2013].

Return excess capital - Capital can be reduced by paying off or returning capital which is in excess of the needs of the company e.g. out of fully paid share of Rs 10, Rs 2.50 per share may be refunded [section 66(1)(b)(ii) of Companies Act, 2013]. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares. Thus, capital can be paid off on condition that it may be called up again if necessary e.g. in aforesaid case, company can recall Rs 2.50 per share, if found necessary.

In RS Livemedia P Ltd., In re (2014) 127 SCL 1 = 45 taxmann.com 551 (Del HC DB), proposal to return excess capital was allowed. In this case, share capital was reduced in disproportionate manner and consideration payable to different shareholders were at different rates. The varying rates were on basis of time period and also on basis of type of investors (exit was allowed to foreign investor shareholders). The proposal was accepted by all. It was held that this is permissible.

Reduction by any other way - Share capital can be reduced 'by any other way' also e.g. adjustment of securities premium account.

No reduction of capital if company is in arrears in respect of repayment or interest on deposits - Company cannot reduce its capital if it is in arrears in the repayment of deposits (accepted before or after commencement of Companies Act, 2013) or interest thereon - proviso to section 66(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

[Normally, companies incurring loss will only be going for reduction of capital. Many of these may be in arrears of repayment of deposits or interest thereon].

Accounting treatment as per accounting standards - The accounting treatment proposed by the company for reduction of capital shall be as per Accounting Standard and certificate of company's auditors shall be filed before Tribunal - proviso to section 66(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

Forfeiture of shares is not reduction of capital - Forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls is not treated as reduction of capital and hence does not require confirmation from NCLT.

Buy back is not reduction of capital - Provisions relating to reduction of capital are not applicable in respect of buy back of securities under section 68 of Companies Act, 2013 - section 66(6) of Companies Act, 2013.

8.1-1 Redemption of preference shares by reduction of capital

In Birla Global Finance Ltd. In re (2004) 50 SCL 387 (Bom HC), it was held that even if redemption of preference shares is possible as per specific provisions of Companies Act, preference shares can be redeemed by following procedure for reduction of capital, as redemption of preference shares will result in reduction of capital. In this case, company had passed necessary special resolution in general meeting and consent of preference shareholders for redemption was obtained and hence Court granted permission to redeem preference shares by reduction of capital.

8.1-2 Adjustment of securities premium account

Securities premium account can be used for reduction of capital.

28.5 Payment of dividend out of capital, prohibited

Dividend pay-out not to bring about capital erosion

28.5-1 As noticed before, section 205(1) impliedly prohibits payment of dividends out of capital when it says as a cardinal principle of law that no dividend shall be declared or paid except out of the profits of the company, profits in this connection understood as ‘revenue profits’ in a financial year, while there is no rule of law or of accounting that capital profits partake the character of capital itself not available for distribution as dividends; and section 205 comes into operation only when the company is a going concern, Globe Motors Ltd. v. Globe United Engg. & Foundry Co. Ltd. [1975] 45 Comp. Cas. 429 (Delhi). For the purpose of prohibition of payment of dividend out of capital, capital means capital according to the Act and not the goods or things on which capital is laid out, Lubbock v. British Bank of South America (1892) 2 Ch. 198 (CA). Where the expenses or payments are improperly charged to capital to swell the apparent profits so as to make it appear that dividends may be properly declared, the dividends declared and paid on that basis cannot be treated as legitimately paid, Dovey v. Cory (1901) AC 477 (HL). If the directors show profits where there are none by manipulating the accounts, and dividends are paid, the directors may be compelled to replace the dividend thus paid out, Exchange Banking Co., In re (1882) 21 Ch. C. 519.

What are profits in general is a question which has many answers

28.5-2 Then, the question is about what are ‘profits’. In regard to what are profits, the Act and Rules refer to the term variously, and the contribution from the court interpretations is not of much help to reach to any clarity. For example, in Lee v. Neuchatel Ashphalte Co. (1886-90) All. ER 947 (CA), it was held that in the case of a wasting asset, it is not necessary to make provision for its replacement before declaring dividends, and if so done, dividends cannot be said to be paid out of capital. Again, in Verner v. General & Commercial Investment Trust (1894) 2 Ch. 239 (CA), the view expressed was that dividend may be paid out of excess ‘receipts’ over current expenses, even if fixed capital is sunk and lost—circulating and floating capital must be kept up. The meaning of the expression ‘profits’ as explained by the Court Spanish Prospecting Co. Ltd., In re (1911) 1 Ch 92 was : "Profit implies a comparison between the state of business at two specific dates usually separated by an interval of a year. The fundamental meaning is the amount of gain made by the business during the year…….If the total assets of the business at the two dates be compared, the increase which they show at the later date as compared with the earlier date (due allowance, of course, being made for capital introduced into or taken out of the business in the meanwhile) represents, in strictness, the profits of the business during the period in question".

Net excess in the worth of the company at the end of the year over that at the beginning is not the profit

28.5-3 The net excess in the worth of the company thus arrived at is not in fact the meaning of ‘profit’, and the meaning of profit in law is maintaining the capital without any reduction (as purported in section 78) and taking out the surplus of current year’s income over expenditure, Lawrence v. West Somerset Rly. Co. (1918) 2 Ch 250. The profit referred to in section 205(1) is the residue of profit after providing for depreciation current and past, past losses and the required transfers to the reserves on the one hand and the exclusion of not only the capital but the premium, if any, on it collected meanwhile during the year, as provided in section 78. Similarly, goodwill when brought into the books is not available as distributable profit by the decision in the Spanish Prospecting Co. case cited above.

Again, profits available for distribution and those distributed are not the same

, that is likely to be a situation !

1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

u Under-subscription : A subscription lower than the minimum subscription devolving on the under-writers in a public issue.

u Paid-up capital : It forms the amount paid on the shares subscribed, whether in cash or for non-cash. If the issued capital is fully subscribed and paid in an issue at par as a condition for allotment of shares, then the capital paid-up will be equal to the capital issued and subscribed. u Capital out of loans : Section 81(4)/94A of the Act provide that debentures issued to or loans drawn from the Government (Central or any State) irrespective of the option and public financial institutions with an option for it attached, by companies, may be ordered by the Central Government to be converted into shares which by itself effects automatic increase of the authorized capital of companies commensurately, with the loans wiped out.

u Uncalled capital : If the issue terms are such that only a part of the nominal value of the shares is payable for allotment the balance being payable against future calls to be made by the board of directors, the difference between the full value of the capital issued to the extent of the shares subscribed and the amount paid-up is called the uncalled capital. This category remaining so for long is now rare.

u Capital called-up but not paid or calls unpaid : It refers to the balance amount remaining unpaid on the first or further or final call made after the allotment of shares by the board of directors as of the last day of the financial year with reference to the balance sheet of that year but within the time allowed, and not amounting to calls in arrear.

u Calls in arrear : The amount of call or calls referred to above remaining unpaid beyond the time allowed.

u Calls in advance or unpaid capital : Section 92 and regulation 18 of Table A provide that moneys advanced and accepted though uncalled in respect of shares may bear interest at 6% p.a. but discounted for voting rights or dividend etc.

u Share premium : If shares are issued at a premium, that is, at a price higher than their face value, the excess is called share premium which forms part of capital for most purposes of assessing the financial position of the company. It does not count for dividend and it is not available for distribution as dividend but is available towards issue of bonus shares or meeting the premium payable on redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures or towards the write-off of preliminary expenses or commission paid on issue of shares or discount allowed on shares or debentures, section 78 of the Act.

u Discount on shares : If shares are issued at a discount, that is, at a price lower than their face value, it is called shares issued at a discount and the total amount of such discount has to be written off in a specified period, section 79 of the Act; and, it would appear that neither for dividend payment nor for voting it would not count anytheless, and the discount legally allowed is in the nature of an upfront dividend paid.

u Forfeited shares : If the calls made on shares allotted as partly-paid become bad debts, such shares may be forfeited by the board of directors to enforce the company’s lien on the shares subject to there being an enabling provision in the articles. When such action is taken, the amount to the extent paid as on the date of forfeiture ranks as capital at par with share premium and is separately displayed as an addition to the share capital in the balance sheet.

u The total of share premium and the amount of forfeiture on forfeited shares when added to the paid-up share capital may exceed the capital authorized in the capital clause in the memorandum.

[1984] 145 ITR 740 held that it is not deductible after referring to various differing judgments. It also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in Poona Electric Supply Co. Ltd v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 521, in which case, the company had set apart a certain amount towards consumer benefit reserve account, which represented excess over reasonable return in terms of the said Act. They are business profits and not statutory profits The real profit of a businessman under section 10(1) of the 1922 Act [corresponding to section 28(i) of the Act] cannot include amounts returned by way of rebate under statutory compulsion. It is as if it has received only the original amount minus the amount to be returned. The amount returned is not a part of the profits at all.

Thus, whether an amount set apart represents a reserve or provision will have to be decided and determined on the basis of the requirement relating thereto. However, for the purposes of section 115J of the Act, as it was an ascertained liability, the same is to be excluded while computing book profit.

1.8-1 Starting Point - Section 115JA attempts to define them by laying down the manner in which they are required to be computed. As said above, the starting point is 'net profit' as shown in the profit and loss account prepared as per the Schedule.

"Although the book profit has not exactly been defined in the Act, it is, however, supposed to be the profit as shown in the profit and loss account of the company for the relevant previous year and as prepared in accordance with the different provisions of the Companies Act. A normal profit and loss account starts with the trading account, incorporates the actual profit and loss account and generally ends with the profit and loss appropriation account. Therefore, the figure of net profit/loss as shown at the bottom of the combined profit and loss account (including the profit and loss appropriation account) should mean the book profit as referred to in section 115J.

[1984] 145 ITR 740 held that it is not deductible after referring to various differing judgments. It also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in Poona Electric Supply Co. Ltd v. CIT [1965] 57 ITR 521, in which case, the company had set apart a certain amount towards consumer benefit reserve account, which represented excess over reasonable return in terms of the said Act. Such an amount was required to be returned to customers in the form of rebate. The Supreme Court held that the amount credited to the said reserve did not form part of the real profit of the company. Under the Act, profits of the business are required to be computed and they are not profits regulated by any statute but profits in the business computed on commercial principles. They are business profits and not statutory profits The real profit of a businessman under section 10(1) of the 1922 Act [corresponding to section 28(i) of the Act] cannot include amounts returned by way of rebate under statutory compulsion. It is as if it has received only the original amount minus the amount to be returned. The amount returned is not a part of the profits at all.

Thus, whether an amount set apart represents a reserve or provision will have to be decided and determined on the basis of the requirement relating thereto. Based on the above decisions and in the light of the provisions of the Schedule, it could be said that the amount set apart towards contingency reserve could be considered as a reserve and not a provision and further, the amount set apart towards consumers benefit could be considered as a provision and that too for a known liability.

In National Rayon Corporation Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 51 ITD 621 the issue before the Bombay Tribunal was whether a provision made for liability relating to earlier years, which had accrued during the earlier year but not provided, could be deducted in computing the profits? The Tribunal held that under normal provisions, claim for such liability was not allowable. However, for the purposes of section 115J of the Act, as it was an ascertained liability, the same is to be excluded while computing book profit.

The above cited Supreme Court's decision also throws more light on the concept of net profit based on working results to be reflected in the profit and loss account as per the requirements of the Schedule.

Thus, the working results, as contemplated by the Schedule, could be the one which a commercial man would not misunderstand and therefore reflects commercial profits, which would be usually computed on the basis of the accepted principle of conservatism and after providing for all known liabilities and losses.

Book Profits

1.8 Book Profits (as defined) are required to be computed in accordance with Explanation below sub-section (2) and the first and the second proviso to subsection (2) of section 115JA of the Act. Two provisions create an impression that they are defined twice and could cause some confusion or technical litigation.

1.8-1 Starting Point - Section 115JA attempts to define them by laying down the manner in which they are required to be computed. As said above, the starting point is 'net profit' as shown in the profit and loss account prepared as per the Schedule.

There is no clarity about the starting point. Would it mean profit before appropriation or profit after appropriation or the final figure carried to balance sheet or anywhere in between. Based on the adjustment prescribed by Explanation, it appears that it should be after tax and appropriations, like, dividends, etc.

This issue was considered by the Bangalore Bench of the Tribunal in Sipani Automobiles Ltd. v. DCIT [1993] 46 ITD 280, wherein the Tribunal observed as follows:

"Although the book profit has not exactly been defined in the Act, it is, however, supposed to be the profit as shown in the profit and loss account of the company for the relevant previous year and as prepared in accordance with the different provisions of the Companies Act. The expression 'Profit and Loss Account' has also not been defined anywhere. A normal profit and loss account starts with the trading account, incorporates the actual profit and loss account and generally ends with the profit and loss appropriation account. All these three accounts, in accountancy parlance, are said to constitute the actual profit and loss account in its entirety. Therefore, the figure of net profit/loss as shown at the bottom of the combined profit and loss account (including the profit and loss appropriation account) should mean the book profit as referred to in section 115J.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Further, the term used in section 66 is 'pay-off', which has been defined in Random House Dictionary as "to pay (someone) everything that is due to that person; To pay (debt) in full." Thus, the term 'pay-off' suggests that there is a due to the shareholder to the extent of his interest in the company that is been paid-off. It appears that this cannot be equated with purchase of shares in which there is nothing due to the seller till the sale transaction takes place.

According to the other view, the payment upon reduction is also purchase of shares. Section 2(22)(d) provides that dividend includes any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of capital. However, the definition also provides that dividend does not include any payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The fact that there is a specific exclusion of payment upon purchase of shares shows that in the absence of such exclusion, purchase of shares under section 77A could have been regarded as reduction of capital. Conversely, reduction of capital should also be construed as purchase of shares by the company.

It appears that the better view is that reduction of capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not a purchase within the meaning of section 115QA, although as a consequence of this view, the shareholder could be liable to

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

◆ The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

◆ Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

◆ As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

◆ As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

◆ The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

◆ This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

◆ Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

28.3 Divisible Profits

Companies limited by shares : Dividend policy structured as a strategy

28.3-1 Since dividend is a return, rather a recurring and periodical return, on the amount invested in shares, no question of any payment arises in respect of companies not limited by shares and created for profit. Even amongst the companies which are limited by shares, it is not as if every company distributes dividends even if it is in profits, and the preponderant choice seems to be rather against it. A majority of the registered companies are private companies, and a majority of public companies are closely held public companies, where in both the kinds of companies the promoter or principal shareholders are also the controllers, directors and managers, preferring to be remunerated by way salaries, perquisites and benefits secured for themselves, and the surplus, if any, left after such drawal from out of the yearly profits allowed to accumulate such that it goes to increase the net worth of the company on the one hand and reduce the interest outgo on borrowings towards working capital to that extent on the other, put in place as a strategy. Strictly speaking, in regard to the flourishing but non-dividend paying companies of high net worth, there is no impairment caused to their shareholders insofar as the shareholders are free to bargain independent of the company for a higher price for their shares or for enhanced loan facility based on the premium commanded by the shares in the market in those circumstances.

Accretion of ‘interest’ value in guarantee companies

28.3-2 As to the companies limited by guarantee, though in business and operating for profit, what can accrue to the benefit of the promoters and principal controllers as members in common with the other members is not the yearly dividends but the advantage of unspecified accrual in the marketable price of their respective shares of interest of no par value in the undertaking of the company, and in that behalf section 37(1) declares that every provision in the memorandum and articles or in any resolution of the company—whether of the Board or of the general meeting-purporting to give any person a right to participate in the ‘divisible profits of the company’ otherwise than as a member, shall be void, implying thereby that such right runs with membership, of the existing members and prospective persons admitted to membership by the company directly, but not indirectly by voluntary transfer of interest in its entirety (by substituting another who is a non-member or even a member) by any existing member without purporting to divide the undertaking of the company into shares or interests of unspecified nominal amount of each as also the total number of shares or interests referred to in section 37(2), an act which has been declared void if the company intends to remain as limited by guarantee, or if there is any provision in the memorandum or articles made or it arises in any resolution of such a company it shall be treated as a provision for a share capital.

28.3-4 Consequently, the rules of law in their full rigour apply to dividends and its other form bonus against the remainder of the larger unlisted public companies and the listed public companies forming about a twentieth of the registered companies, numbering about 25,000. Even so, dividend and bonus are matters of the widest interest amongst the investing public and the Regulators as the decisions in respect of these two kinds of pay-backs, made by the Board of directors and adopted by the general meeting, have the potential to defeat the very purpose of the stringent rules of law enjoined on companies limited by shares and indivisibility of the company’s undertaking into shares in respect of companies limited by guarantee, in common, solely directed for the maintenance of capital or corpus as a safeguard against the dangers of the privilege of limited liability conferred on the members under the Act, particularly in the interest of the unsecured trade creditors.

Accordingly, it is felt that, inter alia, the following taxes paid cannot be added back :

Any tax payable by the company on its foreign income pursuant to a levy by the foreign country or government.

Any agricultural income-tax paid or payable by the company.

Any gift-tax.

Any interest tax. 1.9-2 Reserves adjustment under Explanation (b)/(i) - One of the adjustments required to be made relates to amounts carried to any reserve by whatever name called. The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

Securities premium account and capital redemption account for bonus shares - A securities premium account and a capital redemption reserve account may be used for purpose of issue of fully paid bonus shares - Regulation 39(ii)(D) of Model Articles of Association Table-F of Companies Act, 2013.

7.3-3 Board to act on the basis of ordinary resolution in general meeting Bonus shares are first approved in the meeting of Board. Once bonus issued is announced on basis of Board resolution, the company cannot subsequently withdraw the same - Rule 14 of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014.

The company in general meeting, upon recommendation of Board, can pass following resolution as ordinary resolution - (a) that it is desirable to capitalise any part of the amount for the time being standing to the credit of any of the company's reserve accounts, or to the credit of the profit and loss account, or otherwise available for distribution; and (b) that such sum (capitalized profit) be accordingly set free for distribution in the manner specified in Regulation 39(ii) amongst the members who would have been entitled thereto, if distributed by way of dividend and in the same proportions [Regulation 39(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

After such ordinary resolution, Board can give effect to the resolution by doing all necessary acts [Articles 39(ii)(E) and 40 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Return of allotment - After allotment, return of allotment has to be filed with ROC, as per procedure prescribed in rule 12 of Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 as amended on 20-1-2023.

7.3-4 Fractional certificate or payment of cash

The ratio of issue of bonus shares may be such that some members may be entitled to fractional share.

In such case, the Board may make provisions in respect of such fractional entitlement (a) by the issue of fractional certificates or (b) by payment in cash or (c) otherwise as it thinks fit [Regulation 40(ii)(a) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

For this purpose, Board may authorise any person to enter into an agreement with the company for the allotment to the members additional shares credited as fully paid up. Alternatively, company can pay, on behalf of members to any unpaid amount on their existing shares [Regulation 40(ii)(b) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Such agreement is binding on the members.

Normally, such fractional rights are consolidated into shares and sold by the person authorised by the Board. The proceeds are then distributed among members in proportion to their fractional rights.

7.3-5 Effect of issue of bonus shares

Bonus shares is an excellent way of bringing the paid up capital of the company in line with actual capital employed in the business. It broadens the capital base and improves image of the company.

Only fully paid bonus shares can be issued. Partly paid bonus shares cannot be issued, as it will create liability on members which they may not want.

Bonus shares are same as normal shares and members are entitled to get dividend on such shares. They can also sell the shares, if they wish. A bonus share is thought of as a gift from the company. In fact, a bonus issue simply divides the existing shares into smaller units e.g. assume that equity share capital of company is Rs. one crore and free reserves are Rs. 2.5 crores. The company is declaring dividend of 30%. If bonus shares in ratio of 1:1 are issued, the share capital will be Rs. 2 crores and free reserves will be reduced to 1.5 crores. Thus, actually, there is neither any cash payment to members nor any cash receipt from members. If market price of shares was Rs. 100 per share before issue of bonus shares, it will come down to Rs. 50 per share. Thus, the shareholder is neither a loser nor a gainer. If the company now declares 15% dividend, the shareholder will get the same amount which he was getting earlier.

Issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of reserve but only as part of capital - Hunsur Plywood Works v. CIT (1997) 95 Taxman 460 = 229 ITR 112 (SC) - quoted with approval in Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. CIT (2009) 176 Taxman 142 (SC), where it was held that there is no element of gift in a company issuing bonus shares.

company on buyback of shares which are not listed on recognised stock exchange.

Prior to the amendments by Finance Act, 2016

(a)

distributed income was defined to mean the consideration paid by the company on buy back of shares as reduced by the amount which was received by the company for issue of such shares;

(b)

buyback had been defined to mean the purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. Thus the definition of buyback did not cover buybacks undertaken by a company under other provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013.

Again there could be situations where shares may have been issued by the company in tranches, for different considerations, at different point of time or may have been issued in lieu of existing shares of another company under amalgamation, merger or demerger. In all these cases there was lack of clarity in determination of consideration received by the company at the time of issue of shares being bought back by the company (as per Explanatory Memorandum to Finance Bill, 2016).

In Capgemini India (P.) Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

may be redeemed on the terms on which they were issued or later varied with approval of preference shareholders. The approved terms of redemption can be any of the following - (a) at a fixed time or on the happening of a particular event (b) Any time at the company's option or (c) Any time at the shareholder's option - Rule 9 of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014.

Thus preference shares can be issued with put or call option. Company in infrastructural projects can issue preference shares for a period exceeding 20 years but not exceeding 30 year. However, minimum 10% of shares shall be redeemed per year from 21st year or earlier, on proportionate basis, at the option of preference shareholders - Rule 10 of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014.

Partly paid up preference shares cannot be redeemed.

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT 89 Comp Cas 28 (SC) = (1997) 11 SCL 121 (SC) = 224 ITR 422 = 1997 AIR SCW 731 = 90 Taxman 509 = (1997) Comp LJ 362, it was observed that redemption of shares amounts to purchase of own shares by the company. Redemption of preference shares is an exception to section 77 of the 1956 Act, which provides that company cannot purchase its own shares.

Redeem out of profits - Redeem out of profits of the company. Only that profit which is otherwise available for dividend can be used for this purpose [second proviso (a) to section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013]

Restrictions on purchasing own securities by the company, as contained in section 67 of Companies Act, 2013, do not apply to such redemption - section 67(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

A sum equivalent to nominal amount of the preference shares to be redeemed is required to be transferred to a reserve called 'Capital Redemption Reserve Account'. This reserve must be preserved. The reserve can be reduced only as if it is reduction in share capital [second proviso (c) to section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013]

The capital redemption reserve account can be used to issue fully paid bonus shares to members - section 55(4) of Companies Act, 2013.

If there is any reserve which is available for dividend, it can be transferred to Capital Redemption Reserve Account and then can be used to redeem preference shares.

Redeem by issue of fresh shares - If company is not in position to redeem preference shares or pay dividend, such shares will be termed as 'unredeemed preference shares'. The company can issue further redeemable preference shares equal to amount due including dividend unpaid on such unredeemed preference shares. Such issue is permissible only with consent of three-fourth in value of such preference shares and approved by NCLT [section 55(3) of Companies Act, 2013]

If some shareholders do not consent to such issue, NCLT can direct redemption of preference shares held by persons who do not consent to issue of further redeemable preference shares - proviso to section 55(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

Issue of such further redeemable shares will not be considered as increase or reduction in share capital - Explanation to section 55(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

Thus, no filing fees are payable for increase in capital in such cases.

Section 55(3) of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 1-6-2016, as NCLT has been constituted w.e.f. 1-6-2016.

Thus, approval of NCLT is required.

As per section 80 of the 1956 Act, redemption of preference shares by issue of fresh shares was permissible.

Procedure for petition before NCLT - Procedure for petition before NCLT has been specified in rule 69 of NCLT Rules, 2016. Application should be made in form NCLT.1 with documents as specified in Annexure B and rule 69(1) of NCLT Rules, 2016.

Fees of Rs 5,000 are payable with application.

NCLT can order redemption of preference shares to persons who had not consented to further issue of redeemable preference shares.

Payment of premium on redemption out of securities premium account - Companies which are not required to follow accounting standard can pay premium payable on redemption of redeemable preference shares, if any, out of profits or out of company's 'Securities Premium Account' - section 52(2)(d) and second proviso (d)(ii) to section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

However, companies required to follow accounting standards cannot use securities premium account for this purpose - section 52(3) of Companies Act, 2013 [The possible reason is accounting standards do not permit such use of securities premium account].

Companies required to follow accounting standards can pay premium, if any, shall be provided out of profits of the company, before shares are redeemed - second proviso (d)(i) of section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

CHAPTER 121

ISSUE OF BONUS CUMULATIVE REDEEMABLE PREFERENCE SHARES *ISSUE OF BONUS CUMULATIVE REDEEMABLE PREFERENCE SHARES*

121.1 Background note121.1 Background note

The provisions usually found in the Articles of any company regarding capitalization of profits correspond to Regulations 96 and 97 of Table A in the First Schedule to the Act, providing for issue of ‘fully paid bonus shares’ whether out of reserves created out of profits or the ‘share’ (now ‘securities’ as per section 78 of the Act as amended by the Companies Amendment Act, 1999 with effect from 31-10-1998) premium account. Since the enabling provision refers to issue of ‘fully paid bonus shares’ these can be fully paid preference shares and not necessarily equity shares, though the issue is to existing ‘equity’ holders entitled to it in the proportion of their respective equity holdings in the company.

121.2 Authority121.2 Authority

The proposed issue of bonus cumulative redeemable preference shares has to be on the strength of a provision existing in the Articles, and in its absence the first step would be to alter the Articles by passing a special resolution providing for it in the manner set out in Chapters 45 and 54.

121.3 Procedure & Compliance121.3 Procedure & Compliance

The rest of the procedure to be followed and compliance to be observed are the same as given in Chapters 45, 54, 113 and 120.

HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Income tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1935-36 company ‘R’ had accumulated substantial reserve and resolved to capitalize it - It was also decided that capitalized fund would later on be distributed amongst shareholders as bonus share - Company ‘R’ purchased share of company ‘A’ - Later on; it resolved to reduce its capital by returning to shareholder share in company ‘A’, which was confirmed by District Court - Revenue held that whole transaction was illusory and share of company ‘A’ allotted to assessee shareholders had never become capital and it would represent profits of company ‘R’ which would be taxable in hands of assessee - Whether department was competent to go behind order of court confirming reduction of capital and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced of its share capital was release of profits - Held, No - Whether value of shares of company ‘A’ received by assessee was not liable to be included in his income - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

On reference:

HELD: As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

Therefore, the value of shares of the Company ‘A’ received by the assessee was not liable to be included in the assessee’s income.

If the second condition had not been introduced, bonus shares issued credited as fully paid up would have been liable to be regarded as "dividend" within section 2(6A)(a) but the legislature obviously did not want to tax such bonus shares as dividend and it, therefore, introduced the second condition in section 2(6A)(a) of the 1922 Act. When accumulated profits are capitalized and redeemable preference shares are issued as bonus shares credited as fully paid-up, the capitalized accumulated profits are converted into preference share capital. The balance-sheet thereafter shows the profit and loss account or reserves at a reduced figure and the issued capital at a correspondingly increased figure, the only effect being that one item on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet becomes replaced in whole or part by another item, namely, preference share capital, while the assets side of the balance-sheet remains unaffected. Now it is a fundamental principle of company law that the capital of a company must be maintained intact, for the company being a mere abstraction of law distinct from its members and the liability of the members being limited, it is the capital of the company which provides a minimum safeguard to third parties dealing with the company and the law, therefore, requires that no part of the capital shall be returned to the shareholders except under certain circumstances and by following a certain procedure requiring the scrutiny of the Court and, it is only if the Court sanctions, that there can be repayment to the shareholders in reduction of the capital. But notwithstanding this fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, redeemable preference shares can be repaid in accordance with the terms of issue otherwise than on a formal reduction of capital approved by the Court. The preference share capital collected from the holders of redeemable preference shares or credited as fully paid up out of capitalised accumulated profits can be returned to the shareholders without going through the procedure of reduction of capital, though such return of preference share capital would amount to reduction of capital. This would appear to constitute a departure from the fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, but if one look at section 105B of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, which was the section which governed redemption at the time when the redeemable preference shares in the present case were redeemed, it is found that the purity of this principle is not only not violated but is, on the contrary, preserved in effect, if not in name, by the stringent provisions contained in the section. Redeemable preference shares, according to these provisions, can be repaid out of profits or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. If they are redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue, the capital raised on that issue will obviously replace the capital redeemed and, consequently, the capital of the company will be maintained at the original yardstick. If on the other hand they are redeemed out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, then out of profits an amount equivalent to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed is required to be transferred to a reserve fund to be called "The capital redemption reserve fund" which is to be treated as equivalent to paid up capital. Hence, although the redeemable preference shares disappear on redemption, the capital which they represent is retained for accounting purposes and there is no reduction of the capital yardstick. This analysis of the mechanics of redemption clearly shows that when redeemable preference shares are redeemed, the preference share capital is returned to the shareholders and since such return of the preference share capital would deplete the capital of the company and consequently affect the sanctity of the principle of maintenance of capital which is regarded as a principle of paramount importance, the law requires that the preference share capital so returned should be replaced by other capital either provided by a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or transferred out of the profits of the company in case redemption is made out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. It is undoubtedly true that redemption cannot be made except out of profits of the company or out of proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, but these merely indicate the sources of the moneys which may be utilised for the purpose of returning the preference share capital to the shareholders. The only inhibition is that if a company wants to return the preference share capital to the shareholders the company must do so out of moneys earned by the company as profits or derived by the company from a fresh issue of shares or obtained by the company by selling any property belonging to it and if there are no such moneys, the company cannot return the preference share capital to its shareholders. But what is returned to the shareholders on redemption, what is distributed amongst them, is the preference share capital and not the profits of the company, or proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or sale proceeds of the property belonging to the company which merely provide the moneys for return of the preference share capital.

the transfer of the amounts standing to the credit of development rebate reserve to the share capital account does not involve any disbursement of money by the company. Nothing comes out of the till of the company to the shareholder. The entire amount of money shown as development rebate reserve is retained by the company in another account. It cannot be said that by the issue of bonus shares, the company has distributed its reserve fund to the shareholders even though it has retained the entire amount with it in the share capital account. When a shareholder gets a bonus share, the value of the original share held by him goes down. In effect, the shareholder gets two shares instead of the one share held by him and the market value as well as the intrinsic value of the two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as the value of the original share before the bonus issue.

It appears from the various decisions that issuance of bonus shares does not amount to distribution of accumulated profit of a company. The shareholder derives some benefit by the process of capitalising of the accumulated profits but at the same time, the value of his original shareholding goes down.

Viewed from any angle, it could not be said that in this case the assessee-company had distributed any part of its development rebate reserve fund when it issued the bonus shares. The accumulated profit lying to the credit of the development rebate reserve had been retained by the company. The amount had been transferred to the share capital account. If that was not done, the intrinsic value of the shares held by the shareholders would have been more. After the issue of the bonus shares, the intrinsic value of the original shares had gone down rateably. The accumulated profits of the company had remained with the company in one account or another. In the instant case, neither in form nor in substance, had there been any distribution of profits by the company in making the bonus issue. If the substance and not the form of the transaction was looked to, the issue of bonus shares was in the language of Rowlatt J., 'a bare machinery' for capitalising profits and there was no distribution of profits to the shareholders.

Therefore, the High Court's view that the issue of bonus shares amounted to distribution of accumulated profits of the company shown as development rebate reserve fund was not upheld and the appeals were allowed.

Dissenting view as per Bachawat J.

The distribution contemplated by section 2(6A)(d) is a distribution by a company 'on the reduction of its capital'. The word 'on' has no fixed meaning, but in the context of the sub-section, it must be given the meaning 'at the time of', as 'on entering', 'on the 1st of the month'. The distribution contemplated by the sub-section is, therefore, distribution at the time of the reduction of its capital, that is to say, when the resolution for reduction of its capital under section 55(1)(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, takes effect. As soon as the resolution for reduction of capital and consequential refund of the surplus capital to the shareholders takes effect, the capital stands reduced, the surplus ceases to be capital and stands allotted to the shareholders, each shareholder obtains a vested right to the refund of his share of the surplus, and a liability arises on the part of the company to make the refund. This liability arises as soon as the reduction of capital takes effect, and it matters not that the company has not made the necessary book entries showing the reduction of capital and the transfer of the surplus to the account of the shareholders. The word 'distribution' has several dictionary meanings. In the context of section 2(6A)(d), of the 1922 Act it means allotment or apportionment of the surplus amongst the shareholders; this allotment takes place and each shareholder gets a vested right to his portion of the surplus as soon as the capital stands reduced.

A close scrutiny of section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act reveals that (a) the distribution takes place on a single date and (b) the expression 'accumulated profits' means profits accumulated up to the date of the distribution. These two basic ideas which are implicit in section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act are forcibly brought out in the Explanation to the corresponding section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Thus the entire distribution of the surplus amongst the shareholders takes place on a single date. Now if the distribution is to have certain single date, that date can only be the date when the reduction of capital becomes effective. The payments to the shareholders either actual or notional by credit entries in the books of account are made subsequently. The payments need not be made on one date; they may be and often are made on several dates. The successive payments cannot be the distribution contemplated by section 2(6A)(d) of the 1922 Act. The accumulated profits are to be ascertained on the date of the distribution. But the accumulated profits must be ascertained on the date of the reduction of capital. Thus the two events, namely, the distribution and the reduction of capital must synchronise, and the accumulated profits must also be ascertained at the same point of time. The synchronisation is also obvious on a plain reading of the abridged text 'any distribution on the reduction of capital to the extent of accumulated profits'.

Thirdly, proviso (i)( a) makes it clear that the rebate shall be allowed in the case of a company which satisfies the condition that it must have ‘made the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment within India of the dividends payable out of such profits and for the deduction of the super-tax from the dividends in accordance with section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The words ‘prescribed arrangements’ could only mean arrangements prescribed either by the Act or the rules made thereunder or by the Companies Act or the rules made thereunder or under the articles of the company. Such prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends could not mean notional or deemed dividends such as were contemplated in section 23A section 18(3D) is not also concerned with deemed or notional dividends but with deducting super-tax on the amount of the dividend as increased in accordance with section 16(2). The two parts of proviso (i)(a ) are clearly separate, namely, the part that makes for ‘prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends payable out of such profits’ on the one hand and the part ‘for the deduction of super-tax on dividends in accordance with the provision of section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The first part cannot include deemed or notional dividends at all. As the language clearly says, it means dividend which has been declared and paid by the prescribed arrangements. The second part under section 18(3D) may include consideration of deemed dividend as the section itself provides. In order to succeed, therefore, the revenue had to establish in the instant case that the dividend taken to be dividend in this case was a dividend according to prescribed arrangements within the meaning of proviso (i)(a ) of Paragraph D of the Finance Act. On the facts the revenue could not do this in the instant case. Therefore, the contention of the revenue to come within clause (a) of proviso (i) could not succeed. No doubt, the ITO, had tried to describe as accumulated profit a certain figure, manifestly under a misconception because he tried to include contingency reserve, accumulated balance under the profit and loss account and provision for income-tax which could by no means be considered as accumulated profits of the company. Even profits from the sale of machinery could not be said to be accumulated profits without something more and mere appreciation of the original value of the machinery will not bring it within the expression ‘accumulated profits of the company’. Accumulation of profits is a deliberate act and implies a conscious volition to accumulate the profits. It is well known that reduction of share capital can be effected in company law by various methods, particularly classified as (i) with sanction of the court, and (ii) without such sanction. Forfeiture or surrender of shares of cancellation of unissued shares are examples of reduction of share capital for which sanction of the court is not necessary. In other cases, where the company wants to reduce its share capital, it can do so after obtaining sanction of the court. Section 2(6A) did not expressly mention or even impliedly include the concept of deemed dividend. The express section dealing with deemed dividend, and specially with super-tax on such deemed dividend, is section 23A. Explanation (ii ) of Paragraph D of Part II of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, expressly says that the expression ‘dividend’ shall be deemed to include any distribution included in the expression ‘dividend’ as defined in clause (6A) of section 2. In the instant case, the reduction of share capital had not produced or had not been shown to have produced on any evidence an income by way of ‘dividend’ as contended by the revenue, according to the extended connotation of the word ‘dividend’. Before the Tribunal came to any finding of following rebate on super-tax, it had to be satisfied that the super tax was leviable on the total income of the company under Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, because it was only in that event that the question of rebates on that super tax could arise. This primary condition, had not been satisfied in the instant case and, therefore, the Tribunal was not right in holding that any rebate of super-tax was allowable in the sense that no super-tax itself was leviable on the reduction of share capital which occurred in the facts and circumstances of the case. As the first condition had not been satisfied the consequential question of allowing rebate on super tax really did not arise. Further, this reduction of share capital had not produced an income on which a super-tax could be attached nor was it a dividend within the meaning of the Act or Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. Further there was no evidence to hold that this reduction of share capital in the particular case meant any return of ‘accumulated profits’

distribution must be such as entails release of assets of the company and if, therefore, the distribution does not entail release of assets of the company, though the first condition would be satisfied, the second would not be and the distribution would not, therefore, be dividend within section 2(6A)(a) 1922 Act. Now admittedly there was release of assets of the company on redemption since moneys were actually paid out of the coffers of the company and received by the shareholders. A company must state in its memorandum of association the amount of capital with which the company desires to do business and the number of shares into which that capital is to be divided. The company need not issue all its capital at one time. It may issue only a part of its capital initially and issue the rest of the unissued capital or a part of it at a later date. Now if a company prospers and earns profits it may do one of two things with the profits. It may either distribute the profits by way of dividend among the shareholders or accumulate them. Generally, when a company accumulates profits it carries them to various reserves which appear on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet. Ordinarily, these undistributed profits are employed in the business either in acquisition of fixed assets or as working capital and really represent an increase in the capital employed in the business. When these increase to a considerable extent, the issued capital of the company ceases to bear a true relation to the real capital employed in the business. The company may, in such a case, decide to bring its issued capital into a truer relationship with the capital actually employed in the business or, to use the words of Gower, "more into line with the true excess of assets over liabilities" and may for that purpose capitalise its accumulated profits and issue fully paid up bonus shares of a nominal value equal to the amount capitalised to its shareholders. These bonus shares may be either ordinary or preference shares on the one hand or redeemable preference shares on the other. The company may also instead of issuing bonus shares issue bonus debentures by capitalising its accumulated profits. In all these cases the accumulated profits which are capitalised remain in the coffers of the company and no part of them actually goes into the pockets of the shareholders : the only change that takes place is that the accumulated profits which prior to capitalisation were employed in the business as accumulated profits are thenceforth employed as part of the issued or loan capital of the company according as the issue is of bonus shares or bonus debentures. The accumulated profits which might have been divided among the shareholders as dividend are impounded to increase the capital of the company and what the shareholders get is not any payment out of the accumulated profits but bonus shares or bonus debentures credited as fully paid up. The transaction, to use the words of Viscount Cave in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. John Blott [1921] 8 Tax Cas. 101, 135, takes "nothing out of the company’s coffers and "puts" nothing into the shareholders’ pockets" but what happens is that the accumulated profits which are capitalized are applied in paying up the amounts due on bonus shares or debentures to be issued to the shareholders as fully paid up bonus shares or debentures. This analysis of the mechanism of issue of bonus shares or debentures is, apart from the abundance of authority to support it, clearly based on sound principle. It is clear law that when shares are issued and allotted by a company the liability for the amount due on the shares is always on the allottee and that liability must be satisfied from some source external to the company in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or if the allottee has to his credit any amount due by the company, such credit may, with his consent, be applied in discharge of the allottee's liabilities on the shares. Now admittedly no moneys are paid by the shareholders for the bonus shares issued to them and it must, therefore, follow that when bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up, the liability for payment in full on allotment which the shareholders would otherwise have had to discharge is paid by the company by applying the accumulated profits to the discharge of such liability for the benefit of the shareholders. There is of course no payment of the accumulated profits to the shareholders since no part of the accumulated profits is liberated to them: the company does not part with any of the accumulated profits nor do the shareholders receive any part of them. But the accumulated profits are applied in paying up the capital sums which the shareholders would otherwise have had to contribute for the purpose of new shares. The shareholders receiving bonus shares credited as fully paid up are given credit for the capital sums which they would otherwise have had to contribute in respect of the bonus shares allotted to them if those shares had not been issued credited as fully paid up and this credit is given by application of the capitalised accumulated profits in payment of such capital sums. As observed by Hidayatullah J. in CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC), after the accumulated profits are converted into capital and bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up "the company employs that money not as reserves of profits, but as its proper capital issued to and contributed by the shareholder"

HEADNOTE: Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1983-84 - While computing capital, in addition to paid-up capital, and general reserve, assessee added proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876 on account of bonus shares issued on 15-10-1982 - Whether any increase in paid-up capital by virtue of issue of bonus shares out of general reserve was counter-balanced by an equal decrease in reserves and, therefore, aforesaid amount of Rs. 6,32,876 had to be excluded while computing capital - Held, yes - Whether the assessee’s contention that out of profit made during the accounting period a sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was transferred from the profit and loss account to the general reserve and, therefore, it should be taken to have transferred the capital on account of issue of bonus shares amounting to Rs. 30 lakhs’ out of the aforesaid profits was tenable - Held, yes.

FACT: For the assessment year 1983-84, while computing capital as per the Second Schedule, the assessee, in addition to the paid-up capital and general reserve, added proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876 on account of bonus shares declared on 15-10-1982. The AO held that any increase in the paid-up capital by virtue of issue of bonus shares out of general reserve was counter-balanced by an equal decrease in the reserves and, therefore, rule 3 of the Second Schedule did not come into operation. He, accordingly, computed the capital. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the AO’s order.

On second appeal, the assessee also took up a new plea that out of profit made during the accounting period a sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was transferred from the profit and loss account to the general reserve and, therefore, it should be taken to have transferred the capital on account of issue of bonus shares amounting to Rs. 30 lakhs out of the aforesaid profits.

HELD: In the case of CIT v. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1978] 111 ITR 6 , the Bombay High Court has held that when bonus shares are issued as fully paid-up shares by capitalisation of a part of the amount standing to the credit of the general reserve, the capital, as computed in the manner provided by rule I of the Second Schedule, is not increased in any manner whatsoever. It was, thus, clear that so far as computation of capital was concerned, that had been correctly done by the AO by not taking into consideration the proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876.

As regards the new plea, the assessee’s argument, though attractive, was without any substance. The entries made in the books of account of the assessee had their importance and relevance and could not be wished away. As per the entries recorded in the balance sheet, general reserve as per such balance sheet came to Rs. 93,09,997. Out of this amount, a sum of Rs. 30 lakhs was reduced being utilised for issue of bonus shares; thus leaving a balance of Rs. 63,09,997. This was the position in books as on 15-10-1982. A sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was credited to the reserves account much later on 31-12-1982. So, on the face of it, it was not possible to accept the contention of the assessee that the withdrawal of the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs on account of bonus shares should be attributed to the profit earned during the year. The facts were clear that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had been utilised for the issue of bonus shares out of the brought forward balance of Rs. 93,09,997 in the general reserves account. This argument of the assessee, therefore, was not acceptable.

In the result, the conclusions of the Commissioner (Appeals) were upheld, and the assessee’s appeal was dismissed.
