Section 2(22), read with sections 46A, 115-O and 246, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend (Clause (d)) - Assessee-company was engaged in business of development of computer software and related services and export - During year 2016, assessee sought order of Court to buy back its own shares - Said scheme got approved by Court and, accordingly, consideration for such buy-back was paid to shareholders - Gain arising to shareholders in course of buy-back was offered to taxation as capital gain under section 46A - Department submitted that buy-back of share was nothing but distribution of accumulated profit and it had to be treated as dividend under section 2(22)(d) and Dividend Distribution Tax at 15 per cent was required to be paid by assessee under section 115-O - Assessee filed writ petition on ground that gain on buy-back of shares could not be categorized as a dividend and it was capital gain as per section 46A - Whether profit on shares purchased pursuant to order of Court would amount to dividend and would not amount to capital gain - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had an appeal remedy under section 246, and attempt had been made by it to bypass said appeal remedy, writ petition failed and same was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 30-32] [In favour of revenue]

Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964, read with section 80J of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment years 1973-74 and 1974-75 - Whether appropriation made by board of directors by recommending payment of dividend, would constitute a 'reserve' - Held, no - Whether amount of dividend, declared by company could be included in its capital base - Held, no - Whether capital for purpose of Surtax Act is to be reduced by amount representing capital for relief under section 80J - Held, no

Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1971-72 - Whether there is proportionate increase in capital of company for purpose of capital computation when part of it is capitalised and bonus shares are issued - Held, no

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 - Shares capital - Reduction of - If a company in voluntary liquidation, after repaying its preference and ordinary share capital is revived with fresh share capital which is less than earlier capital, it does not amount to reduction of capital

Section 2(22) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1989-90 - Assessee was shareholder of company AIPL - There had been two amalgamations whereby group companies including some wholly-owned subsidiaries of company ‘AIPL’ had amalgamated with AIPL under supervision of High Court - Subsequently, during previous year relevant to assessment year 1989-90, AIPL effected reduction of its capital from Rs. 100 per equity share to Rs. 45 per equity share - There was specific provision in Articles of AIPL to effect that capital profits of company could not be distributed - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer worked out accumulated profits of AIPL by including capitalised part of share capital issued in exchange of shares of subsidiaries, surplus arising on account of cancellation of shares of subsidiaries held by each other; excess of distribution over book value of shares of certain wholly owned subsidiaries from liquidators; and provision for tax and existing disputed tax liability - He held that payment of Rs. 55 per share on account of reduction of share capital was made out of these accumulated profits and thereby provision of section 2(22)(d) was attracted - Whether where High Court had approved amalga-mations it could not be said that series of amalgamations was carried out as a tax planning device and to avoid capital gains tax - Held, yes - Whether expression ‘accumulated profits’ used in section 2(22)(d) is to be construed as commercial profits computed in accordance with principles of commercial accounting and these profits are not to be treated as equivalent to assessable income - Held, yes - Whether surplus arising on amalgamation of companies results in revenue gain and can be treated as accumulated profits of amalgamated company - Held, no - Whether profits in balance sheet of amalgamating company can be treated as accumulated profits of amalgamated company - Held, no - Whether, insofar as profits of capital nature are concerned arising from sale of capital assets, such profits are to be excluded for purpose of ascertaining accumulated profits under section 2(22) unless such capital profits have been subjected to capital gains under section 45 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, surplus realised by amalgamating company 
 and capitalised by issue of paid-up capital would not be covered under the expression ‘accumulated profits or capitalised profits’ for purpose of section 2(22)(d) - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, in instant case, Assessing Officer was wrong in working out accumulated profits by including aforementioned surpluses, and reworked profits being negative, provisions of section 2(22)(d) were inapplicable - Held, yes

Second Schedule of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1972-73 - Assessee-company created debenture redemption reserve out of its profits and payment to debenture-holders on account of principal and interest was made out of funds other than said debenture redemption reserve - Further an amount equal to cash applied in redeeming debentures was transferred from profit and loss account to capital redemption reserve fund in order to conserve working capital - Whether such debenture redemption reserve was a reserve and not a provision and was to be taken into account for purpose of computation of capital according to Second Schedule - Held, yes

Rule 1 to the Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 -Capital - Computation of- Assessment years 1970-71 and 1973-74 - Whether issue of bonus shares after first day of previous year out of general reserve should be considered for purposes of capital computation and share capital be increased proportionately - Held, no - Whether general reserve be reduced by amount of proposed dividend for purposes of capital computation - Held, yes

Section 2(22)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(6A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] read with schedule I, para D, of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - Deemed dividend - Assessment year 1957-58 - On orders of High Court share capital of company was reduced, and company distributed amounts to shareholders in consequence of such reduction - ITO held that company had accumulated profits and to that extent distribution by company on reduction of share capital would be regarded as dividend - Tribunal held that rebate of super-tax was allowable to assessee under clause (iii) of first proviso to para D of Part II of First Schedule to Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - However, there was no evidence to hold that reduction of share capital in particular case meant any return of "accumulated profits" and there was no question in instant case of any dividend from any subsidiary Indian company within meaning of Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, and its provisos - Whether reduction of share capital did not produce any income on which super tax could be levied nor it was dividend within meaning of Act or Paragraph D of Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957 - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was not right in holding that any rebate of super-tax was allowable in sense that no super-tax itself was leviable on reduction of share capital which occurred in facts and circumstances of case - Held, yes

Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1971-72 - During assessment year 1971-72 on 27-2-1970 assessee-company issued bonus shares out of its general reserves with result that paid-up share capital of assessee-company increased proportionately with corresponding reduction in its general reserve - Whether rule 3 of Second Schedule could be invoked in assessee's case when it issued bonus shares by capitalising a certain amount out of its general reserves which were not affected in any manner on first day of previous year - Held, no

Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1964-65 - Whether amounts set apart for proposed dividend, profit sharing bonus, and pension scheme have to be treated as provision - Held, yes - Whether amount credited to depreciation fund in excess of amount actually allowed in income-tax assessment has to be treated as a reserve - Held, yes

Rule 2 of the Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment years 1970-71 and 1971-72 - Assessee transferred an amount representing difference between depreciation claimed in returns and depreciation debited in books from general reserve account to general reserve account No. 1 - In subsequent year, assessee capitalised certain sum by utilising total amount in general reserve account No.1 and balance from general reserve and issued bonus shares - As a result, it had become paid-up capital - Whether entire difference between depreciation actually allowed to assessee and actually provided for in accounts should be deducted from capital computation base for subsequent assessment years - Held, no

Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment years 1983-84 and 1984-85 - Whether development rebate reserve written back to general reserve should be reduced from capital base under rule 1(iii) - Held, no

Second schedule to the companies (profits) surtax act, 1964-Capital-Computation of -Whether development and contingency reserve is a reserve and should be taken into account while computing capital-Held, on facts, yes-Whether difference between written down value of assets as allowed in income-tax assessments and as shown in assessee's books, representing depreciation reserve, should be treated as reserve for capital computation -Held, on facts, yes.

Section 115JB, read with sections 115J and 115JA, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and Parts II and III of Schedule VI of the Companies Act, 1956 - Minimum alternate tax - Assessment years 2003-04 to 2005-06 - Whether for purposes of section 115JB Assessing Officer has powers to go behind accounts of a company and see as to whether same have been prepared in accordance with requirements of Parts II and III of Schedule VI of Companies Act, 1956 - Held, yes - Assessee earned profit on sale of shares - It did not credit same to profit and loss account but directly credited to capital reserve account in balance sheet - Assessing Officer formed an opinion that as per sub-section (2) of section 115JB assessee was required to prepare profit & loss account in accordance with Parts II and III of Schedule VI of Companies Act, 1956 and that profit on sale of shares should have been part of that profit and loss account - Consequently, he computed book profit under section 115JB and brought profit on sale of shares to taxation under MAT provisions of section 115JB - Whether not crediting profit on sale of shares to profit & loss account was contrary to significant accounting policy of assessee itself as well as against requirements of Accounting Standard AS-13 and requirements of Parts II and III of Schedule VI of Companies Act, 1956 - Held, yes - Whether therefore, Assessing Officer had rightly brought profit on sale of shares to taxation under MAT provisions of section 115JB - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

Second Schedule of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Whether only an amount which is in excess of what is reasonably necessary for meeting a known liability can be treated as reserve - Held, yes - Whether amount set apart for redemption of debentures which was less than assessee's liability on this account, could be regarded as reserve - Held, no

Section 2(8)  of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Statutory deductions- Whether development rebate reserve in excess of statutory requirement has to be treated as ‘other reserve’, for purpose of computing capital base in determining statutory deductions under section 2(8) - Held, yes

Rule 1 of second schedule to the companies (profits) surtax act, 1964-capital-computation of-whether, for purposes of inclusion in capital base, amount standing to credit of general reserves on first day of relevant previous year should be reduced by sum proposed to be capitalised by issue of bonus shares, for which requisite resolution was passed only subsequently-held, no-whether amount shown under 'reserve for bad and doubtful debts account' which had never been utilised since bad debts were debited directly to profit and loss account, should be treated as a provision and excluded from capital base-held, no

Rule 1 Schedule II of the Super Profits Tax Act, 1963 - Capital - Computation of - Whether surplus in profit and loss account and provision for taxation would not constitute 'reserve' - Held, yes - Whether, however, provision for gratuity and excess of reserve for development rebate over reserve statutorily required to be maintained constitute reserve for purpose of computation of capital - Held, yes

Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1931-32 - Respondents-assessees received certain fully paid-up bonus debentures issued to them in respect of their shareholding in certain companies including one 'ABC' - According to various resolutions passed by said company, bonus debentures were issued for capitalizing its reserve fund - Similar was procedure adopted by other companies too - Whether by transactions in question, any income, profits or gains accrued or arose to or were received by assessees within meaning of section 4 of 1922 Act - Held, no

Section Second Schedule of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1972-73 - Whether when a part of amount standing to credit of general reserve is, during course of previous year, capitalised by issue of fully paid-up free bonus shares, there is no increase by any amount in capital computed in accordance with provisions of Second Schedule - Held, yes

III. Rule 1, Schedule II to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Computation of capital - Whether excess development rebate reserve is includible in capital computation for purpose of surtax - Held, yes
Circulars and Notifications : CBDT Circular No. 53 (F. No. 7/2/68-TPL), dated 11-1-1971

Section 34(3)(a)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Development rebate - Withdrawal of - Whether issue of bonus shares amounts to distribution of profits within meaning of section 34(3)(a)(i) - Held, yes

Second Schedule of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Computation of capital -  Whether dividend reserve qua ordinary shares could not be treated as reserve for purpose of capital computation under Act - Held, yes - Whether gratuity reserve in excess of known or determinate liability of assessee in respect of gratuity would be treated as reserve for purpose of capital computation - Held, yes

Section Second Schedule of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Computation of capital -  Assessment years 1967-68 to 1970-71 - Whether loan taken by assessee qualified for inclusion in computation of its capital for purposes of surtax chargeable - Held, yes - Whether proposed dividend should be deducted from general reserve while computing capital employed - Held, yes - Whether before rule 3 of second schedule can be pressed into service by assessee-company, it must be shown that capital base for said company as on first day of previous year relevant to assessment year as per rule 1 undergoes a hike after that day, during relevant assessment year - Held, yes - Whether where bonus shares were issued by capitalising part of general reserve and consequently original amount of capital base considering paid up capital and general reserve remained same, assessee-company would not be entitled to benefit of rule 3 of second schedule - Held, yes

Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Share capital - Reduction of - Petitioner, a public company proposed to reduce its share capital by extinguishing and cancelling 25 crore preference shares - Board of Directors of a company passed a resolution approving reduction of share capital - Members of petitioner-company had also approved said reduction by passing special resolution in its Extraordinary General Meeting - It was observed that company had duly complied all requisite statutory requirements - Further, accounting treatment proposed by company for such reduction was in conformity with accounting standards specified in section 133 and other provisions of Act - Whether since proposed reduction did not prejudicially affect interest of any shareholder nor it had any adverse effect on public at large, special resolution to that effect was to be confirmed - Held, yes [Para 15]CL: Where proposed reduction of share capital did not prejudicially affect interest of any shareholder nor it had any adverse effect on public at large and all requisite statutory requirements in respect to said reduction had been complied, reduction of share capital was to be allowed

Section 4 of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Surtax - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether if there is some amount set apart from profit and is not earmarked for being utilised for any particular purpose and if marked for being utilised for a particular purpose, purpose is not to meet any known or existing liability and is thus not kept for being appropriated to meet such a liability it shall be a reserve and shall qualify for being computed in capital for purposes of Act - Held, yes - Whether it is incorrect, to say that merely because a fund has been set apart for debenture redemption, a specific liability, it is a provision, it is equally wrong to hold that since it is not a provision it is a reserve which qualifies for computation of capital - Held, yes -Assessee-public limited company created a debenture redemption reserve - While completing assessment for surtax ITO rejected assessee’s contention that reserve created for debenture redemption should also be treated as apart of capital, mainly on ground that said reserve had been created for purpose of meeting a specific liability, viz., repayment of debenture loan - On appeals, Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal held that amount set apart for repayment of debentures was a reserve and not a provision - On instant reference, it was, however, seen that there was no information about nature of funds except name ‘debenture redemption reserve’ - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, matter was to be matter remanded back to Tribunal for fresh consideration - Held, yes [-Matter remanded]

Section 4 of Super Profits Tax Act, 1963 - Charge of tax - Whether where there was no indication that sum shown as ‘Reserves and Surplus’ in balance-sheet of assessee-company - Constituted a reserve of any kind, sum was nothing more than a mass of undistributed profits and could not be taken into consideration in computing capital of assessee-company for the purpose of determining standard deduction as contemplated in section 2(9) - Held, yes

Section 100, read with sections 78 and 103, of the Companies Act, 1956 - Share capital - Reduction of - Petitioner, a profit-making company, passed a special resolution for adjustment of debit balance of its intangible accounts against credit balance of its share premium account and general reserve account under provisions of Act - A petition was filed under section 78 and sections 100 to 103 seeking confirmation to proposal of capital reduction of company in form of utilizing its securities premium account as well as general reserve - Whether since said proposal did not prejudicially affect any one as it did not involve extinguishment or diminution of capital of company nor did it involve pay-off of any capital received by company, special resolution to that effect was to be confirmed - Held, yes

facts.text:
The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

On reference:

The Assessing Officer noticed from the balance sheet of the assessee-company that it had made a transfer of sums from the development rebate reserve to share capitalisation account by issue of bonus shares and concluded that the issuance of bonus shares amounted distribution of profits by capitalisation and, therefore, section 155(5 )(ii)( a) applied to the assessee's case as the development rebate reserve had been utilised for distribution by way of dividend or profits. He, accordingly, withdrew the development rebate claim allowed earlier to the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal held that there was no distribution by way of dividend or profits in the issue of bonus shares. The High Court held that the issue of bonus shares resulted in distribution of profits and, therefore, the statutory requirement of section 34(3)(a)(i) had been violated.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

For the assessment year 1983-84, while computing capital as per the Second Schedule, the assessee, in addition to the paid-up capital and general reserve, added proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876 on account of bonus shares declared on 15-10-1982. The AO held that any increase in the paid-up capital by virtue of issue of bonus shares out of general reserve was counter-balanced by an equal decrease in the reserves and, therefore, rule 3 of the Second Schedule did not come into operation. He, accordingly, computed the capital. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the AO’s order.

On second appeal, the assessee also took up a new plea that out of profit made during the accounting period a sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was transferred from the profit and loss account to the general reserve and, therefore, it should be taken to have transferred the capital on account of issue of bonus shares amounting to Rs. 30 lakhs out of the aforesaid profits.

The petitioner-company filed a petition under sections 100, 101 and 102 seeking approval of the minutes for transfer of capital reserves to the profit and loss account. It was pleaded that the company had also unanimously passed a special resolution in its extraordinary general meeting resolving for transfer of balance of (i) share premium account and (ii) debentures forfeited account to the profit and loss account thereby transferring the capital reserves to the profit and loss account to be treated as deemed reduction of capital. The Registrar of Companies also submitted that the Central Government had no objection to the proposed transfer of capital reserves to the profit and loss account.

In the assessment year 1971-72 the assessee-company had issued bonus shares by capitalising part of the general reserves. The assessee claimed that the bonus shares were in addition to the paid-up capital of the company and since any increase in the paid-up capital was to be properly reckoned for purpose of computation of capital under rule 3 of the Second Schedule, the proportionate amount must be taken into account for the purpose of capital computation. The assessee's claim was rejected by the revenue but accepted by the Tribunal.

The High Court held that the process of conversion of reserves into bonus shares did not either reduce the overall capital or increase it. It was held that in order to attract rule 3 of Schedule II there must be a fresh influx of capital and the mere act of capitalising a part of the reserve and issuing bonus shares did not mean that there was any influx of additional capital. Therefore, the High Court rejected the assessees claim.

On appeal:

During the assessment years 1981-82 to 1987-88 the assessee provided for depreciation in its books, on basis of straight-line method whereas under, the Income-tax Act, 1961 it was allowed on reducing basis and thus a difference arose in depreciation as per income-tax records and depreciation as per books. The STO reduced the capital base of the assessee by the difference in depreciation as per income-tax records and depreciation as per books. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), relying on the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Zenith Steel Pipes Ltd. [1978] 112 ITR 215 upheld the STO’s order. He, however, accepted the contention of the assessee that the difference between the depreciation actually allowed and claimed in the books, which had been actually capitalised by the assessee by way of issue of bonus shares would form part of the capital and directed the STO to ascertain the said excess.

On second appeal, the assessee’s contended that the difference in depreciation was not liable to be reduced from the general reserve. According to the assessee, it had declared dividend and also created investment allowance reserve out of the general mass of profit before transferring the amount to the general reserve and in the absence of anything prescribed to the contrary the right of appropriation should be given to the assessee. It further contended that the amount of dividend declared and the investment allowance created were much more than the difference in the amount of depreciation allowed under the Income-tax Act and debited in the books of account and, therefore, nothing should have been excluded from the general reserve. It was further submitted that the Commissioner (Appeals), having accepted the claim of the assessee for the issuance of the bonus shares out of such difference of depreciation, was not justified in rejecting the assessee’s claim for the dividend and investment allowance, having gone out of the differential depreciation. In any case, it was submitted that only the amount of the respective years’ difference should be deducted and not the cumulative difference of all the years.

The assessee was a shareholder of the company, ‘AIPL’. During the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, AIPL had effected reduction of its share capital from Rs. 100 per equity share to Rs. 45 per equity share. Before this reduction of capital, there had been two amalgamations where other companies of the same group, including some wholly-owned subsidiaries of AIPL, had amalgamated with AIPL. On account of amalgamation, equity shares of AIPL were issued in exchange of shares of subsidiaries and, thus, surplus was capitalised. Further, the subsidiaries held shares of each other which were cancelled on amalgamation and the surplus arising in the process was christened as capital reserve account No. 1. Next, excess of distribution over the book value of the shares of certain wholly-owned subsidiaries was received from liquidators of those subsidiaries which was entered in the books as capital reserve account No. 2. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer held that the capitalised part of the share capital of AIPL and the above said two reserve accounts were accumulated profit within the meaning of section 2(22)(d). He worked out accumulated profit of AIPL by further including proportionate current year profit of the company, provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L Account and existing tax liability raised by the income-tax authorities but disputed by the company and not provided in books. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, concluded that the payment of Rs. 55 per share was out of accumulated profits and taxed the amount of distribution as deemed dividend. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) worked out the accumulated profits at a negative figure and, hence, held that distribution made by the company to its shareholders on reduction of share capital did not attract provisions of section 2(22)(d). He further held that since the company had not received any amount in excess of what was paid for acquiring the share, no capital gains tax was leviable in the matter.

On appeal by the revenue :

The assessee made a profit of Rs. 90,44,677 subject to the provisions for depreciation and taxation. After making provisions for there, balance of Rs. 5,08,637 was carried to the balance sheet. On 28-2-1946, the directors recommended that out of aforesaid sum Rs. 4,92, 426 should be distributed as a dividend and balance should be carried forward to next year's account. The recommendation was accepted by shareholders in their meeting on 3-4-1946 and dividend was distributed. Two contentions were raised on behalf of the assessee before the ITO, the first being whether the aforesaid sum could be called a "reserve" within the meaning of rule 2 (1) of the Rules in Schedule II and it should be included in its reserves while determining the capital on the 1-4-1946; the second that the proportionate profits of the assessee for three months, between the 1-1-1946, and the 1-4-1946, should also be included in the said reserves. The ITO rejected the contentions holding that a 'reserve' represents profits set apart for some specific or general purpose and, therefore, profits which had not been so set apart could not be treated as forming part of reserves for the purpose of inclusion in the capital. This order was confirmed on appeal by the AAC but was set aside by the Tribunal. The High Court, on reference, held that the amount of Rs. 5,08,637 was a part of the 'reserves' of the assessee-company as on 1-4-1946, within the meaning of rule 2 (1) and that the profits of the assessee-company from 1-1-1946 to 1-4-1946, should not be included in the said reserves as on 1-4-1946.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

On the orders of the High Court as a consequence of the take-over by the State of the assessee’s business of generation and supply of electricity, the share capital of the assessee-company was substantially reduced, and the company distributed the amounts in cash to its shareholders in consequence of such reduction. The ITO having found accumulated profits, regarded the distribution as dividend to the extent of the accumulated profits. He, concluded that since no part of these profits were allowed to have arisen before 1-4-1933, the company would be deemed to have declared dividend in the assessment year 1957-58 under section 2(6A)(d). Tax was calculated accordingly. On appeal, the two contentions namely, (a) that the definition in clause (d) of section 2(6A) means a distribution out of the accumulated profits and not any distribution on the reduction of its capital; and (b) that the distribution in clause (c) of the second proviso to paragraph ‘D’ of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, means actual distribution and did not include notional distribution, were dismissed by the AAC as without merit. On second appeal, the Tribunal observed that section 2(6A)(d) is general and applied to any distribution by the company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possessed accumulated profits and it did not matter whether the reduction of capital was bona fide or with a view to avoidance of super-tax by the shareholder. However, it opined that the rebate allowable to the assessee could not be withdrawn under the terms of the second proviso to Para D of the 1957 Act, and that the assessee being a company in which public are not substantially interested the rebate admissible was 20 per cent as mentioned in clause (iii) of the first proviso, and there was no question of any further withdrawal of the rebate.

On reference :

For the assessment years 1971-72 and 1972-73, the assessee-company had created, what was designated as 'bonus reserve' and in the computation of the assessee's capital, the ITO excluded the said amount. On appeal, the AAC reversed the ITO's decision. On further appeal, the Tribunal noted that the bonus paid by the assessee for these two years had been separately and independently debited to the profit and loss account and the bonus reserves had not been drawn upon for making such payment. In view thereof, the Tribunal confirmed the AAC's order.

On reference:

The assessee-company issued bonus shares out of the development rebate reserve and claimed development rebate for the relevant assessment years. The ITO rejected the assessee's claim on the ground that the issuance of bonus shares amounted to distribution of profits by capitalisation and could not be considered to be for the purpose of the business. On appeal, the AAC annulled the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal affirmed the AAC's order.

On reference :

The assessee-company had, during the middle of the accounting year, capitalised part of its general reserves by issuing bonus shares and claimed that since the bonus shares constituted an addition to its paid-up share capital under rule 3 of the Second Schedule, such increase worked out on proportionate basis must be added to the capital at the commencement of the year for the purposes of computation of capital. Though the ITO rejected the claim, the Tribunal allowed it.

On reference:

During the course of the previous year (on 31-7-1962), the assessee-company issued bonus shares to the amount equivalent to the paid-up capital. According to the revenue under rule 2 of the Second Schedule of the Act, the capitalised part of the reserve as a result of the issue of bonus shares was also to the proportionately added to the paid-up capital.

The Super Profits Tax Officer did not increase the total capital, as according to him the proportionate increase in paid up capital led to proportionate decrease in reserve. The failure on the part of the Super Profit Tax Officer to do so led to payment of more tax for which the assessee-company objected. The AAC dismissed appeal. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that it was incumbent upon the revenue to increase the paid-up capital due to the issue of bonus shares. As such there was proportionate increase in the total capital. The super profits for tax liability were held to decrease.

On reference :

The assessee-company had a certain general reserve at the close of its accounting year ended on 30-6-1966. The directors' report for that year contained a mention about capitalising a major portion of this reserve by issuing bonus shares, but the necessary resolution in this respect was passed only on 31-10-1966. While computing the capital of the company as on 1-7-1966 for the purpose of surtax, the ITO reduced the sum proposed to be capitalised from the general reserves, on the ground that since this amount had been earmarked as early as 30-6-1966 for capitalisation, it was not a 'reserve' but was in the nature of a 'provision'. The company was also carrying forward a certain sum standing to the credit of 'reserve for bad and doubtful debts account' since 1955, and it was explained that the debts when becoming bad were debited directly to the profit and loss account, and the said reserve was not being utilised at all. The ITO treated this too as a provision and excluded it from the computation of capital. The Tribunal allowed the assessee's appeal and held that (i) that the amount standing to the credit of the reserves for bad and doubtful debts account was a reserve and not provision and, hence, includible in the capital computation ; and (ii) that the entire amount standing to the credit of the General Reserves as on the first day of the previous year should be included in the capital computation for the purposes of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, without reducing therefrom any sum in respect of the amount capitalised subsequently during the succeeding year for issuing bonus shares.

On reference :

The assessee, a sitting judge of the Delhi High Court, held shares in Punjab National Bank Ltd. The Bank was nationalised in 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and received compensation of Rs. 10.20 crores as against its share capital of Rs. 2 crores. The bank, however, continued business even after nationalisation, and decided to purchase the shares from shareholders, if they so desired, so as the reduce its capital. The assessee exercised this option, and received in 1974 Rs. 6,400 from the Bank for his shares originally costing Rs. 2,910. The reduction in share capital was also approved by the High Court in January 1974. The assessee-company was engaged in owning and operating container freight services, (CFS) at various places and warehousing services. The assessee filed its original return of income declaring total income at Rs.50.37 crores. Subsequently, the assessee filed its revised return of income declaring total income at Rs.49.85 crores. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that a sum of Rs.73.99 crores had been debited to the profit & Loss Account, being 'Exceptional Items' on account of investments, written off, in certain companies.

■

The Assessing Officer noticed that in the calculation of taxable income, such amount of exceptional items had been added back, while calculating income under the regular provisions of the Act. However, such amount was not added back in computation of the tax payable under the provisions of section 115JB. As per clause (i) of Explanation 1 to sub-section 2 of section 115JB, the 'book profit' shall further be increased by the amount or amounts set aside, as provisions for diminution in the value of any asset. However, as stated above, such adjustment to the book profit had not been made, while working it, as per the provisions of section 115JB.

■

As per the facts of the case, such reduction in investment in share tantamount to diminution in the value of assets and accordingly required to be added back, while working the 'Book profit' under the provisions of section 115JB. Accordingly, the 'Book profit' was required to be altered to that extent. The assessee was, therefore, requested to explain, as to why such sum of Rs.7399.28 lakhs, should not be added back while working the 'Book profit' under the provisions of section 115JB.

■

The assessee submitted that 'write off' of Rs.7399.28 lacs, was on account of capital reduction of investment in equity shares and preference shares in the group companies. This capital reduction was carried out under section 100 to 104 of the Companies Act, 1956. The assessee submitted that the capital reduction was duly approved by the Bombay High Court. The assessee submitted that when the balances of the assets at the end of the year are reflected at a reduced value, then amount of such reduction shall be treated as 'actual write off' and not 'provision'.

■

Hence, once the amount of diminution in the value of investments was written off against the asset, there could be no use of any amount having been set-aside for diminution in the value of assets. Based on these facts, the assessee submitted that the fundamental premise of existence of asset to treat the amount under clause (i) of Explanation 1 of Section 115JB(2) was lacking, and hence no addition should be made in the hands of the assessee.

■

However, the Assessing Officer rejected the above contention of assessee and observed that assessee had done these transactions under a larger scheme of planning to avoid taxes. Therefore, Assessing Officer did not accept the plea of the assessee that such reduction in value of investment cannot be added back, while computing the book profit under section 115JB.

■

That is, Assessing Officer held that such reduction in value of investment was a part of clause (i) of Explanation 1 of section 115JB(2), and it should be added while computing the book profit under section 115JB. Accordingly, the book profit, as per the provisions of section 115JB, was worked out by the Assessing Officer to the tune of Rs.7399.28 lakhs and added as per clause (i) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

The Tribunal held that the sum advanced to the shareholders being the deemed dividend should be deducted from the accumulated profits in the hands of the company and that no capital gains accrued to the assessee as there was no extinguishment of any right of the assessee. On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee-firm carried on the business of manufacture and sale of ice and aerated waters and also acted as the managing agents of a company. Under the managing agency agreement, the assessee had been appointed as the managing agents of the company for a period of thirty years, subject to the condition that it would continue to hold the company's shares having value of not less than 1,00,000. The assessee purchased 2,000 shares at Rs. 50 each in February, 1942 and 4,000 more shares at Rs. 50 each in June 1946. This claim of revenue loss was disallowed by the ITO, the AAC and the Appellate Tribunal on the ground that the loss was a loss of capital.

As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

Therefore, the value of shares of the Company ‘A’ received by the assessee was not liable to be included in the assessee’s income.

It is perfectly competent to a joint stock company to convert its surplus profits into capital and give the benefit of such conversion to the shareholders in any manner, either by the issue of new shares as bonus shares or by the issue of debentures, or in cash there was no evidence before the Income-tax authorities that the various transactions, which resulted in the transfer of shares in the company A, to the assessee, were illusory. Act requiring that the distribution in order to fall within the section must entail release of assets of the company. If the second condition had not been introduced, bonus shares issued credited as fully paid up would have been liable to be regarded as "dividend" within section 2(6A)(a) but the legislature obviously did not want to tax such bonus shares as dividend and it, therefore, introduced the second condition in section 2(6A)(a) of the 1922 Act. When accumulated profits are capitalized and redeemable preference shares are issued as bonus shares credited as fully paid-up, the capitalized accumulated profits are converted into preference share capital. The balance-sheet thereafter shows the profit and loss account or reserves at a reduced figure and the issued capital at a correspondingly increased figure, the only effect being that one item on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet becomes replaced in whole or part by another item, namely, preference share capital, while the assets side of the balance-sheet remains unaffected. Now it is a fundamental principle of company law that the capital of a company must be maintained intact, for the company being a mere abstraction of law distinct from its members and the liability of the members being limited, it is the capital of the company which provides a minimum safeguard to third parties dealing with the company and the law, therefore, requires that no part of the capital shall be returned to the shareholders except under certain circumstances and by following a certain procedure requiring the scrutiny of the Court and, it is only if the Court sanctions, that there can be repayment to the shareholders in reduction of the capital. But notwithstanding this fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, redeemable preference shares can be repaid in accordance with the terms of issue otherwise than on a formal reduction of capital approved by the Court. The preference share capital collected from the holders of redeemable preference shares or credited as fully paid up out of capitalised accumulated profits can be returned to the shareholders without going through the procedure of reduction of capital, though such return of preference share capital would amount to reduction of capital. This would appear to constitute a departure from the fundamental principle of maintenance of capital, but if one look at section 105B of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, which was the section which governed redemption at the time when the redeemable preference shares in the present case were redeemed, it is found that the purity of this principle is not only not violated but is, on the contrary, preserved in effect, if not in name, by the stringent provisions contained in the section. Redeemable preference shares, according to these provisions, can be repaid out of profits or out of the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. If they are redeemed out of the proceeds of a fresh issue, the capital raised on that issue will obviously replace the capital redeemed and, consequently, the capital of the company will be maintained at the original yardstick. If on the other hand they are redeemed out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, then out of profits an amount equivalent to the nominal amount of the shares redeemed is required to be transferred to a reserve fund to be called "The capital redemption reserve fund" which is to be treated as equivalent to paid up capital. Hence, although the redeemable preference shares disappear on redemption, the capital which they represent is retained for accounting purposes and there is no reduction of the capital yardstick. This analysis of the mechanics of redemption clearly shows that when redeemable preference shares are redeemed, the preference share capital is returned to the shareholders and since such return of the preference share capital would deplete the capital of the company and consequently affect the sanctity of the principle of maintenance of capital which is regarded as a principle of paramount importance, the law requires that the preference share capital so returned should be replaced by other capital either provided by a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or transferred out of the profits of the company in case redemption is made out of profits or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company. It is undoubtedly true that redemption cannot be made except out of profits of the company or out of proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or out of sale proceeds of any property of the company, but these merely indicate the sources of the moneys which may be utilised for the purpose of returning the preference share capital to the shareholders. The only inhibition is that if a company wants to return the preference share capital to the shareholders the company must do so out of moneys earned by the company as profits or derived by the company from a fresh issue of shares or obtained by the company by selling any property belonging to it and if there are no such moneys, the company cannot return the preference share capital to its shareholders. But what is returned to the shareholders on redemption, what is distributed amongst them, is the preference share capital and not the profits of the company, or proceeds of the fresh issue of shares made for the purpose of redemption or sale proceeds of the property belonging to the company which merely provide the moneys for return of the preference share capital.

It was, thus, clear that so far as computation of capital was concerned, that had been correctly done by the AO by not taking into consideration the proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876.

As regards the new plea, the assessee’s argument, though attractive, was without any substance. The entries made in the books of account of the assessee had their importance and relevance and could not be wished away. As per the entries recorded in the balance sheet, general reserve as per such balance sheet came to Rs. 93,09,997. Out of this amount, a sum of Rs. 30 lakhs was reduced being utilised for issue of bonus shares; thus leaving a balance of Rs. 63,09,997. This was the position in books as on 15-10-1982. A sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was credited to the reserves account much later on 31-12-1982. So, on the face of it, it was not possible to accept the contention of the assessee that the withdrawal of the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs on account of bonus shares should be attributed to the profit earned during the year. The facts were clear that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had been utilised for the issue of bonus shares out of the brought forward balance of Rs. 93,09,997 in the general reserves account. This argument of the assessee, therefore, was not acceptable.

In the result, the conclusions of the Commissioner (Appeals) were upheld, and the assessee’s appeal was dismissed.

The Bombay High Court in the case of CIT v. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1978] 111 ITR 6 after analysing the provisions of the Second Schedule, took the view that with reference to the definition of chargeable profits, section 2(5) and 2(8) refers to statutory deductions and that when a part of the amount standing to the credit of general reserve is, during the course of the previous year, capitalised by issue of fully paid-up free bonus shares, there is no increase by any amount in the capital computed in accordance with the provisions of rules 1 and 2 of the Second Schedule. Following the said decision in the instant case, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the capital should not be increased to the extent of bonus shares issued out of the general reserves.

The assessee created a development rebate fund to avail of the deduction under section 33. Section 34(3)( a) does not prohibit the assessee from using any amount credited to the fund for the purpose of its business but he cannot utilise the amount for eight years for 'distribution by way of dividends or profits'. If the ITO finds that the assessee has utilised any amount out of the reserve fund for distribution by way of dividends or profits, he can withdraw the allowance given under section 33 by proceeding under section 155.

In the instant case, there was no allegation that the assessee had distributed any dividend out of the amounts standing to the credit of the fund. But the assessee issued bonus shares and for that purpose transferred the amount standing to the credit of the fund to the share capital account. One view is that issue of bonus shares to the shareholders involves a dual operation by which an amount is released to the shareholders from a reserve fund but is retained by the company and applied in payment of the bonus shares which are issued as fully paid up. The shareholders are treated as having paid for the bonus shares and the supposed payments by the shareholders are taken to share capital account from the reserve fund of the Company. In effect, the shareholders have not paid the face value of the bonus shares. It is to all intents and purposes equivalent to distribution of accumulated profits in cash by the company.

The second view is that when bonus shares are issued, an amount equal to the face value of the shares cannot be regarded as having been received by the shareholders. The issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of the company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of the reserve but only as part of the capital.

The correct view could be that the profits made by the company may be distributed as dividends or retained by the company as its reserve which may be used for improvement of the company's works, buildings and machinery. That will enable the company to make larger profits. There cannot be any dispute that the shareholders will benefit from the improvements brought about in the profit-making apparatus of the company. Likewise, if the accumulated profits are capitalised and capital base of the company is enlarged, this may enable the company to do its business more profitably. The shareholders will also benefit if the share capital is increased. They may benefit immediately by issue of bonus shares. But neither in the case of improvement in the profit-making apparatus nor in the case of expansion of the share capital of the company, can it be said that the shareholders have received any money from the company. They may have benefited in both the cases. But this benefit cannot be treated as distribution of the amount standing to the credit of any reserve fund of the company to its shareholders.

In fact, the transfer of the amounts standing to the credit of development rebate reserve to the share capital account does not involve any disbursement of money by the company. Nothing comes out of the till of the company to the shareholder. The entire amount of money shown as development rebate reserve is retained by the company in another account. It cannot be said that by the issue of bonus shares, the company has distributed its reserve fund to the shareholders even though it has retained the entire amount with it in the share capital account.

When a shareholder gets a bonus share, the value of the original share held by him goes down. In effect, the shareholder gets two shares instead of the one share held by him and the market value as well as the intrinsic value of the two shares put together will be the same or nearly the same as the value of the original share before the bonus issue.

It appears from the various decisions that issuance of bonus shares does not amount to distribution of accumulated profit of a company. The shareholder derives some benefit by the process of capitalising of the accumulated profits but at the same time, the value of his original shareholding goes down.

Viewed from any angle, it could not be said that in this case the assessee-company had distributed any part of its development rebate reserve fund when it issued the bonus shares. The accumulated profit lying to the credit of the development rebate reserve had been retained by the company. The amount had been transferred to the share capital account. If that was not done, the intrinsic value of the shares held by the shareholders would have been more. After the issue of the bonus shares, the intrinsic value of the original shares had gone down rateably. The accumulated profits of the company had remained with the company in one account or another. In the instant case, neither in form nor in substance, had there been any distribution of profits by the company in making the bonus issue. If the substance and not the form of the transaction was looked to, the issue of bonus shares was in the language of Rowlatt J., 'a bare machinery' for capitalising profits and there was no distribution of profits to the shareholders.

Regarding capital reserve account No. 2, a part of the said reserve had been admitted by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) as forming part of the accumulated profits and, therefore, no grievance whatsoever could be raised in second appeal. Insofar as the remaining portion of the said reserve was concerned, the assessee submitted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had deleted the capital gains tax on said portion following the Tribunal’s order to the same effect in respect of one of the wholly-owned subsidiaries of the assessee in an earlier case. In the circumstances, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly excluded this portion for the purposes of section 2(22)(d).

The current profits had been excluded from the computation of accumulated profits by the Commissioner (Appeals) without discussing the issue. In the 1961 Act definition of ‘dividend’ contained under section 2(22) is materially different from the definition contained under section 2(6A) of the 1922 Act due to the presence of Explanation 2 which enacts that the expression ‘accumulated profits’ in sub-clauses (a), (b), (d ) and (e) shall include all profits of the company upto the date of distribution or payment. Therefore current profits had been rightly included by the Assessing Officer.

Regarding the provision for taxation included in debit balance of P&L account and existing tax liability raised by the IT authorities but disputed by the assessee and not provided in the books, the accumulated profits are to be construed as commercial profits for the purposes of section 2(22). Since tax liabilities had been created by the I.T. authorities and assessment orders as well as demand notices in support of the said liabilities had been produced during the assessment proceedings, such liabilities were to be taken note of, even if not provided in the books for ascertaining the accumulated profits. In the absence of specific reserves for taxation created by the company those liabilities might have to be met from the general reserves. In such circumstances to take the figure of general reserve from the balance sheet for ascertaining the accumulated profits would not be a correct procedure for the quantum of the general reserves would not represent the accumulated profits. Having regard to the aforesaid reasons, deduction was liable to be made for ascertaining accumulated profits.

However, the accumulated profit worked out in this way being a negative figure, it could not be said that the company possessed accumulated profits and, hence, provisions of section 2(22) were not applicable.

As regards the issue of levy of capital gains, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held against levy of capital gains without discussing facts and issues involved and without indicating reasons in support of his finding in the impugned order.

The basic issue for the purposes of levy of capital gains is whether reduction of share capital by a company results in extinguishment of rights in shares held by shareholders covered by the expression ‘transfer’ as defined in section 2(47). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of the capital thereby reducing the face value of the shares, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividend of his share capital and the right to share is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in capital. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to consider the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45 as a result of reduction of share capital since he came to the conclusion that accumulated profits possessed by the company exceeded the distribution made to the shareholders on reduction of share capital. While reversing the conclusion of the Assessing Officer and deleting the addition on account of dividend under section 2(22)(a) the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply his mind to the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45, particularly since the distribution made by the company on reduction of share capital had been treated as transfer by the Supreme Court in the various decisions. In the circumstances the issue of levy of capital gains was set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with the direction that the issue of levy of capital gains might be re-examined by him.

It is evident as stated under condition (c ) of Rule 2 that the capital computed in accordance with rule 1 and nothing short of it was to be increased. The revenue authorities intended to reduce the reserve to the extent of the amount of bonus share which according to them was the amount added to paid-up share capital. They could not do so under the plain language used in rule 2. It is the "capital computed in accordance with rule 1" which is to be increased and nothing less than that. The capital would necessarily mean the sum total of the paid-up capital as well as the reserve. To this figure shall be added the proportionate increase in the paid-up share capital. From this enhanced capital, ‘standard deduction’ has to be made which is equal to six per cent of the total capital of the company.

The language used in rule 2 is explicit and the capital computed in accordance with rule 1 has to be increased by the proportionate increase in the paid-up share capital. This capital necessarily includes the reserve as it stood on the first day of the previous year. In other words the reserve could not be reduced to the extent of its capitalisation and if the reserve was computed as it was on the fist day of the previous year, the proportionate increase had to be made in the share capital leading to a benefit which according to the revenue authorities is under and which they preferred to submit as ‘double benefit’. The capitalised part of reserve was to be added to the share capital, while reserve was not to be reduced to that extent. By increasing the base capital the percentage of standard deduction was enhanced. This gave relief to the taxpayer. It was, therefore, held that the expression ‘paid-up capital’ occurring in the Act does include therein even such reserve as has been capitalised without corresponding decrease in the reserve as computed with reference to the first day of the previous year.

The creation of the reserve contemplated by section 34(3)(a) is a condition precedent for obtaining the allowance of development rebate. The grant of allowance is made subject to the condition that the amount shall not be utilised by the assessee for distribution by way of dividends or profits. Where, therefore, conditions are expressly imposed to entitle an assessee to an allowance, the conditions cannot be ignored on any theory of beneficial construction. Where the assessee fails to satisfy the conditions requisite for obtaining the allowance, it will not be for the Court or Tribunal to state that in substance the action of the assessee should be looked into although technically the action falls within the embargo. The conditions, in other words, should be strictly construed because development rebate is a special concession or relief granted by the Act which cannot be availed of unless the statutory condition attached to it is satisfied. That means, the reserve shall not be used for distribution by way of dividends or profits. There are only two ways by which profit could be distributed by a company -one by way of distribution of dividends to the shareholders and another by way of issue of bonus shares. The latter category certainly is not distribution of dividend but nonetheless it is also distribution of profit. By the distribution of bonus shares, capital is created and reserve is depleted. When capital is created by issuing the bonus shares, the shareholders are enriched. Shareholders could be enriched by issue of dividends or by issue of bonus shares. Changing the terminology of profits into shares cannot, therefore, take the distribution out of the embargo imposed by section 34(3)(a)(i). It may not, therefore, be correct to state that by issue of bonus shares the company has utilised the profits for the purpose of business. Issue of bonus shares, is, therefore, nothing but distribution of profits and clearly violates the statutory requirement of section 34(3)(a)(i). Therefore, the Tribunal was not justified in its view.

When a company is prosperous and accumulates a large surplus, it converts that surplus into capital and divides the capital amongst the members in proportion to their rights. That is done by issuing fully paid-up shares representing the increased capital. The shareholders to whom the shares are allotted have to pay nothing. The purpose is to capitalize profits which may be available for division. Bonus shares go by the modern name of 'capitalization shares'. If the Articles of a company empower the company, it can capitalise profits or reserves and issue fully paid-up shares of nominal value, equal to the amount capitalized, to its shareholders. The idea behind the issue of bonus shares is to bring the nominal share capital into line with the excess of assets over liabilities. A company would like to have more working capital but it need not go into the market for obtaining fresh capital by issuing fresh shares. The necessary money is available with it and that money is converted into shares which really means that the undistributed profits have been ploughed back into the business and converted into share capital. Therefore, fully paid-up bonus shares are merely a distribution of capitalized undivided profit. It would be a misnomer to call the recipients of bonus shares as donees of shares from the company. [Para 13]

In using the expression ‘actual cost to the assessee’, the legislature wanted to indicate the sum of money or money’s worth which it cost the assessee to acquire the asset. In special cases however the legislature indicated that the ‘actual cost to the assessee’ might be determined at some other figure. The word ‘actual’ means existing in act or fact, really acted or acting, carried out, real as opposed to potential, possible, virtual, theoretical, ideal, etc." Again it may mean ‘in action of existence at the time, present, current’. ‘Actual cost’ means ‘real cost’ – the cost which the assessee incurred in act or fact. Under section 211 of the Indian Companies Act, balance-sheet of the company has to be prepared in the form prescribed in Schedule VI. The heads of reserve there shown are: ‘(1) capital reserves, (2) capital redemption reserve, (3) share premium account, (4) other reserves specifying the nature of each reserve and the amount in respect thereof, (5) surplus, i.e., balance in profit and loss account after providing for proposed allocations, namely, dividend, bonus or reserves, (6) proposed additions to reserves, and (7) sinking funds.’ Depreciation does not find a place there but in Part III clause 7(1)(b) the expression ‘reserve’ shall not, subject as aforesaid, include any amount written off or retained by way of providing for depreciation, renewals or diminution in value of assets or retained by way of providing for any known liability. It would thus, appear that a provision for depreciation was not to be included in any reserves.

If the company is not obliged to show depreciation in its balance-sheet by way of reserves and indeed ought not to do so under the form prescribed by section 211, depreciation cannot be considered in the context of reserves.

In this view of matter, the proviso (b ) to section 23A(1) of the 1922 Act was not applicable to the assessee for the relevant assessment year on the facts of the case and the company was entitled to the rebate on the undistributed balance of the profits as provided in clause (i) of the proviso to item (b) of Part I of the Schedule to the Finance Act of 1955. The objection to the rebate was based only on the ground of applicability of section 23A. That being out of the way, the assessee was rightly held entitled to the rebate.

Now admittedly there was release of assets of the company on redemption since moneys were actually paid out of the coffers of the company and received by the shareholders. A company must state in its memorandum of association the amount of capital with which the company desires to do business and the number of shares into which that capital is to be divided. The company need not issue all its capital at one time. It may issue only a part of its capital initially and issue the rest of the unissued capital or a part of it at a later date. Now if a company prospers and earns profits it may do one of two things with the profits. It may either distribute the profits by way of dividend among the shareholders or accumulate them. Generally, when a company accumulates profits it carries them to various reserves which appear on the liabilities side of the balance-sheet. Ordinarily, these undistributed profits are employed in the business either in acquisition of fixed assets or as working capital and really represent an increase in the capital employed in the business. When these increase to a considerable extent, the issued capital of the company ceases to bear a true relation to the real capital employed in the business. The company may, in such a case, decide to bring its issued capital into a truer relationship with the capital actually employed in the business or, to use the words of Gower, "more into line with the true excess of assets over liabilities" and may for that purpose capitalise its accumulated profits and issue fully paid up bonus shares of a nominal value equal to the amount capitalised to its shareholders. These bonus shares may be either ordinary or preference shares on the one hand or redeemable preference shares on the other. The company may also instead of issuing bonus shares issue bonus debentures by capitalising its accumulated profits. In all these cases the accumulated profits which are capitalised remain in the coffers of the company and no part of them actually goes into the pockets of the shareholders : the only change that takes place is that the accumulated profits which prior to capitalisation were employed in the business as accumulated profits are thenceforth employed as part of the issued or loan capital of the company according as the issue is of bonus shares or bonus debentures. The accumulated profits which might have been divided among the shareholders as dividend are impounded to increase the capital of the company and what the shareholders get is not any payment out of the accumulated profits but bonus shares or bonus debentures credited as fully paid up. The transaction, to use the words of Viscount Cave in Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. John Blott [1921] 8 Tax Cas. 101, 135, takes "nothing out of the company’s coffers and "puts" nothing into the shareholders’ pockets" but what happens is that the accumulated profits which are capitalized are applied in paying up the amounts due on bonus shares or debentures to be issued to the shareholders as fully paid up bonus shares or debentures. This analysis of the mechanism of issue of bonus shares or debentures is, apart from the abundance of authority to support it, clearly based on sound principle. It is clear law that when shares are issued and allotted by a company the liability for the amount due on the shares is always on the allottee and that liability must be satisfied from some source external to the company in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or money’s worth. The allottee may pay the amount due on the shares in money or if the allottee has to his credit any amount due by the company, such credit may, with his consent, be applied in discharge of the allottee's liabilities on the shares. Now admittedly no moneys are paid by the shareholders for the bonus shares issued to them and it must, therefore, follow that when bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up, the liability for payment in full on allotment which the shareholders would otherwise have had to discharge is paid by the company by applying the accumulated profits to the discharge of such liability for the benefit of the shareholders. There is of course no payment of the accumulated profits to the shareholders since no part of the accumulated profits is liberated to them: the company does not part with any of the accumulated profits nor do the shareholders receive any part of them. But the accumulated profits are applied in paying up the capital sums which the shareholders would otherwise have had to contribute for the purpose of new shares. The shareholders receiving bonus shares credited as fully paid up are given credit for the capital sums which they would otherwise have had to contribute in respect of the bonus shares allotted to them if those shares had not been issued credited as fully paid up and this credit is given by application of the capitalised accumulated profits in payment of such capital sums. As observed by Hidayatullah J. in CIT v. Dalmia Investment Co. Ltd [1964] 52 ITR 567 (SC), after the accumulated profits are converted into capital and bonus shares are issued credited as fully paid up "the company employs that money not as reserves of profits, but as its proper capital issued to and contributed by the shareholder"

The transaction of issue of bonus shares cannot be equated with the transaction of issue of additional capital by the company. The question, then is as To whether the payment made for raising authorised capital necessitated as a consequence decision to issue bonus shares brings in any benefit of permanent nature thereby forfeiting the claim for allowability under section 37(1) . This would require brief discussion on aspects of powers of directors and shareholders and importance of interplay of reserves in corporate finance. The directors have got unfettered power to decide regarding distribution of dividends either in cash or in specie or assets or reserve or even non-distribution of same. Without taking the decision of capitalising reserves they can perennially continue to carry on without in any way affecting interplay of finances at their disposal. Their decision to transfer, by way of accounting entry, part of reserves to issued capital, also does not affect the existing interplay of finances at their disposal because the decision of issue of bonus shares by way of capitalising reserves is only an accounting entry in substance and form both. While considering vis-à-vis fresh issue of capital the decision of issuing the bonus shares should, therefore, be considered as a prudent decision based on financial wisdom and commercial expediency. Thus, if for the purpose of issue of bonus shares the company has to raise the limit of authorised capital, it is only incidental to carrying on of business. It neither adds to the profit earning process nor adds to the Profit-earning apparatus and, hence, cannot be considered capital. The main reason being there is no augmentation of finance.

Accordingly, it was to be held in the present case, that aforesaid expenditure Incurred for the issue of bonus share was an allowable expenditure and the Commissioner (Appeals ) was. not justified in rejecting the assessee’s claim.

Section 205A applies to unpaid dividend to be transferred to special dividend account and thereafter, if a dividend has been declared by the company, but has not been paid or claimed within thirty days from the date of such declaration, the company shall within seven days from the date of expiry of the said period of thirty days transfer the total amount of dividend which remains unpaid or unclaimed within thirty days to the special account opened by the company in that behalf in a scheduled bank to be called ‘unpaid dividend of the company’. In the instant case, the amount which was sought to be converted into bonus debenture was not an amount which was declared as a dividend and unpaid to the shareholders. Therefore, the said objection had no substance and section 205A was not attracted to the facts of the instant case. [Para 8]

The last objection raised was that the issuance of bonus debentures out of the free reserves of the company was against the provisions of section 77, as subscription to securities issued by the company was funded from company’s sources. Section 77 prescribes restrictions on purchase by company, or loans by company for purchase of its own or its holding company’s shares. Section 77A deals with the power of the company to purchase its own securities. Therefore, per se the aforesaid sections had no application, but the grievance of the Regional Director appeared to be that the bonus debentures that were issued out of the reserves of the company were not permitted in law. [Para 9]

Section 2(12) defines ‘what a debenture is?’ . Debenture includes debenture stock, bonds and any other securities of a company, whether constituting a charge on the assets of the company or not. Section 82 provides for nature of shares and debentures. In the entire scheme of the Act, there is no reference to a bonus debenture. [Para 10]

When a company prospers and earns profits, it may do one of the two things with the profits; it may either distribute the profits by way of dividend among the shareholders or accumulate them. Ordinarily, these undistributed profits are employed in the business either in acquisition of fixed assets or as working capital and really represent an increase in the capital employed in the business. When these increase to a considerable extent, the issued capital of the company ceases to bear a true relation to the real capital employed in the business. The company may, in such a case, decide to bring its issued capital into a true relationship with the capital actually employed in the business and may for that purpose capitalise its accumulated profits and issue fully paid-up shares or debentures, of a nominal value equal to the amount capitalised to its shareholders. These new shares or debentures are called as bonus shares or bonus debentures. They are not a gift from the company. They are not issued gratuitously. Their nominal value is paid in full from the capitalized profits or reserves of the company, which could otherwise have been distributed to the shareholders. [Para 14]

The Division Bench of the Bombay High Court held that for the purpose of calculating profits within the meaning of the phrase "accumulated profits" under section 2(6A)(e), an allowance of depreciation should be made by way of a deduction at the rates provided for by the Income-tax Act itself.
