The statutory requirement

2. Upon close reading of sub-section (2) of section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 it requires every company assessee to draw its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI of the Companies Act. The proviso to such sub-section (2) further requires that the accounting policies, the accounting standards and method and rates of depreciation adopted in the preparation of profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB must be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts as laid down before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act. Sub-section (2) reads as under :

"(2) Every assessee, being a company, shall, for the purposes of this section, prepare its profit and loss account for the relevant previous year in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided that while preparing the annual accounts including profit and loss account,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts including profit and loss account and laid before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with the provisions of section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided further that where the company has adopted or adopts the financial year under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), which is different from the previous year under this Act,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall correspond to the accounting policies, accounting standards and the method and rates for calculating the depreciation which have been adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account for such financial year or part of such financial year falling within the relevant previous year."

In other words nothing prevents a company to draw a separate profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB subject, however, to the fact that the accounting policy, accounting standards and the depreciation formula adopted is identical to the accounts prepared for AGM show. This is more so when the accounting period adopted by a company for the purposes of the Companies Act, is other than the financial year.

Requirements under accounting standards

3. Upon close reading of the accounting standards it can be found that the accounting treatment to certain items is made flexible. In other words companies have a choice to provide accounting entry in the manner found suitable to the subject.

The Pooling of Interests Method

4. Let us take an example of a company who has acquired the business of another company under an amalgamation scheme approved by the Court. Accounting Standard 14 has application in such cases. Under the Pooling of Interests Method the amalgamated company is required to disclose the assets and liabilities of the transferor company at their book values. Para 16/35 of AS-14 further requires the transferee-company to adjust the difference in the book value and the purchase consideration against the reserves. Para 35 reads as under :

"35. The difference between the amount recorded as share capital issued (plus any additional consideration in the form of cash or other assets) and the amount of share capital of the transferor-company should be adjusted in reserves."

Now the term ‘reserves’ have been further defined elsewhere in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI as including both capital and revenue reserves. Thus, para 35 provides a flexibility in the matter of adjustment of additional price paid either against capital reserves or general reserves including profit and loss account surplus.

In the subsequent years, it shall be regarded as revaluation of assets.

Further Discussion on Net Worth Having adopted Ind AS, another pertinent question will be, whether gains/losses sitting in the "Other Comprehensive Income" will be regarded as a part of net worth. Here it may be noted that Ind AS 109 allows reporting entities allow some of the financial instruments to be fair valued through Other Comprehensive Income (OCI). Any changes in the fair value of these instruments are effected through OCI, which is carried to the Balance Sheet as Other Equity.

It may be noted that the definition of net worth allows inclusion of only such profits which flow from the Profit and Loss. Unrealized OCI do not form part of the profits/ losses earned/ incurred by the reporting entity in a particular as the OCI are shown separately in the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss. As per the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss, after the Profit earned by a reporting entity is arrived at, the same is added with the OCI during the year to show the Total Comprehensive Income of the reporting entity.

Therefore, just because the OCI is shown in the Statement of Profit and Loss does not mean that the same must be considered as Profits earned by the reporting entity. Hence, for the purpose of computation of net worth, OCI cannot be considered as a part of the net worth.

However, as per Ind AS 109, once the unrealized profits trapped in the form of OCI gets realized due to sale of financial asset or otherwise, it gets transferred from Equity to Profit and Loss. In such a situation, the same must be considered as a part of net worth.

Should the retained earnings be Considered Free Reserve?

Section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 defines Free Reserves:

"2(43) ?free reserves means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend: Provided that—

(i)

any amount representing unrealized gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise, or

(ii)

any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability recognized in equity, including surplus in profit and loss account on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value, shall not be treated as free reserves."

The definition of Free Reserves says that the reserves should be available for dividend distribution as per latest audited balance sheet. It specifically excludes notional or unrealized gains and gains on revaluation of assets. It also states that change in carrying amount of asset or liability recognized in equity and surplus in profit and loss account due to restatement of asset or liability at fair value shall not be included in free reserves.

The definition does not include the unrealized part of the gains. It also excludes the surplus arising on restatement of asset or liability fair value restatement. Hence, the retained earnings which is adjusted for any differences in fair value measurement of assets and liabilities during first time Ind AS adoption cannot be considered as free as these are not realized in nature. The definition of net worth does not distinguish between realized and unrealized gains but the definition of Free Reserves does. Hence although it is a part of Net Worth as explained above, it cannot be a part of free reserves as it excludes unrealized and notional gains.

Hence the amount transferred to Retained Earnings as adjustments during transition of Financial Statements from GAAP to IND AS cannot be considered as Free Reserves.

Introduction:

Reduction of share capital is a process by which a company decreases it's issued, subscribed, or paid-up share capital. This can be undertaken for various purposes, including restructuring, correcting an overcapitalized balance sheet, or returning excess funds to shareholders. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the reduction of share capital requires the approval of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as per the provisions of the mentioned in the Act.

Legal Framework:

The reduction of share capital is governed by Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with The National Company Law Tribunal (Procedure for reduction of share capital of Company) Rules, 2016 which lays down the procedures, requirements, and conditions for reducing share capital.

Reasons for Reduction of Share Capital:

Reduction of share capital can be carried out for various reasons, including but not limited to:

1. Return of Excess Paid-up Capital:

When the company has surplus paid-up capital that is not being utilized, it can be returned to shareholders. This is beneficial as dividends are paid on paid-up capital, and retaining unnecessary capital increases the company's financial burden.

2. Cancellation of Uncalled Share Capital:

Share capital that has been issued but not called for payment can be cancelled to streamline the company's capital structure and reflect actual capital requirements. For example, partly paid shares can be made fully paid without calling for balance call money and accordingly reducing the face value of shares.

3. Cancellation of Unpaid Share Capital:

The unpaid portion of the share capital that shareholders are yet to pay can be cancelled to reduce liabilities and simplify financial accounts.

4. Adjustment for Capital Lost or Diminished:

When the company's assets lose value (reflected as a reduction in book value), the company can adjust its share capital by returning the reduced amount to shareholders. This aligns the share capital with the actual value of the company's assets.

Procedure for Reduction of Share Capital:

Board Meeting & Special Resolution

Board Approval: The Company's Board of Directors must approve the proposal to reduce share capital.

Special Resolution: A special resolution (approved by at least 75% of shareholders) must be passed at a general meeting to approve the reduction. The resolution should specify the method and extent of the reduction.

Filing of Application for Reduction of Share Capital with NCLT:

Form and Fee:

An application to the Tribunal for confirming a reduction of share capital must be made in Form RSC-1, along with the applicable fee as prescribed in the fee schedule i.e., Rs. 5000/-

Accompanying Documents:

The application should be accompanied by the following documents:

Special resolution copy.

Memorandum of association and articles of association.

List of Creditors: A list, certified by the Managing Director (or two directors), showing creditor details (name, address, amounts owed), dated no more than 15 days before filing.

Auditor's Certificate on Creditor List: A certificate from the company's auditor verifying the accuracy of the creditor list.

No Arrears Declaration: A certificate from the auditor and a director's declaration confirming that the company has no pending deposits or interest arrears.

Accounting Treatment Compliance: A certificate from the auditor confirming that the proposed accounting treatment for share capital reduction complies with Section 133 of the Companies Act or relevant provisions.

Issuance of Notices and Directions by NCLT for Reduction of Share Capital:

Notice by Tribunal:

Within 15 days of receiving the application (Form RSC-1), the Tribunal will issue notices or direct that notice to be given in:

Form RSC-2: To the Central Government and Registrar of Companies (RoC) in all cases.

Form RSC-2: To SEBI, if the company is listed.

And Direct the Company to send Notices to each creditor (as per the submitted list) must be within 7 days of the Tribunal's direction in form Form RSC-3. The notice will include:

Details of the proposed reduction of share capital including an amount.

The amount owed to the creditor or contingent claim, if any.

A deadline for sending objections.

Public Notice:

The Tribunal will direct the company to publish a notice in Form RSC-4 within 7 days from the directions given by the tribunal in:

A widely circulated English newspaper.

A widely circulated vernacular newspaper in the state of the registered office.

The company's website (if applicable).

The notice will invite creditor objections and provide hearing details.

The notice must mention:

The amount of share capital reduction.

Locations where the creditor list can be inspected.

The deadline (fixed by the Tribunal) for submitting objections.

In all these cases involving substantial expenditure on replacement of parts of machinery like revamping of an old textile unit for improvement of business operations, which capitalised in books in some cases, it was held that the expenditure is allowable as deduction by way of current repairs. The items of equipment replaced under a modernisation scheme are of two types, the first category being of cases where the replacements do not result in adding to the existing production capacity but only result in increasing the efficiency and improving the profit-earning capacity, either by way of savings in fuel cost or improving the yield of the product, etc., and the other category being of cases where the replacements result in increase in capacity as well as efficiency. The cost of both these categories of items can be capitalised in the accounts in accordance with AS 10, while for tax purposes the expenditure on the former is allowed as deduction as current repair. It may be noted that according to the legal authorities, except in the case of a claim for deduction under section 37, in order to claim any expenditure as deduction under any of the sections 30 to 36 of the Act, it is not necessary that such expenditure should be of revenue nature, as there is no prohibition for allowing as deduction even capital expenditure, if it falls under any of the categories provided in those sections, as in the case under section 37. Examples are provided by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of India Cements Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 60 ITR 52 and decisions of several High Courts (interest on borrowings utilised for acquisition of an asset not put to use or for setting up a new project not commissioned). There are similar decisions in the case of current repairs - Hanuman Motor Service v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 88 , 91 (Mys.) and Nathmal Banketlal Parikh & Co. v. CIT [1980] 122 ITR 168 (AP)(FB). In the case of Madras Cements v. CIT [1990] 42 TTJ 175 , the Madras Bench of the Tribunal has held that the cost of replacement of an entire Cement Mill, out of several existing mills, is an allowable deduction as current repair. These two measures if utilised properly would go a long way in not only reducing taxable income to nil but also in providing a hedge against future tax liability, as in such cases there would be substantial loss for tax purposes in spite of there being substantial income in accounts.

Accounting for Government Grants - AS 12

11. As per this standard, Government grants should be recognised prudently, considering receipt and fulfilment of conditions attached thereto, and they can be treated either as capital reserve or reduced from cost of assets or can be treated as deferred revenue, depending on facts of each case and choice of method. Under the Act, their treatment is similar again, varying with facts of each case. Needless to mention that the treatment given in books is of no consequence in this regard. The long-pending issue regarding investment subsidy has been finally settled by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. P.J. Chemicals Ltd. [1994] 210 ITR 830, holding that it need not be reduced from cost. Subsidy, when given as an incentive to encourage growth of industry, has been considered capital - Sadichha Chitra v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 774 (Bom.), CIT v. Dusad Industries [1986] 162 ITR 784 (MP) which was followed by the same High Court in CIT v. Plastichem [1988] 174 ITR 546 (MP), Godia Wires v. CIT [1989] 178 ITR 596 (MP) and CIT v. R.C.C. Hume-Pipe & Products [1991] 188 ITR 187 (MP). A far reaching decision in this respect is found in Tamil Nadu Sugar Corpn. Ltd. v. ITO [1994] 48 ITD 345 (Mad.) where it was held that the rebate of excise duty granted under an incentive scheme for establishing new sugar factories is a capital receipt not liable to tax. When subsidy is related to profitable conduct of business, it was held to be revenue in Merinoply & Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 209 ITR 508 (Cal.).

Conclusion:

Benefits of Share Capital Reduction:

Reduction of share capital offers significant benefits to companies, such as improving financial ratios, returning surplus funds to shareholders, and aligning the company's capital base with its actual requirements. It can also help increase shareholder value by improving earnings per share (EPS).

Tribunal's Oversight and Protection of Interests:

The involvement of NCLT ensures that the process is conducted transparently and legally. The Tribunal balances the interests of both shareholders and creditors, making sure that creditors' rights are protected before confirming the reduction of share capital.

Strategic Financial Tool:

Reduction of share capital, when carried out properly, serves as an effective tool for a company to restructure its finances, improve its financial health, and return value to shareholders. It is a carefully regulated process that allows companies to maintain optimal capital structure while ensuring legal compliance and fairness.

Future Outlook:

With growing awareness and increasing financial flexibility, more companies may consider share capital reduction as a strategy for improving their capital structure. As the regulatory environment evolves, the NCLT will continue to play a crucial role in facilitating and supervising these financial adjustments.

In this article, the author discusses the purpose and method of revaluation of certain fixed assets by various companies and the accounting practices followed in this regard Since the depreciation charge goes up on upward revaluation of the concerned assets, certain companies take a transfer from revaluation reserve to offset the increase in the depreciation charge and thereby inflate their profits. The author is critical of this practice. The main thrust of the article, however, pertains to the question of making a bonus issue out of revaluation reserve which is barred by the existing SEBI guidelines. The author sees no harm in allowing a bonus issue of shares to be made out of the revaluation reserve, as the profit on revaluation is real profit and not fictitious. The lifting of the ban will, obviously, also promote entrepreneurial freedom in decision-making - EDITOR

Purpose of revaluation

1. Accounting data are mostly generated using the historical cost valuation base. In an inflationary environment it is highly likely that the carrying amount of some fixed assets does not reflect their current costs. It is possible that some fixed value of assets has impaired and their current costs fall below the written historical costs. It is also possible that current costs of some fixed assets are much more than the written down historical costs. In both the situations net asset value of equity is not correctly reflected. Therefore, periodic revaluation of fixed assets is considered necessary to reflect the current value of fixed assets.

Presenting fixed assets at historical cost in an inflationary environment is a somewhat obscure practice. The historical cost balance sheet fails to reflect a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the reporting entity. Periodic revaluation of fixed assets to reflect their current value is not prohibited in the company law. In this article, we shall discuss only the issue of upward revaluation of fixed assets and treatment of revaluation profit.

Process of revaluation

2.1 Adjustment of increase in value - Revaluation is commonly done through an appraisal by competent valuers. Sometimes revaluation may be done by using the price index appropriate to the concerned fixed assets. Para 13.3 of Accounting Standard-10 (AS-10) states that the revalued amount of fixed assets is presented in the financial statements by restating the gross book value and accumulated depreciation. It is also recorded by estating the net book value adding therein the net increase on account of revaluation.

However, Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 requires that where sums have been added by writing up the assets, every balance sheet subsequent to such writing up shall show the increased figures with the date of the increase in place of the original cost. Each balance sheet for the first five years subsequent to the date of writing up shall also show the amount of increase made. For every fixed asset it is required to show (i) the original cost, (ii) additions thereto and deductions therefrom during the year, and (iii) depreciation written off or provided for up to the end of the year. Accordingly, as per company law additions to original cost by revaluation should be disclosed. It is not possible to adjust the increase in value with the net book value.

2.2 Selective revaluation - It is not judicious to revalue fixed assets selectively. This process may result in misleading valuation. It is then possible to revalue such assets wherein writing up results, ignoring such other assets where writing down becomes necessary.

Para 27 of AS-10 requires that when a fixed asset is revalued in financial statements, an entire class of assets should be revalued, or the selection of assets for revaluation should be made on a systematic basis.

2.3 Revaluation above the net recoverable amount -The net recoverable amount of a fixed asset indicates the maximum amount which can be fetched by disposal of that particular asset. As a prudential accounting policy it is suggested that upward revaluation should be restricted to the net recoverable amount.

Para 28 of AS-10 requires that the revaluation in financial statements of a class of assets should not result in the net book value of that class being greater than the recoverable amount of that class.

A comparison of revalued figure with the recoverable amount with reference to a class of fixed assets may result in excess revaluation profit (for a valuation above recoverable amount) against an individual asset falling within a class. This possibility should be avoided by requiring comparison of the revalued figure with the recoverable amount for each individually identifiable item of assets separately.

2.4 Revaluation profit - In case of upward revaluation of fixed assets, revaluation profit arises. Accumulated depreciation existing at the date of revaluation cannot be adjusted with such revaluation profit (Para 29). In Part I of Schedule VI it is required that the total depreciation written off should be shown.

The Revised Schedule VI has no Part III as it omits Parts III (definitions of 'reserve', 'provision', 'revenue reserve' and 'capital reserve') and Part IV ('Balance Sheet Abstract of Company's General Business Profile'). Therefore, section 115JB(2) required amendment by omission to 'Part III' of Schedule VI to bring it line with Revised Schedule VI. Further, proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act,1956 permits certain companies, e.g. insurance, banking or electricity company to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions specified in their regulatory Acts. Also, Courts and ITAT have held in a catena of decisions that since profit and loss account for MAT purposes is required by section 115JB(2) to be prepared as per Schedule VI, banks, electricity companies etc. which are exempt from Schedule VI are not liable to MAT. For instance, in Krung Thai Bank PCL v. Jt. DIT (International Taxation) [2011] 16 taxmann.com 239 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that the provisions of section 115JB can only come into play when the assessee is required to prepare its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act. The starting point of computation of MAT under section 115JB is the result shown by such a profit and loss account. In the case of banking companies, however, the provisions of Schedule VI are not applicable in view of exemption set out under proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act. The final accounts of the banking companies are required to be prepared in accordance with the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The provisions of section 115JB cannot thus be applied to the case of a banking company. In Kerala State Electricity Board v. Dy. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 118/[2011] 196 Taxman 1 (Ker.), the Kerala High Court held that section 115JB stipulates that the accounting policies, accounting standards, etc., shall be uniform, both for the purpose of income-tax as well as for the information statutorily required to be placed before the annual general meeting conducted, in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956. However, the assessee though was by definition a company under the Income-tax Act and deemed to be a company for the purpose of the Income-tax Act, by virtue of the declaration under section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act, it was not a company for the purpose of the Companies Act. Therefore, it was not obliged either to convene an annual general meeting or place its profit and loss account in such general meeting. As a matter of fact, a general meeting contemplated under section 166 of the Companies Act, 1956 was not possible in the case of the assessee, as there were no shareholders for the assessee-board. On the other hand, under section 69 of the Electricity Supply Act, the assessee was obliged to keep proper accounts, including the profit and loss account, and to prepare an annual statement of accounts, balance sheet, etc., in such form as had been prescribed by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Thus, it could be seen that coming to the maintenance of the accounts, the assessee, though was deemed to be a 'company' - both by virtue of operation of section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act for the purpose of Income-tax Act and by virtue of the definition of the expression 'company' under the Income-tax Act, yet it was required to keep and maintain its accounts in a manner specified by the Central Government, but not in the manner specified in the Companies Act. Therefore, MAT would not apply to electricity companies.

So, to bring section 115JB(2) in line with Companies Act,1956 and to overcome judicial pronouncements as above, the Finance Act, 2012 has substituted section 115JB(2) with effect from A.Y. 2013-14. Section 115JB(2) as substituted provides that companies which are not required under the proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the Schedule VI of the Companies Act, 1956, profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of their regulatory Acts shall be taken as a basis for computing the book profit under section 115JB and also omits reference to Part III of Schedule VI. It is submitted that since Revised Schedule VI is applicable from 1-4-2011, the amendment dropping reference to Part III of Schedule VI needs to be given retrospective effect from 1-4-2012(A.Y.2012-13). Therefore, such interest cost would not be tax deductible under MAT. The FAQ, however, does not explicitly deal with the treatment from the holders' perspective. By analogy, the interest income should also be excluded from computation of book profit for MAT.

The FAQ also does not deal with the equity component that arises on initial recognition of the redeemable preference shares that is either bearing dividend rate below-market interest or bearing discretionary dividend (and considered as compound instrument). Many Indian companies fund their group companies through preference shares. In this short article, the author examines the question as to whether deferred tax liability is covered as a permissible adjustment while determining book profits under section 115JB of the Income-tax Act. Analyzing the relevant provisions, as well as the relevant Accounting Standards and judicial views, the author concludes that deferred tax liability is ‘Outside the list of adjustments’ to be made in terms of the Explanation to section 115JB, while determining book profits - EDITOR

Introduction

1. In the determination of book profits under section 115JB, the starting figure is the net profit after tax as per profit and loss account. Such a profit is arrived at after providing for both current year tax and deferred tax liability. The current tax provision requires an adjustment though but whether deferred tax too needs to be added back for the purpose of computation of book profits is a point in issue.

The Supreme Court decision

2. In a recent decision dated 3-5-2002 in the case of Apollo Tyres Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 255 ITR 273/ 122 Taxman 562 , the Supreme Court held that the Assessing Officer has the limited power of making increases and reductions to such net profit as provided for in the Explanation to section 115J. Thus, the Assessing Officer does not have the jurisdiction to go behind the net profits shown in the profit and loss account except to the extent provided in the Explanation.

The permitted adjustments

3. Such Explanation provides for adjustment of the following sums if debited to the profit and loss account :—

(a)The amount of income-tax paid or payable, and the provision therefor; or

(b)The amounts carried to any reserves, by whatever name called other than a reserve specified under section 33AC; or

(c)The amount or amounts set aside to provisions made for meeting liabilities, other than ascertained liabilities; or

(d)The amount by way of provision for losses of subsidiary companies; or

(e)The amount or amounts of dividends paid or proposed; or

(f)The amount or amounts of expenditure relatable to any income to which section 10 or section 10A or section 10B or section 11 or section 12 apply.

Position qua deferred tax liability

4. Clause (a) above essentially refers to current tax liability. Clause (43) of section 2 also defines ‘tax’ meaning income-tax chargeable under the provisions of the Act. Even AS-22 defines such current tax as ‘the amount of income-tax determined to be payable in respect of taxable income for a period’ akin to the language used in such clause (a). Further, such clause has remained in its original form all through in the history of taxation on book profits since 1987. The statutory requirement for provision of deferred tax liability has however come into effect from 1-4-2001 and this certainly cannot assume the same treatment as applicable in the case of current tax or as part of income-tax payable under the Act as provided for in clause (a).

Position qua Accounting Standards (AS)

5. Further, AS-22 read such debit as a charge to the profit and loss account and not by way of amounts withdrawn for reserves requiring any adjustment as per clause (b) above. Also, AS-22 clearly mean that such liability is ascertainable and for this purpose also provide for the manner of determination of tax effect of timing difference (deferred tax), hence, such sum falls outside the purview of adjustment referred to in clause (c) as per supra. The remaining three clauses (d), ( e) and (f) have no application either.

Judicial views

6. Further, the Supreme Court in Harshad Shantilal Mehta v. Custodian [1998] 231 ITR 871/ 99 Taxman 216 held that tax, penalty and interest are different concepts under the Income-tax Act. The definition of ‘tax’ under section 2(43) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, does not include penalty or interest. In CIT v. Fertilisers & Chemicals Travancore Ltd. [2003] 126 Taxman 145, the Kerala High Court in the context of admissibility of deduction of interest on income-tax for the purpose of computation of book profits under section 115J held that the adjustment clause (a) in the Explanation only refers to income-tax paid or payable and that does not include interest.

It was argued on the Revenue's side that a conjoint reading of sub-clause (1) and sub-clause (2) of Section 92 of the Act indicates that what is sought to be taxed is the cost incurred in passing on the benefit to the holding company and not the share premium received. It was highlighted that the difference between the ALP and the price charged for the issue of shares was the benefit being passed on to VTSHL. The High Court held thus: "This manner of reading a provision by ignoring/rejecting certain words without any finding that in the absence of so rejecting, the provision would become unworkable, is certainly not the permitted mode of interpretation…This rejecting of words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible."

2.2-4 Applicability of Chapter X to Share Subscription - With respect to applicability of Transfer Pricing provisions to share subscription the High Court observed as under :

"The charge of Income now has to be found in Section 4 of the Act. If it is income chargeable to tax, under the normal provision of the Act, then alone Chapter X of the Act could be invoked ...the amount received on issue of shares is admittedly a capital account transaction not separately brought within the definition of income, except in cases covered under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act. Thus, such a capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception cannot be brought to tax"

Referring to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India10, it was held that arriving at the value of transaction on the basis of ALP would not convert non-income to income. Tax could be charged only on income and where income would not arise, the point of applying ALP to measure the value of the transaction itself would not arise.

The Hon'ble High Court further observed that the Parliament had consciously not brought to tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad. The High Court went on to hold that, although Section 56(1) of the Act would allow, under the head 'income from other sources', all income which is not otherwise excluded, it does not provide for charging to tax capital receipts in respect of issue of shares as it has been specifically provided for in Section 45 or Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act.

It further explained that while income is a flow, capital is a fund. The decision of the Privy Council in CIT v. Shaw Wallace & Co. Ltd.11 was referred to by the High Court to bring out this distinction, wherein it was observed thus:

"…income has been likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree or the crop of a field. It is essentially the produce of something which is often loosely spoken of as capital"

The High Court further rejected the contention that Chapter X was a complete Code by itself. It held thus:

"It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be found specifically mentioned in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act."

Relying on the Constitutional Bench's Judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vatika Township (P.) Ltd.12, the High Court held that there was no charge whether express or implied, in letter or in spirit, to tax the issue of shares at a premium. The High Court also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty13 to explain that the difference between charging provisions and computing provisions is qualitative in nature and computation provisions cannot substitute the charging provisions. In B.C. Srinivasa Shetty14, the transaction was not taxed as, even though there was a charging provision, yet the computation provision failed. The High Court concluded that the facts of the instant case were on a higher pedestal as there was no charging provision to tax issue of shares at premium to a non-resident, thus, there could be no occasion to invoke computational provisions.

Such amount is available to be applied either in or towards paying up any amount for the time being unpaid on any shares held by each such member, or paying up in full un-issued shares of the company to be allotted and distributed, credited as fully paid-up, to and amongst such members in their respective proportions, or partly in one way and partly the other. However, a share premium account or a capital redemption reserve account can be applied only in the paying up of un-issued shares to be issued to members of the company as fully paid bonus shares to the members according to their respective entitlements but not as a gift, CIT v. Chunilal Khusaldas [1974] 44 Comp. Cas. 90 (Guj.). The effect of issue of bonus shares from general reserves is to seal off the chances of the amounts being available for distribution as dividend permanently by conversion into share capital without contribution from the shareholders. According to the decision of Supreme Court in Shree Gopal Paper Mills Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1970 SC 1750, bonus shares become vested from the date of the resolution in general meeting and not from the date of subsequent allotment by the Board of directors. For issue of bonus shares, see discussion in Ch 20.

From the DCA Circular 9/1994 dated 6-9-1994 it would appear that the guidelines for issue of bonus shares issued by SEBI under the SEBI (DIP) Guidelines, 2000 for listed companies are applicable to all companies—that is to say, that bonus shares are to be issued out of free general reserves built out of genuine profits or share (securities?) premium account collected in cash, but not out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets. BONUS SHARES

If a company is profit making, its accumulated profits and free reserves go on increasing. Thus, actual capital employed (i.e. share capital plus accumulated profit plus free reserves) is much higher than the share capital as reflected in the balance sheet. Hence, profits earned appear to be much higher compared to the share capital. Hence, part of accumulated profits and free reserves can be distributed among members as fully paid bonus shares.

A company may issue fully paid-up bonus shares to its members, out of — (i) its free reserves (ii) the securities premium account; or (iii) the capital redemption reserve account [section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013] - similar provision in Regulation 39(ii)(D) of Model Articles of Association Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

Bonus shares out of securities premium account - Fully paid bonus shares can be issued out of securities premium account - section 52(2)(a) and 52(3)(a) of Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 39(ii)(D) of the Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

Bonus shares out of capital redemption reserve account - If preference shares are redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to nominal amount of the shares to be redeemed are required to be transferred to capital redemption reserve account under section 55(2) of Companies Act, 2013. This capital redemption reserve account can be used to issue fully paid bonus shares to members - section 55(4) of Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 39(ii)(D) of the Table F of Companies Act, 2013.

The capital redemption reserve arising out of buy back of securities can be utilised to issue fully paid bonus shares - section 69(2) of Companies Act, 2013.

No bonus out of revaluation of reserves - Bonus shares cannot be issued by capitalising reserves created by the revaluation of assets [proviso to section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013] As per SEBI guidelines also, a listed company cannot use revaluation reserves to issue bonus shares.

SEBI guidelines for listed companies - SEBI guidelines for issue of bonus shares should be followed by a listed company.

7.3-1 Conditions for issue of bonus shares by capitalizing profits or reserves

Company can capitalise its profits or reserves for purpose of issue of bonus shares, if following conditions are fulfilled [section 63(2) of Companies Act, 2013] -

(a)

it is authorised by its articles.

(b)

it has, on the recommendation of the Board, been authorised in the general meeting of the company.

(c)

Company has not defaulted in payment of interest or principal in respect of fixed deposits or debt securities issued by it.

(d)

it has not defaulted in respect of the payment of statutory dues of the employees such as contribution to provident fund, gratuity and bonus.

(e)

the partly paid-up shares, if any outstanding on the date of allotment, are made fully paid-up.

(f)

company complies with such conditions as may be prescribed.

The wording of the provision is such that aforesaid conditions are required to be satisfied only if profits or reserves are to be capitalised. It can be argued that these conditions are not required to be satisfied if bonus shares are to be issued out of securities premium account or capital redemption reserve account.

However, really securities premium account or capital redemption reserve account is also 'reserve'. Hence, these conditions should be satisfied [This is one of the examples in the Act of clumsy drafting].

(C)

partly in the way specified in sub-clause (A) and partly in that specified in sub-clause (B)

CHAPTER 125

REDEMPTION OF REDEEMABLE PREFERENCE SHARES OUT OF DISTRIBUTABLE PROFITS *REDEMPTION OF REDEEMABLE PREFERENCE SHARES OUT OF DISTRIBUTABLE PROFITS*

125.1 Background note125.1 Background note

The redemption of preference shares may be effected out of the distributable profits i.e. profits which would otherwise be available for dividend. Redemption is said to be out of profits when a fresh issue of shares for financing the redemption is not made.

125.2 Terms of redemption125.2 Terms of redemption

The redemption must be in accordance with the terms of issue and articles of association of the company.

125.3 Board Resolution125.3 Board Resolution

A Board Resolution should be passed for redemption of preference shares out of distributable profits of the company.

125.4 Transfer to capital redemption reserve125.4 Transfer to capital redemption reserve

A sum equivalent to the nominal value of shares redeemed should be transferred to a reserve fund called "Capital Redemp tion Reserve" account. The capital redemption reserve should be utilised only for issue of fully paid-up bonus shares.

125.5 Making payment125.5 Making payment

Arrangements for payment of amount due on redeemed prefer ence shares should be made. The redemption of preference shares shall not be taken as reduction of capital.

125.6 Entry in register125.6 Entry in register

Particulars of redemption should be made in the Register of Preference Shareholders and other related records and documents.

125.7 Special Requirement in case of listed companies125.7 Special Requirement in case of listed companies

A listed public company should comply with the following additional requirements:

125.7-1 Intimation to Stock Exchange(s)125.7-1 Intimation to Stock Exchange(s)

Intimation regarding redemption of preference shares should be made to each of the stock exchange(s) in which the securities of the company are enlisted.

125.7-2 Publication of advertisement125.7-2 Publication of advertisement

Advertisement regarding redemption should be made in newspapers and three copies thereof should be forward ed to each of the stock exchange(s) in which the securities of the company are enlisted.

125.8 Secretarial Compliance Certificate125.8 Secretarial Compliance Certificate

In case of companies having a paid-up capital of Rs. 10 lakhs or more but upto Rs. 2 crores, the secretarial compliance certificate to be obtained from the practising company secretary shall affirm compliance with the provisions relating to redemption of share.

DIVIDEND

28.1

SHARE OF PROFIT TO MEMBERS

Dividend is basically the share of profit distributed among shareholders.

As per section 2(35) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 2(14A) of the 1956 Act], dividend includes interim dividend.

Thus, the term 'dividend' is not fully defined in the Companies Act.

Ordinary meaning of dividend is a share of profits, whether at a fixed rate or otherwise, allocated to holders of shares in a company - Chelsea Waterworks v. Metropolitan Water Board (1904) 2 KB 77 (CA). It may include 'bonuses' or 'bonus dividends'.

Dividend is a return on investment made in the risk capital of a company, as distinct from interest on borrowed capital, which is in the form of interest. Capitalisation of profits in the form of bonus shares is not dividend. Dividend means a distribution of sums to members out of profits or reserves available for the purpose- Introduction to Secretarial Standard on Dividend SS-3.

A dividend on equity as well as preference shares can be paid only out of profits. Dividend cannot be paid out of capital. Payment of dividend out of capital is breach of trust.

Secretarial Standard on dividends - ICSI has issued new Secretarial Standard SS-3 effective from 1-1-2018. At present, it is not mandatory.

Administration Powers in respect of non-payment of dividend - As per section 24 of Companies Act, 2013 (corresponding to section 55A of the 1956 Act), provisions in respect of issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend will be administered by SEBI in respect of a listed public company or a public company which intends to get their securities listed in any recognised stock exchange. - - In other cases, the provisions will be administered by Central Government.

28.1-1 Source for payment of dividend

Dividend can be paid out of (a1) Profits of current year after providing for depreciation or (a2) out of profits for previous financial year or years after providing for depreciation for previous years, remaining undistributed or (c) Out of both (a1) and (a2) * (b) Out of moneys provided by Central or State Government for payment of dividend in pursuance of guarantee given by that, if any - section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 205(1) of the 1956 Act] [* - The word 'or' is omitted w.e.f. 9-2-2018].

In computing profits, any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets and any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value shall be excluded - proviso to section 123(1)(a) inserted w.e.f. 9-2-2018.

Dividend can also be paid out of free reserves of the company but not from any other reserve - third proviso to section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

However, declaration of dividend out of free reserves can be done only in accordance with prescribed rules - second proviso to section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [word in italics inserted w.e.f. 9-2-2018].

How to calculate 'profits' - Profit of company should be calculated according to commercially acceptable principles and practices, after preparing accounts as per accounting standards.

28.1-2 Payment of dividend out of capital profits

There is no specific provision whether 'profit' is only revenue profit or capital profits.

In absence of any such distinction in the Act, capital profits should be eligible for distribution, if actually realised. Thus, dividend cannot be paid by revaluation of assets, as the surplus has not been actually realised.

28.1-3 Whole of profits need not be distributed

It is not necessary to distribute whole of profits among shareholders. Company can distribute part of the profits among members, part will be transferred to reserves and part will be retained in P&L account itself. Dividend or reserves are appropriation of profits and hence are shown 'below the line'. Profits as per P&L account are carried forward and then its appropriation is shown in annual accounts.

Since profit figure usually appears at the bottom of P&L accounts, it is called 'bottom line'. Improvement in profits is termed as 'improving bottom line'.

28.1-4 Part of accumulated profits as bonus shares

Part of profit can be distributed as bonus shares. This aspect has been discussed in an earlier chapter. Dividend has to be paid by cash/cheque/dividend warrant/direct credit in bank account. Hence, giving bonus shares is not 'dividend'.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

Once bonus issued is announced on basis of Board resolution, the company cannot subsequently withdraw the same - Rule 14 of Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014.

The company in general meeting, upon recommendation of Board, can pass following resolution as ordinary resolution - (a) that it is desirable to capitalise any part of the amount for the time being standing to the credit of any of the company's reserve accounts, or to the credit of the profit and loss account, or otherwise available for distribution; and (b) that such sum (capitalized profit) be accordingly set free for distribution in the manner specified in Regulation 39(ii) amongst the members who would have been entitled thereto, if distributed by way of dividend and in the same proportions [Regulation 39(i) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

After such ordinary resolution, Board can give effect to the resolution by doing all necessary acts [Articles 39(ii)(E) and 40 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Return of allotment - After allotment, return of allotment has to be filed with ROC, as per procedure prescribed in rule 12 of Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014 as amended on 20-1-2023.

7.3-4 Fractional certificate or payment of cash

The ratio of issue of bonus shares may be such that some members may be entitled to fractional share.

In such case, the Board may make provisions in respect of such fractional entitlement (a) by the issue of fractional certificates or (b) by payment in cash or (c) otherwise as it thinks fit [Regulation 40(ii)(a) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

For this purpose, Board may authorise any person to enter into an agreement with the company for the allotment to the members additional shares credited as fully paid up. Alternatively, company can pay, on behalf of members to any unpaid amount on their existing shares [Regulation 40(ii)(b) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Such agreement is binding on the members.

Normally, such fractional rights are consolidated into shares and sold by the person authorised by the Board. The proceeds are then distributed among members in proportion to their fractional rights.

7.3-5 Effect of issue of bonus shares

Bonus shares is an excellent way of bringing the paid up capital of the company in line with actual capital employed in the business. It broadens the capital base and improves image of the company.

Only fully paid bonus shares can be issued. Partly paid bonus shares cannot be issued, as it will create liability on members which they may not want.

Bonus shares are same as normal shares and members are entitled to get dividend on such shares. They can also sell the shares, if they wish. A bonus share is thought of as a gift from the company. In fact, a bonus issue simply divides the existing shares into smaller units e.g. assume that equity share capital of company is Rs. one crore and free reserves are Rs. 2.5 crores. The company is declaring dividend of 30%. If bonus shares in ratio of 1:1 are issued, the share capital will be Rs. 2 crores and free reserves will be reduced to 1.5 crores. Thus, actually, there is neither any cash payment to members nor any cash receipt from members. If market price of shares was Rs. 100 per share before issue of bonus shares, it will come down to Rs. 50 per share. Thus, the shareholder is neither a loser nor a gainer. If the company now declares 15% dividend, the shareholder will get the same amount which he was getting earlier.

Issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of reserve but only as part of capital - Hunsur Plywood Works v. CIT (1997) 95 Taxman 460 = 229 ITR 112 (SC) - quoted with approval in Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. CIT (2009) 176 Taxman 142 (SC), where it was held that there is no element of gift in a company issuing bonus shares.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Further, the term used in section 66 is 'pay-off', which has been defined in Random House Dictionary as "to pay (someone) everything that is due to that person; To pay (debt) in full." Thus, the term 'pay-off' suggests that there is a due to the shareholder to the extent of his interest in the company that is been paid-off. It appears that this cannot be equated with purchase of shares in which there is nothing due to the seller till the sale transaction takes place.

According to the other view, the payment upon reduction is also purchase of shares. Section 2(22)(d) provides that dividend includes any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of capital. However, the definition also provides that dividend does not include any payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The fact that there is a specific exclusion of payment upon purchase of shares shows that in the absence of such exclusion, purchase of shares under section 77A could have been regarded as reduction of capital. Conversely, reduction of capital should also be construed as purchase of shares by the company.

It appears that the better view is that reduction of capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not a purchase within the meaning of section 115QA, although as a consequence of this view, the shareholder could be liable to

(a)

tax under section 115BBDA

(b)

capital gains tax under section 45.

The company may also be liable to DDT under section 115-O.

7.5-5 Computation of distributed income

As mentioned above, the amount received by a company in respect of the shares being bought back shall be determined in the prescribed manner. Explanatory Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance Bill, 2016 states that "rules would thereafter be framed to provide for manner of determination of the amount in various circumstances including shares being issued under tax neutral reorganisations and in different tranches."

Thus, if the buyback is in respect of shares issued at different point of time for different considerations, then the amount which is received by the company for issue of such shares has to be determined individually in the manner as may be prescribed.

Sequentially the computation of distributed income would involve the following steps:

(a)

Identification of the shares purchased

(b)

Determination of the amount received for each such share in the prescribed manner

(c)

Calculation of the consideration paid by the company for purchase of the shares

(d)

Distributed income is equal to (c) - (b).

7.5-6 Redemption of preference shares

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422/90 Taxman 509 (SC), it was held that redemption of preference shares was sale of shares by the shareholder. Conversely, the redemption could be construed as purchase of shares by the issuing company. Hence, redemption of preference shares may also be covered by section 115QA. Will the redemption now enter the computation of capital gains so far as the shareholder is concerned?

Suppose the preference shares costing Rs. 100 were redeemed by the company for Rs. 100. Suppose the indexed cost of acquisition was Rs. 130. Before the amendment in section 115QA, there was a capital loss of Rs. 30 (Rs. 130 less Rs. 100) arising to the shareholder. Will there may be any such capital loss after the amendment to section 115QA?

General reserve.

Again there could be situations where shares may have been issued by the company in tranches, for different considerations, at different point of time or may have been issued in lieu of existing shares of another company under amalgamation, merger or demerger. Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. 1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

ACCUMULATED PROFITS

General - The expression 'accumulated profits' means profits in the commercial sense and not assessable or taxable profits liable to tax as income under the Act [P. K. Badiani v. CIT [1976] 105 ITR 642 (SC)]. Calculation, what to be taken into account and what not - Profits for purpose of ascertaining accumulated profits must be determined after allowing depreciation allowable and allowed under the 1961 Act [Navnitlal C. Jhaveri v. CIT [1971] 80 ITR 582 (Bom.)].

Current profits could not be included in the expression 'accumulated profits' [Girdhardas & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 82 (Bom.), affirmed inCIT v. V. Damodaran [1979] 2 Taxman 397 (SC)].

Distribution made to a shareholder of the company out of non-taxable capital gains of the company would not form part of 'accumulated profits' and anything attributable to such capital gain shall not be deemed to be dividend in the hands of the shareholder [CIT v. Mangesh J. Sanzgiri [1979] 1 Taxman 120 (Bom.)].

This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22) as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)].

Character does not change - Accumulated profits would retain their character as such even though a part of them was not taxed as profit [Tea Estate India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 785 (SC)].

REDUCTION OF CAPITAL AND BUY-BACK OF SECURITIES

8.1

CAPITAL REDUCTION

Share capital of a company gives it strength. Large share capital base means the company is on sound footing. Hence, there are very few restrictions on increase in share capital, but many restrictions on reduction of capital.

Company can reduce share capital, any capital redemption reserve account and any share premium account in any manner subject to provisions of law [Regulation 38 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

In particular, the company can reduce capital by following means, by passing special resolution and on confirmation by NCLT - section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 100(1) of the 1956 Act].

Section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016.

Extinguishment or reduction in liability - Company can extinguish or reduce the liability of members for unpaid capital e.g. if Rs 7.50 are paid in respect of share of Rs 10, the share will be treated as fully paid up for Rs 7.50. Thus, shareholder need not pay the balance amount [section 66(1)(a) of Companies Act, 2013].

Cancel lost capital - Capital which has been lost or is not represented by available assets can be cancelled. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares [section 66(1)(b)(i) of Companies Act, 2013].

Return excess capital - Capital can be reduced by paying off or returning capital which is in excess of the needs of the company e.g. out of fully paid share of Rs 10, Rs 2.50 per share may be refunded [section 66(1)(b)(ii) of Companies Act, 2013]. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares. Thus, capital can be paid off on condition that it may be called up again if necessary e.g. in aforesaid case, company can recall Rs 2.50 per share, if found necessary.

In RS Livemedia P Ltd., In re (2014) 127 SCL 1 = 45 taxmann.com 551 (Del HC DB), proposal to return excess capital was allowed. In this case, share capital was reduced in disproportionate manner and consideration payable to different shareholders were at different rates. The varying rates were on basis of time period and also on basis of type of investors (exit was allowed to foreign investor shareholders). The proposal was accepted by all. It was held that this is permissible.

Reduction by any other way - Share capital can be reduced 'by any other way' also e.g. adjustment of securities premium account.

No reduction of capital if company is in arrears in respect of repayment or interest on deposits - Company cannot reduce its capital if it is in arrears in the repayment of deposits (accepted before or after commencement of Companies Act, 2013) or interest thereon - proviso to section 66(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

[Normally, companies incurring loss will only be going for reduction of capital. Many of these may be in arrears of repayment of deposits or interest thereon].

Accounting treatment as per accounting standards - The accounting treatment proposed by the company for reduction of capital shall be as per Accounting Standard and certificate of company's auditors shall be filed before Tribunal - proviso to section 66(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

Forfeiture of shares is not reduction of capital - Forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls is not treated as reduction of capital and hence does not require confirmation from NCLT.

Buy back is not reduction of capital - Provisions relating to reduction of capital are not applicable in respect of buy back of securities under section 68 of Companies Act, 2013 - section 66(6) of Companies Act, 2013.

8.1-1 Redemption of preference shares by reduction of capital

In Birla Global Finance Ltd. In re (2004) 50 SCL 387 (Bom HC), it was held that even if redemption of preference shares is possible as per specific provisions of Companies Act, preference shares can be redeemed by following procedure for reduction of capital, as redemption of preference shares will result in reduction of capital. In this case, company had passed necessary special resolution in general meeting and consent of preference shareholders for redemption was obtained and hence Court granted permission to redeem preference shares by reduction of capital.

8.1-2 Adjustment of securities premium account

Securities premium account can be used for reduction of capital.

7.3-8 Bonus shares cannot be issued out of revaluation reserves

Proviso to section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 205(3) of the 1956 Act] specifically prohibits issue of fully paid bonus shares by capitalizing reserves created by revaluation of assets.

In the 1956 Act, there was no such specific prohibition.

7.3-9 Bonus shares, dividend are accretions to pledged stock

In Standard Chartered Bank v. Custodian 2000 AIR SCW 1443 = AIR 2000 SC 1488 = 25 SCL 221, it was held that if shares are pledged as security with bank, bonus shares, dividend and interest in respect of pledged securities would be accretion to the pledged stock and have to be regarded as forming part of pledged property. The accretion will remain with the pawnee and the accretion can be dealt with in the same manner as the pledged shares. [As per section 163 of Contract Act, accretions in respect of goods must be returned when the goods bailed are returned]. It was observed - 'Bonus share is an accretion. A bonus share is issued when the company capitalised its profits by transferring an amount equal to the face value of the share from its reserve to the nominal capital. In other words, the undistributed profit of the company is retained by the company under the head of capital against the issue of further shares to its shareholders. Bonus shares have, therefore, been described as a distribution of capitalised undivided profit. - . - A bonus share is a property which comes into existence with an identity and value of its own and capable of being bought and sold as such. - . - Thus, bonus shares is an accretion.

7.3-10 Making partly paid shares fully paid up by bonus issue

As per Regulation 39(ii) of Table F of Companies Act, 2013, amount standing to credit of company's reserve account, or to credit of profit and loss account or otherwise available for distribution, can be used for following - (i) Making partly paid shares as fully paid (ii) Issuing fully paid shares (termed as bonus shares) in proportion to their existing shareholding (iii) Partly for making shares fully paid up and partly for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.

This is also permitted under proviso to section 123(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 205(3) of the 1956 Act].

As per Regulation 39(3) of Table F of Companies Act, 2013, share premium account and capital redemption reserve can be utilised only for issue of fully paid bonus shares. In other words, these reserves cannot be used for making partly paid shares fully paid up. Other reserves and surplus profits can be used either for making partly paid fully paid up or issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.
