12. The Supreme Court has held in Bhagwati Developers v. Peerless General Finance & Investment Co. [2005] 62 SCL 574 that unlisted public companies can issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve.

12.1 FACTUAL MATRIX - The facts of the case are:

The respondent-company issued bonus shares for Rs. 31 crores out of Rs. 73 crores standing in revaluation reserve. The appellant, who was a shareholder of the company, filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that it was not entitled to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve. The appellant challenged the power of the respondent-company to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve on three grounds. viz., (a) that the bonus shares had been issued contrary to SEBI guidelines, (b) that the issue was contrary to the circular issued by the Department of Company Affairs; and (c) that the issue could not have been made as it was contrary to article 182 of the articles of association of the company. The Calcutta High Court, in its impugned order, held that the respondent-company was entitled to issue bonus shares out of revaluation reserve. The shareholder preferred an appeal against the High Court’s order to the Apex Court.

12.2 JUDGMENT - SEBI has clarified on August 13, 1992 that its guidelines do not apply to issue of securities by closely-held private companies and unlisted public companies. (Para 6)

The circular dated September 6, 1994 does not have any mandatory effect. These circulars are merely advisory in character. (Para 7)

The relevant portion of the article 182 of the articles of association of the company, which had been strongly relied upon reads as follows :

"182(1) Any General Meeting may resolve that any amounts standing to the credit of the share premium account or the capital redemption reserve account or any monies, investment or other assets forming part of the undivided profits including profits or surplus monies arising from the realization and (where permitted by law from the appreciation in value of any capital assets of the company) standing to the credit of the General Reserve, or any Reserve Fund or any other fund of the company or in the hands of the company and available for dividend be capitalized:

(i) by the issue and distribution as fully paid-up shares, debentures, debenture stock, bonds or other obligations of the company, or

(ii) by crediting shares of the company which may have been issued and not fully paid-up, with the whole or any part of the sum remaining unpaid thereon :

Provided that any amounts standing to the credit of the share premium account or the capital redemption reserve account shall be applied only in crediting the payment of capital on shares of the company to be issued to members (as herein provided) as fully paid bonus shares." (Para 8)

FACT: In the relevant assessment year, the assessee-company claimed deduction of the expenditure incurred for the issue of bonus shares. The ITO, how- rejected the assessee’s claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The transaction of issue of bonus shares cannot be equated with the transaction of issue of additional capital by the company. The question, then is as To whether the payment made for raising authorised capital necessitated as a consequence decision to issue bonus shares brings in any benefit of permanent nature thereby forfeiting the claim for allowability under section 37(1) . This would require brief discussion on aspects of powers of directors and shareholders and importance of interplay of reserves in corporate finance. The directors have got unfettered power to decide regarding distribution of dividends either in cash or in specie or assets or reserve or even non-distribution of same. Without taking the decision of capitalising reserves they can perennially continue to carry on without in any way affecting interplay of finances at their disposal. Their decision to transfer, by way of accounting entry, part of reserves to issued capital, also does not affect the existing interplay of finances at their disposal because the decision of issue of bonus shares by way of capitalising reserves is only an accounting entry in substance and form both. While considering vis-à-vis fresh issue of capital the decision of issuing the bonus shares should, therefore, be considered as a prudent decision based on financial wisdom and commercial expediency. Thus, if for the purpose of issue of bonus shares the company has to raise the limit of authorised capital, it is only incidental to carrying on of business. It neither adds to the profit earning process nor adds to the Profit-earning apparatus and, hence, cannot be considered capital. The main reason being there is no augmentation of finance.

Accordingly, it was to be held in the present case, that aforesaid expenditure Incurred for the issue of bonus share was an allowable expenditure and the Commissioner (Appeals ) was. not justified in rejecting the assessee’s claim.

HELD: Section 23A of the 1922 Act, which aims at preventing companies to which the provisions of the said section apply from accumulating profits without distributing them as dividend amongst its shareholders, makes it obligatory for the companies to distribute by way of dividend a certain minimum percentage of the balance of income available after deducting from the assessable income the taxes payable thereon.

The expression "paid up capital of the company", though not defined in the Companies Act or in the Income-tax Act, is an expression well-known to people dealing with companies and their affairs. There can be no doubt whatsoever that for considering what is the "paid up capital of the company" an ordinary person will have recourse to the balance-sheet of the company. The ordinary meaning which any one will associate to the expression "paid up capital of the company" is what he would find from the balance-sheet of the company as held by the company at a given time as its paid up capital. In the first place, the expression used in the provision is "the paid up capital of the company". The paid up capital of the company which this proviso requires to be considered is the paid up capital of the company at the time when the application of the provisions of section 23A of the 1922 Act is required to be made to the company. Now, it may be that a company at its inception may start with a larger paid-up capital. The Companies Act contains provisions whereby the company is allowed to reduce its capital. If the company avails of those provisions and reduces its capital, for subsequent times, the company's capital will not be the original capital, but the reduced capital, and it will not be possible to say with reference to any point subsequent to the reduction that the paid up capital of the company is what initially it was before the reduction.

DIVIDEND

28.1

SHARE OF PROFIT TO MEMBERS

Dividend is basically the share of profit distributed among shareholders.

As per section 2(35) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding to section 2(14A) of the 1956 Act], dividend includes interim dividend.

Thus, the term 'dividend' is not fully defined in the Companies Act.

Ordinary meaning of dividend is a share of profits, whether at a fixed rate or otherwise, allocated to holders of shares in a company - Chelsea Waterworks v. Metropolitan Water Board (1904) 2 KB 77 (CA). It may include 'bonuses' or 'bonus dividends'.

Dividend is a return on investment made in the risk capital of a company, as distinct from interest on borrowed capital, which is in the form of interest. Capitalisation of profits in the form of bonus shares is not dividend. Dividend means a distribution of sums to members out of profits or reserves available for the purpose- Introduction to Secretarial Standard on Dividend SS-3.

A dividend on equity as well as preference shares can be paid only out of profits. Dividend cannot be paid out of capital. Payment of dividend out of capital is breach of trust.

Secretarial Standard on dividends - ICSI has issued new Secretarial Standard SS-3 effective from 1-1-2018. At present, it is not mandatory.

Administration Powers in respect of non-payment of dividend - As per section 24 of Companies Act, 2013 (corresponding to section 55A of the 1956 Act), provisions in respect of issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend will be administered by SEBI in respect of a listed public company or a public company which intends to get their securities listed in any recognised stock exchange. - - In other cases, the provisions will be administered by Central Government.

28.1-1 Source for payment of dividend

Dividend can be paid out of (a1) Profits of current year after providing for depreciation or (a2) out of profits for previous financial year or years after providing for depreciation for previous years, remaining undistributed or (c) Out of both (a1) and (a2) * (b) Out of moneys provided by Central or State Government for payment of dividend in pursuance of guarantee given by that, if any - section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [corresponding section 205(1) of the 1956 Act] [* - The word 'or' is omitted w.e.f. 9-2-2018].

In computing profits, any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets and any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value shall be excluded - proviso to section 123(1)(a) inserted w.e.f. 9-2-2018.

Dividend can also be paid out of free reserves of the company but not from any other reserve - third proviso to section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

However, declaration of dividend out of free reserves can be done only in accordance with prescribed rules - second proviso to section 123(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [word in italics inserted w.e.f. 9-2-2018].

How to calculate 'profits' - Profit of company should be calculated according to commercially acceptable principles and practices, after preparing accounts as per accounting standards.

28.1-2 Payment of dividend out of capital profits

There is no specific provision whether 'profit' is only revenue profit or capital profits.

In absence of any such distinction in the Act, capital profits should be eligible for distribution, if actually realised. Thus, dividend cannot be paid by revaluation of assets, as the surplus has not been actually realised.

28.1-3 Whole of profits need not be distributed

It is not necessary to distribute whole of profits among shareholders. Company can distribute part of the profits among members, part will be transferred to reserves and part will be retained in P&L account itself. Dividend or reserves are appropriation of profits and hence are shown 'below the line'. Profits as per P&L account are carried forward and then its appropriation is shown in annual accounts.

Since profit figure usually appears at the bottom of P&L accounts, it is called 'bottom line'. Improvement in profits is termed as 'improving bottom line'.

28.1-4 Part of accumulated profits as bonus shares

Part of profit can be distributed as bonus shares. This aspect has been discussed in an earlier chapter. Dividend has to be paid by cash/cheque/dividend warrant/direct credit in bank account. Hence, giving bonus shares is not 'dividend'.

Any interest tax. 1.9-2 Reserves adjustment under Explanation (b)/(i) - One of the adjustments required to be made relates to amounts carried to any reserve by whatever name called. The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

7.3-4 Fractional certificate or payment of cash

The ratio of issue of bonus shares may be such that some members may be entitled to fractional share.

In such case, the Board may make provisions in respect of such fractional entitlement (a) by the issue of fractional certificates or (b) by payment in cash or (c) otherwise as it thinks fit [Regulation 40(ii)(a) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

For this purpose, Board may authorise any person to enter into an agreement with the company for the allotment to the members additional shares credited as fully paid up. Alternatively, company can pay, on behalf of members to any unpaid amount on their existing shares [Regulation 40(ii)(b) of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

Such agreement is binding on the members.

Normally, such fractional rights are consolidated into shares and sold by the person authorised by the Board. The proceeds are then distributed among members in proportion to their fractional rights.

7.3-5 Effect of issue of bonus shares

Bonus shares is an excellent way of bringing the paid up capital of the company in line with actual capital employed in the business. It broadens the capital base and improves image of the company.

Only fully paid bonus shares can be issued. Partly paid bonus shares cannot be issued, as it will create liability on members which they may not want.

Bonus shares are same as normal shares and members are entitled to get dividend on such shares. They can also sell the shares, if they wish. A bonus share is thought of as a gift from the company. In fact, a bonus issue simply divides the existing shares into smaller units e.g. assume that equity share capital of company is Rs. one crore and free reserves are Rs. 2.5 crores. The company is declaring dividend of 30%. If bonus shares in ratio of 1:1 are issued, the share capital will be Rs. 2 crores and free reserves will be reduced to 1.5 crores. Thus, actually, there is neither any cash payment to members nor any cash receipt from members. If market price of shares was Rs. 100 per share before issue of bonus shares, it will come down to Rs. 50 per share. Thus, the shareholder is neither a loser nor a gainer. If the company now declares 15% dividend, the shareholder will get the same amount which he was getting earlier.

Issuance of bonus shares is nothing but mere capitalisation of the profits of company in respect of which certificates are issued to the shareholders entitling them to participate in the amount of reserve but only as part of capital - Hunsur Plywood Works v. CIT (1997) 95 Taxman 460 = 229 ITR 112 (SC) - quoted with approval in Khoday Distilleries Ltd. v. CIT (2009) 176 Taxman 142 (SC), where it was held that there is no element of gift in a company issuing bonus shares.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

◆ The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

◆ Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

◆ As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

◆ As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

◆ The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

◆ This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

◆ Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

HOW REVALUATION IS DONE? 4. Expert valuers are asked to find out the current value of the fixed assets. These valuers ascertain the guideline value adopted by registration department for land and buildings. The valuers work out the present value for other fixed assets and revalue the fixed assets. The board of directors verify the certificate of revaluation given by the valuers and pass an appropriate resolution for revaluing the assets. The values of the relevant assets are written up and the increase in value is credited to capital reserve account. The company should follow Accounting Standard 10-(Accounting for fixed assets) for revaluing the fixed assets. Revaluation of assets should be done for the entire class of assets and not for individual assets. The basis of revaluation should be disclosed in the balance sheet.

WHETHER BONUS SHARES CAN BE ISSUED OUT OF REVALUATION RESERVE - THE CONTROVERSY

5. Before the abolition of the Capital Issues (Control) Act, 1947, the Controller of Capital Issues had categorically stated in his guidelines for issue of bonus shares that reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets are not permitted to be capitalized. The Department of Company Affairs has issued Circular No. 9 of 1994 dated September 6, 1994 prohibiting issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserves. The text of the circular is given below:

"Prohibition of issue of bonus shares out of reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets

I am directed to say that...it has come to the notice of the Department that a number of unlisted companies (existing private/closely held public companies) are resorting to revaluation of their assets and issuing bonus shares therefrom. The latest Securities and Exchange Board of India’s guidelines on bonus shares dated April 13, 1994, inter alia, stipulate that the bonus issue has to be made out of free reserves built out of the genuine profits or share premium collected in cash only and reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets cannot be capitalized for this purpose. These guidelines are applicable only to listed companies.

This matter has been considered in the Department and the existing private/closely held and unlisted companies are hereby advised not to issue bonus shares out of the reserves created by revaluation of fixed assets."

SOME OBSERVATIONS ON THE ABOVE CIRCULAR

6. There is no provision in the Companies Act, 1956 dealing with the kind of reserve which may be used for the purpose of issue of bonus share except for an enabling provision under proviso to section 205(3) which enables the company to capitalize profits or ‘reserves’ for the purpose of issuing bonus shares. The term ‘reserve’ is negatively defined in Schedule VI, Part III: the expression ‘reserve’ shall not include the amount written of or retained by way of providing for depreciation, renewals or diminution in the value of assets or retained by way of providing for known liability. Revaluation Reserve therefore, cannot be excluded in terms of this definition from being termed as Reserve.

POSITION UNDER ENGLISH LAW

7. The permissibility of capitalizing Revaluation Reserve is judicially recognized in England. This is clear from the authority of the decision in Dimbulla Valley (Ceylon) Tea Co. Ltd. v. Laurie [1961] 1 Ch 353 in which the eminent Judge BUCKLEY J. observed as follows: "It has, I think, long been generally accepted view of the law in this country. (Though not established by judicial authority) that if the surplus on capital account results from a valuation made in good faith by competent valuers, and is not likely to be liable to short term fluctuations, it may properly be capitalised."

SEBI DOES NOT PROHIBIT BONUS OUT OF REVALUATION RESERVE BY UNLISTED COMPANIES

8. SEBI have in the DIP Guidelines recognized the legal position that an unlisted company can issue bonus shares by capitalizing its Revaluation Reserves. This is brought out by clause 4.6.1(ii) of the SEBI (Disclosure & Investor Protection) Guidelines, 2000 (‘the DIP Guidelines) which deal with promoters contribution. Clause 4.6 of the DIP Guidelines reads as under:

"4.6 Securities Ineligible for Computation of Promoters Contribution.

4.6.1 Where the promoters of any company making an issue of securities have acquired equity during the preceding three years, before filing the offer documents with the Board, such equity shall not be considered for computation of promoters contribution if it is:

"(i) acquired for consideration other than cash and revaluation of assets or capitalization of intangible assets is involved in such transaction(s) ; or

(ii) resulting from a bonus issues, out of revaluation reserves or reserves without accrual of cash resources."

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

Further, the term used in section 66 is 'pay-off', which has been defined in Random House Dictionary as "to pay (someone) everything that is due to that person; To pay (debt) in full." Thus, the term 'pay-off' suggests that there is a due to the shareholder to the extent of his interest in the company that is been paid-off. It appears that this cannot be equated with purchase of shares in which there is nothing due to the seller till the sale transaction takes place.

According to the other view, the payment upon reduction is also purchase of shares. Section 2(22)(d) provides that dividend includes any distribution to its shareholders by a company on reduction of capital. However, the definition also provides that dividend does not include any payment made by a company on purchase of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The fact that there is a specific exclusion of payment upon purchase of shares shows that in the absence of such exclusion, purchase of shares under section 77A could have been regarded as reduction of capital. Conversely, reduction of capital should also be construed as purchase of shares by the company.

It appears that the better view is that reduction of capital under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is not a purchase within the meaning of section 115QA, although as a consequence of this view, the shareholder could be liable to

(a)

tax under section 115BBDA

(b)

capital gains tax under section 45.

The company may also be liable to DDT under section 115-O.

7.5-5 Computation of distributed income

As mentioned above, the amount received by a company in respect of the shares being bought back shall be determined in the prescribed manner. Explanatory Memorandum explaining provisions of the Finance Bill, 2016 states that "rules would thereafter be framed to provide for manner of determination of the amount in various circumstances including shares being issued under tax neutral reorganisations and in different tranches."

Thus, if the buyback is in respect of shares issued at different point of time for different considerations, then the amount which is received by the company for issue of such shares has to be determined individually in the manner as may be prescribed.

Sequentially the computation of distributed income would involve the following steps:

(a)

Identification of the shares purchased

(b)

Determination of the amount received for each such share in the prescribed manner

(c)

Calculation of the consideration paid by the company for purchase of the shares

(d)

Distributed income is equal to (c) - (b).

7.5-6 Redemption of preference shares

In Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [1997] 224 ITR 422/90 Taxman 509 (SC), it was held that redemption of preference shares was sale of shares by the shareholder. Conversely, the redemption could be construed as purchase of shares by the issuing company. Hence, redemption of preference shares may also be covered by section 115QA. Will the redemption now enter the computation of capital gains so far as the shareholder is concerned?

Suppose the preference shares costing Rs. 100 were redeemed by the company for Rs. 100. Suppose the indexed cost of acquisition was Rs. 130. Before the amendment in section 115QA, there was a capital loss of Rs. 30 (Rs. 130 less Rs. 100) arising to the shareholder. Will there may be any such capital loss after the amendment to section 115QA?

Section 4 of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 - Surtax - Capital - Computation of - Assessment year 1974-75 - Whether if there is some amount set apart from profit and is not earmarked for being utilised for any particular purpose and if marked for being utilised for a particular purpose, purpose is not to meet any known or existing liability and is thus not kept for being appropriated to meet such a liability it shall be a reserve and shall qualify for being computed in capital for purposes of Act - Held, yes - Whether it is incorrect, to say that merely because a fund has been set apart for debenture redemption, a specific liability, it is a provision, it is equally wrong to hold that since it is not a provision it is a reserve which qualifies for computation of capital - Held, yes -Assessee-public limited company created a debenture redemption reserve - While completing assessment for surtax ITO rejected assessee’s contention that reserve created for debenture redemption should also be treated as apart of capital, mainly on ground that said reserve had been created for purpose of meeting a specific liability, viz., repayment of debenture loan - On appeals, Commissioner (Appeals) as well as Tribunal held that amount set apart for repayment of debentures was a reserve and not a provision - On instant reference, it was, however, seen that there was no information about nature of funds except name ‘debenture redemption reserve’ - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, matter was to be matter remanded back to Tribunal for fresh consideration - Held, yes [-Matter remanded]

Finance Act 2002

Enlargement of deduction under section 33AC to shipping companies

1.3 Under section 33AC, a Government company or a public company formed and registered in India with the main object of carrying on the business of operation of ships is allowed a deduction of 100% of the profits derived from the business of operation of ships and carried to a reserve account, subject to certain conditions. Hitherto, where the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve account from time to time exceeded twice the amount of the paid-up share capital (excluding the amounts capitalized from the reserves) of the assessee, no deduction was allowed in respect of such excess [first proviso to section 33AC].

This proviso has now been amended to extend the benefit by providing that the deduction shall be allowed in respect of the aggregate of the amounts carried to the reserve account up to twice the aggregate of the amounts of the paid-up share capital, general reserve and amount credited to the share premium account of the assessee.

The amendment is effective from assessment year 2003-2004.

In view of the above amendment, the following amounts will now be reckoned for the purpose of entitlement to the deduction :

(a)

Bonus shares.

(b)

Share premium, whether collected in cash or otherwise.

(c)

General reserve.

1.3-1 Surplus in profit and loss account - The amendment refers to general reserve. In the context of surtax, it has been held that a mass of undistributed profits, lying unutilized and not specially set apart for any purpose, does not constitute a reserve [CIT v. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1953] 24 ITR 499 (SC); Aluminium Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1968] 68 ITR 125 (Ker.)]. Hence, apparently surplus in profit and loss account cannot be reckoned for the purpose of the deduction under the amended section 33AC.

Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

Capital gains

1.11 Under the Act, as per section 45, capital gains is deemed to be income, of the previous year in which the transfer takes place. Having regard to that fact and for other reasons discussed. Special Bench of the Tribunal in Sutlej case (supra)took a view that capital gains cannot form part of book profit. One of the grounds discussed for taking such a view was that it affects capital structure of a company and does not affect working results and as per the Schedule cannot form part of book profit.

In Indo Marine Agencies (Kerala) Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1995] 51 TTJ 18, the Cochin Bench of Tribunal has taken a view that profit on sale of capital asset shown in Profit and Loss Account should be reckoned for computing book profit.

A reading of para 3(xii)(a)of Part III of the Schedule to the said Act also reflects the position, that, if it is shown in the profit and loss account, then, it should be reckoned for computing book profits.

In view of the above decisions, it appears that :

ACCUMULATED PROFITS

General - The expression 'accumulated profits' means profits in the commercial sense and not assessable or taxable profits liable to tax as income under the Act [P. K. Badiani v. CIT [1976] 105 ITR 642 (SC)]. Calculation, what to be taken into account and what not - Profits for purpose of ascertaining accumulated profits must be determined after allowing depreciation allowable and allowed under the 1961 Act [Navnitlal C. Jhaveri v. CIT [1971] 80 ITR 582 (Bom.)].

Current profits could not be included in the expression 'accumulated profits' [Girdhardas & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1957] 31 ITR 82 (Bom.), affirmed inCIT v. V. Damodaran [1979] 2 Taxman 397 (SC)].

Distribution made to a shareholder of the company out of non-taxable capital gains of the company would not form part of 'accumulated profits' and anything attributable to such capital gain shall not be deemed to be dividend in the hands of the shareholder [CIT v. Mangesh J. Sanzgiri [1979] 1 Taxman 120 (Bom.)].

This would clearly exclude return of a part of the capital by the company from section 2(22) as the same cannot be regarded as profits capable of being capitalised, the return being of the capital itself [CIT v. G. Narasimhan [1999] 102 Taxman 66 (SC)].

Character does not change - Accumulated profits would retain their character as such even though a part of them was not taxed as profit [Tea Estate India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 785 (SC)].

INCOME TAX: Where assessee, having reduced share capital during year to absorb accumulated losses, computed book profit under section 115JB by setting off brought-forward losses, relevant date for determining such brought-forward loss was beginning of year, i.e. losses as on 1-4-2004, and reduction of share capital effected during year could not be reckoned with reference to loss position as on 31-3-2005

REDUCTION OF CAPITAL AND BUY-BACK OF SECURITIES

8.1

CAPITAL REDUCTION

Share capital of a company gives it strength. Large share capital base means the company is on sound footing. Hence, there are very few restrictions on increase in share capital, but many restrictions on reduction of capital.

Company can reduce share capital, any capital redemption reserve account and any share premium account in any manner subject to provisions of law [Regulation 38 of Model Articles of company limited by shares as contained in Table-F of Schedule I of Companies Act, 2013].

In particular, the company can reduce capital by following means, by passing special resolution and on confirmation by NCLT - section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 100(1) of the 1956 Act].

Section 66 of Companies Act, 2013 has been notified and made effective on 15-12-2016.

Extinguishment or reduction in liability - Company can extinguish or reduce the liability of members for unpaid capital e.g. if Rs 7.50 are paid in respect of share of Rs 10, the share will be treated as fully paid up for Rs 7.50. Thus, shareholder need not pay the balance amount [section 66(1)(a) of Companies Act, 2013].

Cancel lost capital - Capital which has been lost or is not represented by available assets can be cancelled. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares [section 66(1)(b)(i) of Companies Act, 2013].

Return excess capital - Capital can be reduced by paying off or returning capital which is in excess of the needs of the company e.g. out of fully paid share of Rs 10, Rs 2.50 per share may be refunded [section 66(1)(b)(ii) of Companies Act, 2013]. This can be done with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares. Thus, capital can be paid off on condition that it may be called up again if necessary e.g. in aforesaid case, company can recall Rs 2.50 per share, if found necessary.

In RS Livemedia P Ltd., In re (2014) 127 SCL 1 = 45 taxmann.com 551 (Del HC DB), proposal to return excess capital was allowed. In this case, share capital was reduced in disproportionate manner and consideration payable to different shareholders were at different rates. The varying rates were on basis of time period and also on basis of type of investors (exit was allowed to foreign investor shareholders). The proposal was accepted by all. It was held that this is permissible.

Reduction by any other way - Share capital can be reduced 'by any other way' also e.g. adjustment of securities premium account.

No reduction of capital if company is in arrears in respect of repayment or interest on deposits - Company cannot reduce its capital if it is in arrears in the repayment of deposits (accepted before or after commencement of Companies Act, 2013) or interest thereon - proviso to section 66(1) of Companies Act, 2013.

[Normally, companies incurring loss will only be going for reduction of capital. Many of these may be in arrears of repayment of deposits or interest thereon].

Accounting treatment as per accounting standards - The accounting treatment proposed by the company for reduction of capital shall be as per Accounting Standard and certificate of company's auditors shall be filed before Tribunal - proviso to section 66(3) of Companies Act, 2013.

Forfeiture of shares is not reduction of capital - Forfeiture of shares for non-payment of calls is not treated as reduction of capital and hence does not require confirmation from NCLT.

Buy back is not reduction of capital - Provisions relating to reduction of capital are not applicable in respect of buy back of securities under section 68 of Companies Act, 2013 - section 66(6) of Companies Act, 2013.

8.1-1 Redemption of preference shares by reduction of capital

In Birla Global Finance Ltd. In re (2004) 50 SCL 387 (Bom HC), it was held that even if redemption of preference shares is possible as per specific provisions of Companies Act, preference shares can be redeemed by following procedure for reduction of capital, as redemption of preference shares will result in reduction of capital. In this case, company had passed necessary special resolution in general meeting and consent of preference shareholders for redemption was obtained and hence Court granted permission to redeem preference shares by reduction of capital.

8.1-2 Adjustment of securities premium account

Securities premium account can be used for reduction of capital.

7.3-6 When right to bonus crystallises

In Shri Gopal Paper Mills v. CIT AIR 1970 SC 1750 = 37 Comp Cas 240 = 77 ITR 543 (SC), it was held that shareholder becomes owner of shares on date of resolution. It is not necessary for issue of shares that a share certificate has to be given. It can be given later. Vesting of bonus shares takes place from date of company's resolution and not from date of actual allotment.

7.3-7 Expenses in issue of bonus shares are revenue expenses

In CIT v. General Insurance Corporation (2006) 156 Taxman 96 (SC), it has been held that expenditure incurred in connection with bonus shares is revenue expenditure. - same view in Bombay Burmah Trading v. CIT (1984) 145 ITR 793 = 12 Taxman 178 (Bom HC).

Earlier, in Gujarat Steel Tubes v. CIT (1994) 210 ITR 358 (Guj), it was held that expenses incurred in issue of bonus shares are capital in nature and cannot be allowed as expenditure. - quoted and followed in CIT v. Bharat Vijay Mills (2002) 124 Taxman 60 (Guj HC DB). Now these decisions stand overruled.

7.3-8 Bonus shares cannot be issued out of revaluation reserves

Proviso to section 63(1) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 205(3) of the 1956 Act] specifically prohibits issue of fully paid bonus shares by capitalizing reserves created by revaluation of assets.

In the 1956 Act, there was no such specific prohibition.

7.3-9 Bonus shares, dividend are accretions to pledged stock

In Standard Chartered Bank v. Custodian 2000 AIR SCW 1443 = AIR 2000 SC 1488 = 25 SCL 221, it was held that if shares are pledged as security with bank, bonus shares, dividend and interest in respect of pledged securities would be accretion to the pledged stock and have to be regarded as forming part of pledged property. The accretion will remain with the pawnee and the accretion can be dealt with in the same manner as the pledged shares. [As per section 163 of Contract Act, accretions in respect of goods must be returned when the goods bailed are returned]. It was observed - 'Bonus share is an accretion. A bonus share is issued when the company capitalised its profits by transferring an amount equal to the face value of the share from its reserve to the nominal capital. In other words, the undistributed profit of the company is retained by the company under the head of capital against the issue of further shares to its shareholders. Bonus shares have, therefore, been described as a distribution of capitalised undivided profit. - . - A bonus share is a property which comes into existence with an identity and value of its own and capable of being bought and sold as such. - . - Thus, bonus shares is an accretion.

7.3-10 Making partly paid shares fully paid up by bonus issue

As per Regulation 39(ii) of Table F of Companies Act, 2013, amount standing to credit of company's reserve account, or to credit of profit and loss account or otherwise available for distribution, can be used for following - (i) Making partly paid shares as fully paid (ii) Issuing fully paid shares (termed as bonus shares) in proportion to their existing shareholding (iii) Partly for making shares fully paid up and partly for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.

This is also permitted under proviso to section 123(5) of Companies Act, 2013 [Corresponding to section 205(3) of the 1956 Act].

As per Regulation 39(3) of Table F of Companies Act, 2013, share premium account and capital redemption reserve can be utilised only for issue of fully paid bonus shares. In other words, these reserves cannot be used for making partly paid shares fully paid up. Other reserves and surplus profits can be used either for making partly paid fully paid up or issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.

u Under-subscription : A subscription lower than the minimum subscription devolving on the under-writers in a public issue.

u Paid-up capital : It forms the amount paid on the shares subscribed, whether in cash or for non-cash. If the issued capital is fully subscribed and paid in an issue at par as a condition for allotment of shares, then the capital paid-up will be equal to the capital issued and subscribed. u Capital out of loans : Section 81(4)/94A of the Act provide that debentures issued to or loans drawn from the Government (Central or any State) irrespective of the option and public financial institutions with an option for it attached, by companies, may be ordered by the Central Government to be converted into shares which by itself effects automatic increase of the authorized capital of companies commensurately, with the loans wiped out.

u Uncalled capital : If the issue terms are such that only a part of the nominal value of the shares is payable for allotment the balance being payable against future calls to be made by the board of directors, the difference between the full value of the capital issued to the extent of the shares subscribed and the amount paid-up is called the uncalled capital. This category remaining so for long is now rare.

u Capital called-up but not paid or calls unpaid : It refers to the balance amount remaining unpaid on the first or further or final call made after the allotment of shares by the board of directors as of the last day of the financial year with reference to the balance sheet of that year but within the time allowed, and not amounting to calls in arrear.

u Calls in arrear : The amount of call or calls referred to above remaining unpaid beyond the time allowed.

u Calls in advance or unpaid capital : Section 92 and regulation 18 of Table A provide that moneys advanced and accepted though uncalled in respect of shares may bear interest at 6% p.a. but discounted for voting rights or dividend etc.

u Share premium : If shares are issued at a premium, that is, at a price higher than their face value, the excess is called share premium which forms part of capital for most purposes of assessing the financial position of the company. It does not count for dividend and it is not available for distribution as dividend but is available towards issue of bonus shares or meeting the premium payable on redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures or towards the write-off of preliminary expenses or commission paid on issue of shares or discount allowed on shares or debentures, section 78 of the Act.

u Discount on shares : If shares are issued at a discount, that is, at a price lower than their face value, it is called shares issued at a discount and the total amount of such discount has to be written off in a specified period, section 79 of the Act; and, it would appear that neither for dividend payment nor for voting it would not count anytheless, and the discount legally allowed is in the nature of an upfront dividend paid.

u Forfeited shares : If the calls made on shares allotted as partly-paid become bad debts, such shares may be forfeited by the board of directors to enforce the company’s lien on the shares subject to there being an enabling provision in the articles. When such action is taken, the amount to the extent paid as on the date of forfeiture ranks as capital at par with share premium and is separately displayed as an addition to the share capital in the balance sheet.

u The total of share premium and the amount of forfeiture on forfeited shares when added to the paid-up share capital may exceed the capital authorized in the capital clause in the memorandum.

u Reduced capital or company ‘Limited and Reduced’ : The amount of capital lost and not represented by available assets and reduction of capital in any way duly confirmed by the Tribunal under the Act, sometimes with an order that the words ‘and Reduced’ are to be added as the last words in company’s name during a given period, for compulsory use to serve as public notice that the company has effected reduction of its capital.

u Interest out of capital : If authorized by the articles or a special resolution and with previous sanction of the Central Government in terms of section 208 of the Act, a company engaged in the construction of any work or building or the provision of any plant of a long gestation period may pay interest out of capital for the period at a rate not exceeding four per cent per annum, and such a payment while it adds to the cost of the project it shall not operate as a reduction of the amount paid up on the shares in respect of which it is paid, [section 208(1)(b)]; and, the definition of ‘actual cost’ as given in Challapalli Sugars Ltd. v. CIT AIR 1975 SC 97.

u Reserve Capital : A company limited by shares may determine by special resolution that any portion of its uncalled capital shall be called-up only in the event and for the purposes of the company being wound up. On passing such a special resolution, the earmarked part of the uncalled capital becomes irrevocably the reserve capital, section 99 of the Act.

In other words, the interest falling due and payable for the period subsequent to the date of installation of such asset on the outstanding balances of the loans does not form part of the ‘actual cost’, and it has to be charged to the revenues year after year, necessitating on account of this timing difference partial decapitalisation of the interest capitalized earlier as the actual cost. It will not be in accord with sound company practice to utilize the excess amount resulting from the recomputation of depreciation for distribution to members by way of dividend or otherwise. Share premium - Not a capital reserve

Premium obtained on the issue of shares from its very nature is not a part of the capital paid-up on shares ; it is the surplus of the sum received in respect of the share over the amount required to pay up the share to the extent to which it is treated by the company as paid-up. The premium is not the capital paid-up on the share but a sum received by the company in excess of the capital paid-up on the share (see Drown v. Gaumont- British Picture Corporation Ltd. (1937) Ch. 402/[1938] 8 Comp. Cas. 136 and in the matter of Coca-Cola Amatil Ltd. (1998) NSW Lexis 1786, BC 9802902). It is not a capital and has no characteristics of a statutory reserve or reserve; it is however deemed to be paid-up share capital for the purpose of sections 100 to 104 of the Indian Companies Act, 1956 [Global Trust Bank Ltd., In re [2005] 127 Comp. Cas. 604 (AP)]

Issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserve 6.1 Existing prohibition - Section M of the SEBI Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection does not allow issue of bonus shares out of the Revaluation reserve. This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

CIT [1965] 57 ITR 521, in which case, the company had set apart a certain amount towards consumer benefit reserve account, which represented excess over reasonable return in terms of the said Act. Such an amount was required to be returned to customers in the form of rebate. The Supreme Court held that the amount credited to the said reserve did not form part of the real profit of the company. Under the Act, profits of the business are required to be computed and they are not profits regulated by any statute but profits in the business computed on commercial principles. They are business profits and not statutory profits The real profit of a businessman under section 10(1) of the 1922 Act [corresponding to section 28(i) of the Act] cannot include amounts returned by way of rebate under statutory compulsion. It is as if it has received only the original amount minus the amount to be returned. The amount returned is not a part of the profits at all.

Thus, whether an amount set apart represents a reserve or provision will have to be decided and determined on the basis of the requirement relating thereto. Based on the above decisions and in the light of the provisions of the Schedule, it could be said that the amount set apart towards contingency reserve could be considered as a reserve and not a provision and further, the amount set apart towards consumers benefit could be considered as a provision and that too for a known liability.

In National Rayon Corporation Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 51 ITD 621 the issue before the Bombay Tribunal was whether a provision made for liability relating to earlier years, which had accrued during the earlier year but not provided, could be deducted in computing the profits? The Tribunal held that under normal provisions, claim for such liability was not allowable. However, for the purposes of section 115J of the Act, as it was an ascertained liability, the same is to be excluded while computing book profit.

The above cited Supreme Court's decision also throws more light on the concept of net profit based on working results to be reflected in the profit and loss account as per the requirements of the Schedule.

Thus, the working results, as contemplated by the Schedule, could be the one which a commercial man would not misunderstand and therefore reflects commercial profits, which would be usually computed on the basis of the accepted principle of conservatism and after providing for all known liabilities and losses.

AO passed an assessment order limiting the deduction under Section 44C to 5% of the gross total income. The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that to be brought within the ambit of Section 44C, two broad conditions must be satisfied: (i) The assessee claiming the deduction must be a non-resident; and (ii) The expenditure in question must strictly fall within the definition of 'head office expenditure' as provided in the Explanation to the Section. The Explanation prescribes a tripartite test to determine if an expense qualifies as 'head office expenditure' - (i) The expenditure was incurred outside India; (ii) The expenditure is in the nature of 'executive and general administration' expenses; and (iii) The said executive and general administration expenditure is of the specific kind enumerated in clauses (a), (b), or (c) respectively of the Explanation, or is of the kind prescribed under clause (d).

This means that even if such head office expenditure can be allowed as a deduction under Section 37(1), it would not be permitted if it exceeds the ceiling limit set under Section 44C. Section 44C of the Income Tax Act does not create a distinction between common and exclusive head office expenditure. It applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches. The term 'attributable' in Clause (c) does not create a statutory distinction between 'common' and 'exclusive' expenditure.

Thus, the question of law is answered in favour of the Revenue, and it was held that Section 44C applies to 'head office expenditure' regardless of whether it is common expenditure or expenditure incurred exclusively for the Indian branches.

5. Reduction in share capital of subsidiary & subsequent reduction in shareholding is 'transfer' under Section 2(47): SC

Jupiter Capital (P.) Ltd. v. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 170 taxmann.com 305 (SC)

The assessee held shares in an Indian company. The company filed a petition before the High Court for a reduction of its share capital to set off the loss against the paid-up equity share capital. The High Court ordered for a reduction in the share capital of the company. The assessee's share was reduced proportionately, and the company paid an amount to the assessee as consideration. During the year, the assessee claimed a long-term capital loss accrued on the reduction in share capital from the sale of shares of such company.

However, the Assessing Officer (AO) contended that although the number of shares got reduced by virtue of reduction in share capital of the company, yet the face value of each share as well as shareholding pattern remained the same. Thus, reduction in shares of the subsidiary company did not result in the transfer of a capital asset as envisaged in section 2(47).

The matter reached before the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court held that section 2(47) is an inclusive definition providing that relinquishment of an asset or extinguishment of any right therein amounts to a transfer of a capital asset. While the taxpayer continues to remain a shareholder of the company even with the reduction of share capital, it could not be accepted that there was no extinguishment of any part of his right as a shareholder qua the company.

The expression 'extinguishment of any right therein' is of wide import. It covers every possible transaction which results in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation or cancellation, by satisfaction or otherwise, of all or any of the bundle of rights, qualitative or quantitative, which the assessee has in a capital asset, whether such asset is corporeal or incorporeal.

In the instant case, the face value per share remained the same before the reduction of share capital and after the reduction of share capital. However, as the total number of shares were reduced.

Relying upon the decision in case of Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. Commissioner of Income Tax reported in (1997) 7 SCC 524, it was held that reduction of right in a capital asset would amount to 'transfer' under section 2(47). Sale is only one of the modes of transfer envisaged by section 2(47). Relinquishment of any rights in it, which may not amount to sale, can also be considered as transfer and any profit or gain which arises from the transfer of such capital asset is taxable under section 45.

Also, a company under section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 has a right to reduce the share capital, and one of the modes which could be adopted is to reduce the face value of the preference share. When as a result of the reducing of the face value of the share, the share capital is reduced, the right of the preference shareholder to the dividend or his share capital and the right to share in the distribution of the net assets upon liquidation is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in the capital. Such a reduction of the right of the capital asset clearly amounts to a transfer within the meaning of section 2(47).

Thus, it was held that the reduction in share capital of the subsidiary company and subsequent proportionate reduction in the shareholding of the assessee would be squarely covered within the ambit of the expression 'sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset' used in section 2(47).

12. Cognizant liable to pay DDT on its Rs. 19,000 crores buyback: ITAT [Cognizant Technology Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. Asst. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 309 (Chennai - Trib.)]

The assessee (Cognizant Technology) had purchased its own shares from non-resident shareholders in a 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of provisions of Section 391-393 of the Companies Act, 1956.

In accordance with the scheme, the assessee purchased 94,00,534 equity shares from its shareholder at the price of Rs. 20,297 per share and paid a total consideration of Rs. 19,080.26 crores.

The share capital of the assessee company was held by four non-resident shareholders, out of which three shareholders are residents of the USA, and one shareholder is a tax resident of Mauritius. The net effect of the scheme was that post-sanction of the scheme, the only shareholder left was Cognizant Mauritius Ltd.

The AO held that consideration paid by the assessee to its shareholders for the purchase of its own shares was liable to tax as deemed dividend under Section 2(22)(d). Consequently, the assessee was liable to pay Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) under Section 115-O.

On the other hand, the assessee submits that the 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' was sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of Sections 391 to 393 of the Companies Act, 1956. It cannot be considered as a buyback of shares in terms of provisions of Section 77A or a reduction of capital in terms of Sections 100-104/402 of the Companies Act, 1956.

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the findings of AO. The matter reached before the tribunal.

The tribunal held as follows:

Two essential prerequisites must be satisfied to come within the ambit of Section 2(22)(d). First, there must be a distribution to the shareholders on the reduction of the capital, and second, it must be to the extent that the company possess accumulated profits. In the present case, it was evident from the audited financial statement that the share capital has been reduced by around Rs. 9.4 crores, which is equivalent to 54.70% of the total paid-up share capital. The Supreme Court, in CIT v. G. Narasihan 236 ITR 327, has clarified that Section 2(22)(d) is automatically attracted once these parameters are satisfied. Further, Clause 7 of the scheme clarifies that the distribution of money will be out of the general reserves and accumulated credit balance in the profit and loss account. Thus, both conditions are satisfied to treat the transaction within Section 2(22)(d).

The assessee also argued that the scheme of purchase of own shares was made through offer and acceptance. This involves an element of quid pro quo, and thus, there was no 'distribution of the purpose of section 2(22)(d). The tribunal held that the definition of 'distribution' does not contain any aspect of quid pro quo or lack thereof. The prerequisites for distribution are that there must be payment, and the disbursal must be made to more than one person. Section 2(22)(d) does not distinguish whether the reduction of share capital is the intended result of the resultant consequence of the scheme.

The assessee's transaction would either fall under Section 391-393 r.w. Section 77 and Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 or Sections 391-393 r.w Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The scheme clearly states that it is not a buyback under Section 77A. Therefore, once the assessee states it is not buyback under section 77A, it should automatically fall back to Section 77 r.w Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956. If said sections are applied, then said transaction was nothing but the reduction of capital and distribution of accumulated profits.

The assessee also contended that Section 115QA was amended in 2016, and the present transaction would only be taxable per the amended provisions. The assessee's arguments were not accepted for two reasons. Firstly, there is a distinction between the purchase of own shares upon reduction of share capital and buyback. Buyback is a term used only with respect to transactions covered under Section 77A. If all conditions of Section 115-O r.w Section 2(22) are satisfied, the same cannot be impliedly excluded based on the amendment to Section 115QA.

Now the term ‘reserves’ have been further defined elsewhere in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI as including both capital and revenue reserves. Thus, para 35 provides a flexibility in the matter of adjustment of additional price paid either against capital reserves or general reserves including profit and loss account surplus. Normally such difference is very large and it is unlikely that a company would so choose to adjust such difference in the profit and loss account for that would impact the Earning Per Share (EPS) and the market capitalization. Any such company, therefore, would like to prioritize such adjustment against capital reserves such as share premium, etc. But in any case there is nothing that prevents a company to adjust such difference against profit and loss account. And even while it so chooses to make such an adjustment for the purpose of section 115JB, there would be no shift in the manner of treatment since the accounting standard adopted for preparation of profit and loss account in either case would be the same. In other words the treatment meted out in either case would be in accordance with the accounting standard.

Provisioning of deferred tax liability

5. Yet another instance is the provisioning of deferred tax liability when AS-22 so requires such provision for the period prior to the coming into force of standard against the reserves. Para 33 of AS-22 in this regard reads as under :

"33. On the first occasion that the taxes on income are accounted for in accordance with this statement, the enterprise should recognize, in the financial statements, the deferred tax balance that has accumulated prior to the adoption of this Statement as deferred tax asset/liability with a corresponding credit/charge to the revenue reserves, subject to the consideration of prudence in case of deferred tax assets (see paragraphs 15-18). The amount so credited/charged to the revenue reserves should be the same as that which would have resulted if this Statement had been in effect from the beginning."

In that case while the company so chooses to make such provision against general reserves in the balance sheet, yet it can draw a separate profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB after charge to the profit and loss account and take benefit of such deduction. Such an exercise would be well within the ambit of income-tax laws since revenue reserves would always include profit and loss account surplus.
