Corporate Accounting Policies

5.1 Revaluation of land by DCM Ltd. and reversal- During 1990-91 DCM revalued freehold land pertaining to its closed unit, Delhi Cloth Mills, creating a surplus of Rs. 199.25 crores and subsequently, the revaluation was updated by creating an additional surplus of Rs. 74.21 crores. During 1991-92 the company revalued some more land pertaining to its closed unit, Delhi Cloth Mills, creating a surplus of Rs. 6 crores, Revaluation Surpluses were transferred to revaluation reserve.

Thereafter, DCM has converted such land into stock-in-trade and adopted a policy to recognise such lands at their historical costs plus development expenses. It has also reduced the revaluation reserve by necessary adjustments.

The whole accounting process of revaluation of land, recognition of revaluation profit, conversion of land into stock-in-trade and reversing revaluation has made the financial statements non-understandable and unreliable.

Up to the assessment year 1984-85, there was no capital gains tax incidence if any capital asset was converted into stock-in-trade for the difference between market value as on the date of conversion and cost by virtue of the Supreme Court's decision in CIT v. Bai Shirinbai K. Kooka [1962] 46 ITR 86. The tax advantage of converting a capital asset into stock-in-trade has now been eliminated by insertion of section 45(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and notional capital gain arising out of conversion is taxable as capital gains; there was thus no tangible purpose to reverse the revaluation at the time of conversion of land into stock-in-trade.

The prudent concept of valuation of stock-in-trade at the lower of the historical cost and market price is not applicable to real estate AS-2 valuation of inventories is not applicable to real estate.

Through the process of reversal of revaluation, DCM rather undervalued its stock-in-trade and thereby it has generated a set of grossly misleading financial statements in 1992-93 and thereafter. In fact, the choice of accounting policies should be directed to produce relevant and reliable accounting data to aid users' decision-making.

Similar to the case discussed above was the case of "Heritage Housing Finance Ltd" wherein the Central Government raised an objection that the share exchange ratio as proposed in the said scheme was not fair and reasonable. The petitioner filed petition contending that the Central Government could not raise aforesaid objection when in the shareholders' meeting the entire scheme had been approved unanimously. It was held that the plain reading of the provisions did not postulate the nature of the objection required to be raised by the Central Government but what it provided was that the Court before passing any order ,must take into consideration the representations and/or objections raised by the Central Government. It was held that the Central Government was certainly within their competence to raise the objection as they were required to see that no unfairness and/or unreasonableness to be shown either to the creditors or the class of creditors and/or members or the class of members and public interest, which certainly imbibed itself with the power to question the said share exchange ratio. Therefore, there was no force in the submission of the petitioner that the Central Government could not raise objection to the share exchange ratio. It was therefore directed to the official liquidator to engage a Chartered Accountant from its panel, who should submit the report before the court relating to fairness of the share exchange ratio.

As is clearly provided in the Companies Act 2013, regarding issuance of bonus shares and declaration of dividend, only Free Reserves can be utilized. Drawing from the discussion above, the adjustments arising due to transition of assets and liabilities from GAAP to Ind AS cannot be part of first time Ind AS adopted Free Reserves. Hence, this cannot be used for declaration of dividend and issuance of bonus shares.

Conclusion

Summing up the entire discussion above, when a company is moving to Ind AS way of preparing Financial Statements, it may be required to recognize some assets and liabilities on its Balance Sheet and may be required to put other assets and liabilities off balance sheet. Also, some assets and liabilities may be required to be reclassified or re measured. This is brought about by adjusting the Retained Earnings. However, the question is whether such an Ind AS adjusted Retained Earnings be a part of net worth, free reserves and whether it can be used for issuing bonus shares and declaring dividend? The answer is based on the above discussion. Retained Earnings representing the adjustments arising out of restating the assets and liabilities at its fair value due to its first time Ind AS adoption shall be a part of Net Worth as the amount is attributable to the right valuation of assets and liabilities and not revaluation of the same. The adjustments arising out of first time Ind AS adoption reflected in Retained Earnings shall not be a part of Free Reserves as per definition of Companies Act. These adjustments cannot be considered as free reserves as they are unrealized in nature. Hence, it cannot be used for declaration of dividend and issuance of bonus shares. However, upon their subsequent disposal, the positive or negative surplus shall be realized in nature and then shall form part of Free Reserves.

9. Listed companies are governed by the SEBI and its Regulations and Guidelines. The DIP Guidelines in Chapter XIV deal with the issue of bonus shares by a company to which the DIP Guidelines are applicable.

Thus, a listed company cannot capitalize its revaluation reserves in view of SEBI Regulations/DIP Guidelines.

POSITION OF AN UNLISTED COMPANY

11. ICAI’S GUIDANCE NOTE ON AVAILABILITY OF REVALUATION RESERVE FOR ISSUE OF BONUS SHARES

1. In the recent past, a few private companies and closely-held public companies have resorted to the practice of utilizing the reserve created on revaluation of fixed assets for issue of bonus shares. This Guidance Note discusses the nature of revaluation reserves and in this context examines the question whether such reserves can be utilised for issue of bonus shares. It supplements the Guidance Note on Treatment of Reserve Created on revaluation of Fixed Assets, issued in 1982.

2. Revaluation of fixed assets is one of the issues dealt with in Accounting Standard (AS) 10 on ‘Accounting for Fixed Assets’, issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, which states, inter alia, as follows:

"13.1 Sometimes financial statements that are otherwise prepared on a historical cost basis include part or all of fixed assets at a valuation in substitution for historical costs...

13.2 A commonly accepted and preferred method of restating fixed assets is by appraisal, normally undertaken by competent valuers. Other methods sometimes used are indexation and reference to current prices which when applied are cross checked periodically by appraisal method."

3. AS-10 lays down as below:

"29. When a fixed asset is revalued upwards, any accumulated depreciation existing at the date of the revaluation should not be credited to the profit and loss statement.

30. A decrease in net book value arising on revaluation of fixed asset should be charged directly to the profit and loss statement except that to the extent that such a decrease is related to an increase which was previously recorded as, credit to revaluation reserve and which has not been subsequently reversed or utilised, it may be charged directly to that account."

4. It may be noted that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of a book adjustment only. Buy-back of Shares and Company Law

RAJESH DHAWAN

The author is MBA, Finance

In this write-up, the issue for consideration is buy-back of shares under Company Law. After citing relevant provisions, the author has highlighted the conditions for buy-back and prohibition for buy-back in certain circumstances.

INTRODUCTION

1. Not only statute, but also common law, has upheld the ‘sanctity’ of a company’s capital. In 1887, in Trevor v. Whitworth 12 App. Case 409, it was held that a company limited by shares may not purchase its own shares as this would amount to an unauthorized reduction of capital. The rationale for this decision is plain, namely, that the creditors of the company make decisions on its credit-worthiness on several grounds, but an important ground is the amount of its share capital. If the Courts had not established at an early stage that capital was ‘sacrosanct’ and could not be returned to shareholders at their whim, then share capital would not have been protected. Without this protection, creditors could find shareholders depleting share capital, with creditors left to carry all business risks.

RELEVANT PROVISIONS

2. In India, the rule in Trevor v. Whitworth was enshrined in section 77 of the Companies Act, 1956 which prohibited a company from buying or cancelling its own shares, unless it complied with the provisions and followed the procedure for reduction of share capital under sections 100 to 104 of the Companies Act, which involved confirmation by the Court.

However, section 77A of the Companies Act, which was inserted in the Companies Act by the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1999 with retrospective effect from October 31, 1998, is an exception to the prohibition under section 77 and section 100. Section 77A allows companies to buy-back their own shares as well as other specified securities.

Section 77(1) provides that a company limi-ted by shares or a company limited by guarantees having a share capital cannot buy its own shares, as it involves permanent reduction of capital without sanction of the Court.

However, the Companies (Amendment) Act, 1999, has introduced three new sections, viz., sections 77A, 77AA and 77B whereunder companies have been permitted to buy-back their shares or other securities subject to certain conditions. Besides, the SEBI has issued certain guidelines regulating these buy-backs. The provisions relating to buy-back as per the Amendment Act including SEBI guidelines in this regard are as follows :—

Section 77A, inserted by the (Amendment) Act, 1999, allows [subject to provision of section 77B(2)] a company to buy its own shares out of :—

(i) its free reserves; or

(ii) the security premium account; or

(iii) the proceeds of any share or other specified securities.

However, no buy-back of any kind of shares or other specified securities shall be made out of the proceeds of an earlier issue of the same kind of shares or same kind of other specified securities.

In case shares are bought back out of free reserves, then a sum equal to the nominal value of shares bought back shall be transferred to a reserve account to be called the capital redemption reserve account (section 77AA). The details of such transfer shall be disclosed in the balance sheet. The SEBI guidelines stipulate that this account shall be disclosed in the balance sheet. The SEBI guidelines stipulate that this account shall be allowed to be used for issue of fully paid bonus shares.

CONDITIONS FOR BUY-BACK

3. Following are the conditions for buy-back :—

A. Section 77A(2) provides that no company shall purchase its own shares or other specified securities unless :—

(a) the buy-back is authorised by its articles;

(b) a special resolution has been passed in general meeting of the company authorising the buy-back;

The Companies (Amendment) Act, 2001 (with effect from October 23, 2001) has authorised the buy-back by passing a resolution at a meeting of the board of directors, provided the buy-back does not exceed 10 per cent of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves of the company. However, there cannot be more than one such buy-back in any period of 365 days.

(c) the buy-back is less than 25 per cent of the total paid-up capital and free reserves of the company purchasing its own shares or other specified securities. However, the buy-back of equity shares in any financial year must not exceed 25 per cent of its paid up equity capital in that financial year;

Revaluation reserve balance in respect of asset disposed off/retired (proposed amendment to Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2))

3. Explanation 1 to section 115JB has been amended with effect from A.Y. 2013-14 to substitute the words "if any amount referred to in clauses (a) to (i) is debited to the profit and loss account, and as reduced by,—" with the words "(j) the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset, if any amount referred to in clauses (a) to (i) is debited to the profit and loss account or if any amount referred to in clause (j) is not credited to the profit and loss account, and as reduced by,—". Para 14.4 of (AS) 10 "Accounting for Fixed Assets" provides that "The amount standing in revaluation reserve following the retirement or disposal of an asset which relates to that asset may be transferred to general reserve". Since (AS) 10 permits companies to transfer "revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset", to general reserve, companies follow this treatment. The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2012 explains that as a result of this treatment permitted by (AS) 10 "the gains attributable to revaluation of the asset is not subject to MAT liability. It is, therefore, proposed to amend section 115JB to provide that the book profit for the purpose of section 115JB shall be increased by the amount standing in the revaluation reserve relating to the revalued asset which has been retired or disposed, if the same is not credited to the profit and loss account."

Thus, the impact of the proposed amendment is that revaluation increase will act be subject to MAT not in the year of revaluation but in the year of disposal/retirement of revalued asset.

Thus, if on disposal or retirement of a revalued asset, if the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset is not credited to profit and loss account but directly transferred to general reserve or any other reserve without routing it through P&L account or allowed to remain in Revaluation Reserve, the same must be added to net profit to arrive at the book profit. In view of the words "if the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset", the amendment would affect companies who have credited the increase on revaluation to revaluation reserve. It would not affect companies which credit increase on revaluation to capital reserve. Companies could credit revaluation increase to capital reserve only upto financial year 2010-11. With effect from financial year 2011-12, Revised Schedule VI is applicable which requires distinct disclosure of Revaluation Reserve implying that revaluation increase cannot be credited to Capital Reserve.

The above amendment has been made to overcome the decision in ITO v. Galaxy Saws (P.) Ltd. [2011] 13 taxmann.com 179 (Mum.) wherein it was held that no addition could be made to the net profit on account of revaluation reserve directly taken to the balance sheet while computing the book profit (even after revalued asset is sold off and the balance in revaluation reserve represents realized gains). In that case, the assessee, company had sold its premises for Rs. 96 lakhs. Book value of property was Rs. 3,30 lakhs (approx.). Assessee got property revalued and as per report of registered valuer, value of property was Rs. 97.44 lakhs. Gain in book value of property was taken by assessee to balance sheet as revaluation reserve. However, loss arising on sale, i.e., Rs. 1.44 lakhs (Rs. 97.44 lakhs minus Rs. 96 lakhs) was debited by assessee to profit and loss account. Assessing Officer rejected computation of book profit made by assessee based on revalued cost and added gain of Rs. 92.70 lakhs computed on basis of book value of asset originally shown. The ITAT held that since revaluation reserve had been directly taken to balance sheet and not debited to profit and loss account, it could not be added under clause (b) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2).

Gopal Nathani*

This short article will be of interest only to companies which are obliged to pay MAT under the provisions of section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The author has pointed out that the accounting treatment to certain items in the accounting standards is made flexible, so as to offer a choice to the companies to make accounting entries in the manner found suitable to the subject, and has in this context explained two illustrative situations - EDITOR

The Supreme Court ruling

1. The Supreme Court in Apollo Tyres Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 255 ITR 273/ 122 Taxman 562 held that the first and the foremost thing in the computation of the book profits is whether the account statements are drawn in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956.

The statutory requirement

2. Upon close reading of sub-section (2) of section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 it requires every company assessee to draw its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI of the Companies Act. The proviso to such sub-section (2) further requires that the accounting policies, the accounting standards and method and rates of depreciation adopted in the preparation of profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB must be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts as laid down before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act. Sub-section (2) reads as under :

"(2) Every assessee, being a company, shall, for the purposes of this section, prepare its profit and loss account for the relevant previous year in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided that while preparing the annual accounts including profit and loss account,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts including profit and loss account and laid before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with the provisions of section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided further that where the company has adopted or adopts the financial year under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), which is different from the previous year under this Act,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall correspond to the accounting policies, accounting standards and the method and rates for calculating the depreciation which have been adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account for such financial year or part of such financial year falling within the relevant previous year."

In other words nothing prevents a company to draw a separate profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB subject, however, to the fact that the accounting policy, accounting standards and the depreciation formula adopted is identical to the accounts prepared for AGM show. This is more so when the accounting period adopted by a company for the purposes of the Companies Act, is other than the financial year.

Requirements under accounting standards

3. Upon close reading of the accounting standards it can be found that the accounting treatment to certain items is made flexible. In other words companies have a choice to provide accounting entry in the manner found suitable to the subject.

The Pooling of Interests Method

4. Let us take an example of a company who has acquired the business of another company under an amalgamation scheme approved by the Court. Accounting Standard 14 has application in such cases. Under the Pooling of Interests Method the amalgamated company is required to disclose the assets and liabilities of the transferor company at their book values. Para 16/35 of AS-14 further requires the transferee-company to adjust the difference in the book value and the purchase consideration against the reserves. Para 35 reads as under :

"35. The difference between the amount recorded as share capital issued (plus any additional consideration in the form of cash or other assets) and the amount of share capital of the transferor-company should be adjusted in reserves."

Now the term ‘reserves’ have been further defined elsewhere in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI as including both capital and revenue reserves. Thus, para 35 provides a flexibility in the matter of adjustment of additional price paid either against capital reserves or general reserves including profit and loss account surplus.

regarded as a revaluation exercise, as already discussed. Hence, the adjustments arising out of Ind AS adoption in the first year of transition shall be part of net worth as it is not regarded as revaluation of assets. The same shall not hold true for any subsequent adjustments because whatever adjustments were required to be done during alignment of Financials with Ind AS have already been done in the first year itself. In the subsequent years, it shall be regarded as revaluation of assets.

Further Discussion on Net Worth Having adopted Ind AS, another pertinent question will be, whether gains/losses sitting in the "Other Comprehensive Income" will be regarded as a part of net worth. Here it may be noted that Ind AS 109 allows reporting entities allow some of the financial instruments to be fair valued through Other Comprehensive Income (OCI). Any changes in the fair value of these instruments are effected through OCI, which is carried to the Balance Sheet as Other Equity.

It may be noted that the definition of net worth allows inclusion of only such profits which flow from the Profit and Loss. Unrealized OCI do not form part of the profits/ losses earned/ incurred by the reporting entity in a particular as the OCI are shown separately in the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss. As per the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss, after the Profit earned by a reporting entity is arrived at, the same is added with the OCI during the year to show the Total Comprehensive Income of the reporting entity.

Therefore, just because the OCI is shown in the Statement of Profit and Loss does not mean that the same must be considered as Profits earned by the reporting entity. Hence, for the purpose of computation of net worth, OCI cannot be considered as a part of the net worth.

However, as per Ind AS 109, once the unrealized profits trapped in the form of OCI gets realized due to sale of financial asset or otherwise, it gets transferred from Equity to Profit and Loss. In such a situation, the same must be considered as a part of net worth.

Should the retained earnings be Considered Free Reserve?

Section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 defines Free Reserves:

"2(43) ?free reserves means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend: Provided that—

(i)

any amount representing unrealized gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise, or

(ii)

any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability recognized in equity, including surplus in profit and loss account on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value, shall not be treated as free reserves."

The definition of Free Reserves says that the reserves should be available for dividend distribution as per latest audited balance sheet. It specifically excludes notional or unrealized gains and gains on revaluation of assets. It also states that change in carrying amount of asset or liability recognized in equity and surplus in profit and loss account due to restatement of asset or liability at fair value shall not be included in free reserves.

The definition does not include the unrealized part of the gains. It also excludes the surplus arising on restatement of asset or liability fair value restatement. Hence, the retained earnings which is adjusted for any differences in fair value measurement of assets and liabilities during first time Ind AS adoption cannot be considered as free as these are not realized in nature. The definition of net worth does not distinguish between realized and unrealized gains but the definition of Free Reserves does. Hence although it is a part of Net Worth as explained above, it cannot be a part of free reserves as it excludes unrealized and notional gains.

Hence the amount transferred to Retained Earnings as adjustments during transition of Financial Statements from GAAP to IND AS cannot be considered as Free Reserves.

Use of the Free Reserves for issue of Bonus Shares and Declaration of Dividend

Free Reserves is of immense significance because it is used for the purpose of issue of bonus shares and declaration of dividend. With the changes brought in it post Ind AS adoption, its corresponding effect on bonus shares and dividend declaration is also required to be addressed. Introduction:

Reduction of share capital is a process by which a company decreases it's issued, subscribed, or paid-up share capital. This can be undertaken for various purposes, including restructuring, correcting an overcapitalized balance sheet, or returning excess funds to shareholders. Under the Companies Act, 2013, the reduction of share capital requires the approval of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) as per the provisions of the mentioned in the Act.

Legal Framework:

The reduction of share capital is governed by Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with The National Company Law Tribunal (Procedure for reduction of share capital of Company) Rules, 2016 which lays down the procedures, requirements, and conditions for reducing share capital.

Reasons for Reduction of Share Capital:

Reduction of share capital can be carried out for various reasons, including but not limited to:

1. Return of Excess Paid-up Capital:

When the company has surplus paid-up capital that is not being utilized, it can be returned to shareholders. This is beneficial as dividends are paid on paid-up capital, and retaining unnecessary capital increases the company's financial burden.

2. Cancellation of Uncalled Share Capital:

Share capital that has been issued but not called for payment can be cancelled to streamline the company's capital structure and reflect actual capital requirements. For example, partly paid shares can be made fully paid without calling for balance call money and accordingly reducing the face value of shares.

3. Cancellation of Unpaid Share Capital:

The unpaid portion of the share capital that shareholders are yet to pay can be cancelled to reduce liabilities and simplify financial accounts.

4. Adjustment for Capital Lost or Diminished:

When the company's assets lose value (reflected as a reduction in book value), the company can adjust its share capital by returning the reduced amount to shareholders. This aligns the share capital with the actual value of the company's assets.

Procedure for Reduction of Share Capital:

Board Meeting & Special Resolution

Board Approval: The Company's Board of Directors must approve the proposal to reduce share capital.

Special Resolution: A special resolution (approved by at least 75% of shareholders) must be passed at a general meeting to approve the reduction. The resolution should specify the method and extent of the reduction.

Filing of Application for Reduction of Share Capital with NCLT:

Form and Fee:

An application to the Tribunal for confirming a reduction of share capital must be made in Form RSC-1, along with the applicable fee as prescribed in the fee schedule i.e., Rs. 5000/-

Accompanying Documents:

CIT v. Caminco Binoni Zinc Ltd. [1993] 204 ITR 56 (Cal.), Co-operative Sugars Ltd. v. IAC [1993] 47 ITD 188 (Coch.). In all these cases involving substantial expenditure on replacement of parts of machinery like revamping of an old textile unit for improvement of business operations, which capitalised in books in some cases, it was held that the expenditure is allowable as deduction by way of current repairs. The items of equipment replaced under a modernisation scheme are of two types, the first category being of cases where the replacements do not result in adding to the existing production capacity but only result in increasing the efficiency and improving the profit-earning capacity, either by way of savings in fuel cost or improving the yield of the product, etc., and the other category being of cases where the replacements result in increase in capacity as well as efficiency. The cost of both these categories of items can be capitalised in the accounts in accordance with AS 10, while for tax purposes the expenditure on the former is allowed as deduction as current repair. It may be noted that according to the legal authorities, except in the case of a claim for deduction under section 37, in order to claim any expenditure as deduction under any of the sections 30 to 36 of the Act, it is not necessary that such expenditure should be of revenue nature, as there is no prohibition for allowing as deduction even capital expenditure, if it falls under any of the categories provided in those sections, as in the case under section 37. Examples are provided by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of India Cements Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 60 ITR 52 and decisions of several High Courts (interest on borrowings utilised for acquisition of an asset not put to use or for setting up a new project not commissioned). There are similar decisions in the case of current repairs - Hanuman Motor Service v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 88 , 91 (Mys.) and Nathmal Banketlal Parikh & Co. v. CIT [1980] 122 ITR 168 (AP)(FB). In the case of Madras Cements v. CIT [1990] 42 TTJ 175 , the Madras Bench of the Tribunal has held that the cost of replacement of an entire Cement Mill, out of several existing mills, is an allowable deduction as current repair. These two measures if utilised properly would go a long way in not only reducing taxable income to nil but also in providing a hedge against future tax liability, as in such cases there would be substantial loss for tax purposes in spite of there being substantial income in accounts.

DR. T.P. GHOSH

In this article, the author discusses the purpose and method of revaluation of certain fixed assets by various companies and the accounting practices followed in this regard Since the depreciation charge goes up on upward revaluation of the concerned assets, certain companies take a transfer from revaluation reserve to offset the increase in the depreciation charge and thereby inflate their profits. The author is critical of this practice. The main thrust of the article, however, pertains to the question of making a bonus issue out of revaluation reserve which is barred by the existing SEBI guidelines. The author sees no harm in allowing a bonus issue of shares to be made out of the revaluation reserve, as the profit on revaluation is real profit and not fictitious. The lifting of the ban will, obviously, also promote entrepreneurial freedom in decision-making - EDITOR

Purpose of revaluation

1. Accounting data are mostly generated using the historical cost valuation base. In an inflationary environment it is highly likely that the carrying amount of some fixed assets does not reflect their current costs. It is possible that some fixed value of assets has impaired and their current costs fall below the written historical costs. It is also possible that current costs of some fixed assets are much more than the written down historical costs. In both the situations net asset value of equity is not correctly reflected. Therefore, periodic revaluation of fixed assets is considered necessary to reflect the current value of fixed assets.

Presenting fixed assets at historical cost in an inflationary environment is a somewhat obscure practice. The historical cost balance sheet fails to reflect a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the reporting entity. Periodic revaluation of fixed assets to reflect their current value is not prohibited in the company law. In this article, we shall discuss only the issue of upward revaluation of fixed assets and treatment of revaluation profit.

Process of revaluation

2.1 Adjustment of increase in value - Revaluation is commonly done through an appraisal by competent valuers. Sometimes revaluation may be done by using the price index appropriate to the concerned fixed assets. Para 13.3 of Accounting Standard-10 (AS-10) states that the revalued amount of fixed assets is presented in the financial statements by restating the gross book value and accumulated depreciation. It is also recorded by estating the net book value adding therein the net increase on account of revaluation.

However, Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 requires that where sums have been added by writing up the assets, every balance sheet subsequent to such writing up shall show the increased figures with the date of the increase in place of the original cost. Each balance sheet for the first five years subsequent to the date of writing up shall also show the amount of increase made. For every fixed asset it is required to show (i) the original cost, (ii) additions thereto and deductions therefrom during the year, and (iii) depreciation written off or provided for up to the end of the year. Accordingly, as per company law additions to original cost by revaluation should be disclosed. It is not possible to adjust the increase in value with the net book value.

2.2 Selective revaluation - It is not judicious to revalue fixed assets selectively. This process may result in misleading valuation. It is then possible to revalue such assets wherein writing up results, ignoring such other assets where writing down becomes necessary.

Para 27 of AS-10 requires that when a fixed asset is revalued in financial statements, an entire class of assets should be revalued, or the selection of assets for revaluation should be made on a systematic basis.

2.3 Revaluation above the net recoverable amount -The net recoverable amount of a fixed asset indicates the maximum amount which can be fetched by disposal of that particular asset. As a prudential accounting policy it is suggested that upward revaluation should be restricted to the net recoverable amount.

Para 28 of AS-10 requires that the revaluation in financial statements of a class of assets should not result in the net book value of that class being greater than the recoverable amount of that class.

A comparison of revalued figure with the recoverable amount with reference to a class of fixed assets may result in excess revaluation profit (for a valuation above recoverable amount) against an individual asset falling within a class. This possibility should be avoided by requiring comparison of the revalued figure with the recoverable amount for each individually identifiable item of assets separately.

2.4 Revaluation profit - In case of upward revaluation of fixed assets, revaluation profit arises. Accumulated depreciation existing at the date of revaluation cannot be adjusted with such revaluation profit (Para 29). In Part I of Schedule VI it is required that the total depreciation written off should be shown.

The Revised Schedule VI has no Part III as it omits Parts III (definitions of 'reserve', 'provision', 'revenue reserve' and 'capital reserve') and Part IV ('Balance Sheet Abstract of Company's General Business Profile'). Therefore, section 115JB(2) required amendment by omission to 'Part III' of Schedule VI to bring it line with Revised Schedule VI. Further, proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act,1956 permits certain companies, e.g. insurance, banking or electricity company to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions specified in their regulatory Acts. Also, Courts and ITAT have held in a catena of decisions that since profit and loss account for MAT purposes is required by section 115JB(2) to be prepared as per Schedule VI, banks, electricity companies etc. which are exempt from Schedule VI are not liable to MAT. For instance, in Krung Thai Bank PCL v. Jt. DIT (International Taxation) [2011] 16 taxmann.com 239 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that the provisions of section 115JB can only come into play when the assessee is required to prepare its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act. The starting point of computation of MAT under section 115JB is the result shown by such a profit and loss account. In the case of banking companies, however, the provisions of Schedule VI are not applicable in view of exemption set out under proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act. The final accounts of the banking companies are required to be prepared in accordance with the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The provisions of section 115JB cannot thus be applied to the case of a banking company. In Kerala State Electricity Board v. Dy. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 118/[2011] 196 Taxman 1 (Ker.), the Kerala High Court held that section 115JB stipulates that the accounting policies, accounting standards, etc., shall be uniform, both for the purpose of income-tax as well as for the information statutorily required to be placed before the annual general meeting conducted, in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956. However, the assessee though was by definition a company under the Income-tax Act and deemed to be a company for the purpose of the Income-tax Act, by virtue of the declaration under section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act, it was not a company for the purpose of the Companies Act. Therefore, it was not obliged either to convene an annual general meeting or place its profit and loss account in such general meeting. As a matter of fact, a general meeting contemplated under section 166 of the Companies Act, 1956 was not possible in the case of the assessee, as there were no shareholders for the assessee-board. On the other hand, under section 69 of the Electricity Supply Act, the assessee was obliged to keep proper accounts, including the profit and loss account, and to prepare an annual statement of accounts, balance sheet, etc., in such form as had been prescribed by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Thus, it could be seen that coming to the maintenance of the accounts, the assessee, though was deemed to be a 'company' - both by virtue of operation of section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act for the purpose of Income-tax Act and by virtue of the definition of the expression 'company' under the Income-tax Act, yet it was required to keep and maintain its accounts in a manner specified by the Central Government, but not in the manner specified in the Companies Act. Therefore, MAT would not apply to electricity companies.

So, to bring section 115JB(2) in line with Companies Act,1956 and to overcome judicial pronouncements as above, the Finance Act, 2012 has substituted section 115JB(2) with effect from A.Y. 2013-14. Section 115JB(2) as substituted provides that companies which are not required under the proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the Schedule VI of the Companies Act, 1956, profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of their regulatory Acts shall be taken as a basis for computing the book profit under section 115JB and also omits reference to Part III of Schedule VI. It is submitted that since Revised Schedule VI is applicable from 1-4-2011, the amendment dropping reference to Part III of Schedule VI needs to be given retrospective effect from 1-4-2012(A.Y.2012-13). In this short article, the author examines the question as to whether deferred tax liability is covered as a permissible adjustment while determining book profits under section 115JB of the Income-tax Act. Analyzing the relevant provisions, as well as the relevant Accounting Standards and judicial views, the author concludes that deferred tax liability is ‘Outside the list of adjustments’ to be made in terms of the Explanation to section 115JB, while determining book profits - EDITOR

Introduction

1. In the determination of book profits under section 115JB, the starting figure is the net profit after tax as per profit and loss account. Such a profit is arrived at after providing for both current year tax and deferred tax liability. The current tax provision requires an adjustment though but whether deferred tax too needs to be added back for the purpose of computation of book profits is a point in issue.

The Supreme Court decision

2. In a recent decision dated 3-5-2002 in the case of Apollo Tyres Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 255 ITR 273/ 122 Taxman 562 , the Supreme Court held that the Assessing Officer has the limited power of making increases and reductions to such net profit as provided for in the Explanation to section 115J. Thus, the Assessing Officer does not have the jurisdiction to go behind the net profits shown in the profit and loss account except to the extent provided in the Explanation.

The permitted adjustments

3. Such Explanation provides for adjustment of the following sums if debited to the profit and loss account :—

(a)The amount of income-tax paid or payable, and the provision therefor; or

(b)The amounts carried to any reserves, by whatever name called other than a reserve specified under section 33AC; or

(c)The amount or amounts set aside to provisions made for meeting liabilities, other than ascertained liabilities; or

(d)The amount by way of provision for losses of subsidiary companies; or

(e)The amount or amounts of dividends paid or proposed; or

(f)The amount or amounts of expenditure relatable to any income to which section 10 or section 10A or section 10B or section 11 or section 12 apply.

Position qua deferred tax liability

4. Clause (a) above essentially refers to current tax liability. Clause (43) of section 2 also defines ‘tax’ meaning income-tax chargeable under the provisions of the Act. Even AS-22 defines such current tax as ‘the amount of income-tax determined to be payable in respect of taxable income for a period’ akin to the language used in such clause (a). Further, such clause has remained in its original form all through in the history of taxation on book profits since 1987. The statutory requirement for provision of deferred tax liability has however come into effect from 1-4-2001 and this certainly cannot assume the same treatment as applicable in the case of current tax or as part of income-tax payable under the Act as provided for in clause (a).

Position qua Accounting Standards (AS)

5. Further, AS-22 read such debit as a charge to the profit and loss account and not by way of amounts withdrawn for reserves requiring any adjustment as per clause (b) above. Also, AS-22 clearly mean that such liability is ascertainable and for this purpose also provide for the manner of determination of tax effect of timing difference (deferred tax), hence, such sum falls outside the purview of adjustment referred to in clause (c) as per supra. The remaining three clauses (d), ( e) and (f) have no application either.

Judicial views

6. Further, the Supreme Court in Harshad Shantilal Mehta v. Custodian [1998] 231 ITR 871/ 99 Taxman 216 held that tax, penalty and interest are different concepts under the Income-tax Act. The definition of ‘tax’ under section 2(43) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, does not include penalty or interest. In CIT v. Fertilisers & Chemicals Travancore Ltd. [2003] 126 Taxman 145, the Kerala High Court in the context of admissibility of deduction of interest on income-tax for the purpose of computation of book profits under section 115J held that the adjustment clause (a) in the Explanation only refers to income-tax paid or payable and that does not include interest.

It was argued on the Revenue's side that a conjoint reading of sub-clause (1) and sub-clause (2) of Section 92 of the Act indicates that what is sought to be taxed is the cost incurred in passing on the benefit to the holding company and not the share premium received. It was highlighted that the difference between the ALP and the price charged for the issue of shares was the benefit being passed on to VTSHL. The High Court held thus: "This manner of reading a provision by ignoring/rejecting certain words without any finding that in the absence of so rejecting, the provision would become unworkable, is certainly not the permitted mode of interpretation…This rejecting of words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible."

2.2-4 Applicability of Chapter X to Share Subscription - With respect to applicability of Transfer Pricing provisions to share subscription the High Court observed as under :

"The charge of Income now has to be found in Section 4 of the Act. If it is income chargeable to tax, under the normal provision of the Act, then alone Chapter X of the Act could be invoked ...the amount received on issue of shares is admittedly a capital account transaction not separately brought within the definition of income, except in cases covered under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act. Thus, such a capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception cannot be brought to tax"

Referring to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India10, it was held that arriving at the value of transaction on the basis of ALP would not convert non-income to income. Tax could be charged only on income and where income would not arise, the point of applying ALP to measure the value of the transaction itself would not arise.

The Hon'ble High Court further observed that the Parliament had consciously not brought to tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad. The High Court went on to hold that, although Section 56(1) of the Act would allow, under the head 'income from other sources', all income which is not otherwise excluded, it does not provide for charging to tax capital receipts in respect of issue of shares as it has been specifically provided for in Section 45 or Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act.

It further explained that while income is a flow, capital is a fund. The decision of the Privy Council in CIT v. Shaw Wallace & Co. Ltd.11 was referred to by the High Court to bring out this distinction, wherein it was observed thus:

"…income has been likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree or the crop of a field. It is essentially the produce of something which is often loosely spoken of as capital"

The High Court further rejected the contention that Chapter X was a complete Code by itself. It held thus:

"It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be found specifically mentioned in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act."

Relying on the Constitutional Bench's Judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vatika Township (P.) Ltd.12, the High Court held that there was no charge whether express or implied, in letter or in spirit, to tax the issue of shares at a premium. The High Court also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty13 to explain that the difference between charging provisions and computing provisions is qualitative in nature and computation provisions cannot substitute the charging provisions. In B.C. Srinivasa Shetty14, the transaction was not taxed as, even though there was a charging provision, yet the computation provision failed. The High Court concluded that the facts of the instant case were on a higher pedestal as there was no charging provision to tax issue of shares at premium to a non-resident, thus, there could be no occasion to invoke computational provisions.

HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Income tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Accrual of - Assessment year 1935-36 company ‘R’ had accumulated substantial reserve and resolved to capitalize it - It was also decided that capitalized fund would later on be distributed amongst shareholders as bonus share - Company ‘R’ purchased share of company ‘A’ - Later on; it resolved to reduce its capital by returning to shareholder share in company ‘A’, which was confirmed by District Court - Revenue held that whole transaction was illusory and share of company ‘A’ allotted to assessee shareholders had never become capital and it would represent profits of company ‘R’ which would be taxable in hands of assessee - Whether department was competent to go behind order of court confirming reduction of capital and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced of its share capital was release of profits - Held, No - Whether value of shares of company ‘A’ received by assessee was not liable to be included in his income - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was shareholder of a company ‘R’ which had substantial reserve, passed a resolution for capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds and the capitalized fund was to be distributed amongst the members of the company ‘R’ in effect as bonus shares. On the next day the company ‘R’ resolved to purchase shares in the company ‘A’ out of its capitalized reserve. Later on the company ‘R’ resolved to reduce its capital by returning to the shareholders the shares in the company ‘A’ and this resolution was confirmed by an order of the District Court. As a result of this resolution, certain shares in the Company A were allotted to the assessee. The view which the ITO took was that the whole transaction by the company ‘R’ for the increase and subsequent decrease of its capital and purchase and distribution of company ‘A’ shares was illusory, and that accordingly he could treat the company ‘A’ shares allotted to the assessee as never having become capital, but as their representing profits of the company ’R’. Both the Assistant Commissioner and commissioner agreed with the decision of the ITO

On reference:

HELD: As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced, - which was in the next year, - and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The ITO, when he said that the whole transaction was illusory, apparently meant that the real motive of the directors in putting forward those various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but the High Court could not go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders.

It was not competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the reduction of capital made by the District Court and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company ‘R’ for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital.

Therefore, the value of shares of the Company ‘A’ received by the assessee was not liable to be included in the assessee’s income.

Per Rangnekar, J. [Concurrent view]

It is perfectly competent to a joint stock company to convert its surplus profits into capital and give the benefit of such conversion to the shareholders in any manner, either by the issue of new shares as bonus shares or by the issue of debentures, or in cash there was no evidence before the Income-tax authorities that the various transactions, which resulted in the transfer of shares in the company A, to the assessee, were illusory. A company, however, is incapable of having any intention. The intention must be of the share-holders, who are the masters of the Company. But assuming that the motive of the Managing Agents of the Company and of the shareholders was to escape super-tax,-and that seemed to be the ground on which the opinion of the Income-tax authorities was based -, the consideration of such a question was entirely irrelevant and immaterial in construing the legal effect of the transfer of undivided profits to the shareholders by way of capital.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Coltman and Hathising for the Applicant.

In the case of CIT v. Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. [1978] 111 ITR 6 , the Bombay High Court has held that when bonus shares are issued as fully paid-up shares by capitalisation of a part of the amount standing to the credit of the general reserve, the capital, as computed in the manner provided by rule I of the Second Schedule, is not increased in any manner whatsoever. It was, thus, clear that so far as computation of capital was concerned, that had been correctly done by the AO by not taking into consideration the proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876.

As regards the new plea, the assessee’s argument, though attractive, was without any substance. The entries made in the books of account of the assessee had their importance and relevance and could not be wished away. As per the entries recorded in the balance sheet, general reserve as per such balance sheet came to Rs. 93,09,997. Out of this amount, a sum of Rs. 30 lakhs was reduced being utilised for issue of bonus shares; thus leaving a balance of Rs. 63,09,997. This was the position in books as on 15-10-1982. A sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was credited to the reserves account much later on 31-12-1982. So, on the face of it, it was not possible to accept the contention of the assessee that the withdrawal of the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs on account of bonus shares should be attributed to the profit earned during the year. The facts were clear that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had been utilised for the issue of bonus shares out of the brought forward balance of Rs. 93,09,997 in the general reserves account. This argument of the assessee, therefore, was not acceptable.

In the result, the conclusions of the Commissioner (Appeals) were upheld, and the assessee’s appeal was dismissed.

It was also pointed out that the amount of Rs. 60,73,092 had been transferred from the profit and loss account to the general reserve on 31-12-1982 whereas the bonus shares were declared much earlier on 15-10-1982. Our attention was also drawn to the entries made in the balance-sheet which were to the following effect:- It was, therefore, submitted that capital had been properly computed by the Assessing Officer and the first appellate authority had correctly agreed with him.

8. We have carefully considered the rival submissions as also the facts on record. The two authorities of Himachal Pradesh High Court and Bombay High Court are under the Super Profit Tax Act, 1963. The Bombay High Court in the case of Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd. ( supra) had an occasion to examine the provisions of rule 2 of the Second Schedule to the Super Profit Tax Act, 1963 and those of rule 3 of the Second Schedule to the Act, in Century Spg. & Mfg. Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) at page 17. It has been held that the provisions of the two Acts were materially different. On merits, the Bombay High Court has held that if during the course of previous year, a part of the amount standing to the credit of the general reserve is capitalised by issue of fully paid-tip bonus shares, it cannot be said that the capital of the company computed in accordance with rule I of the Second Schedule is increased by any amount of such issue of bonus shares. According to the High Court, what happens in such a case is that a part of the sum standing to the credit of one of the sub-items to be included in the computation of capital is during the previous year transferred to another item to be included in the computation of capital under rule I. Therefore, according to the High Court, when bonus shares are issued as fully paid-up shares by capitalization of a part of the amount standing to the credit of the general reserve, the capital, as computed in the manner provided by rule I of the Second Schedule is not increased in any manner whatsoever.

9. The Calcutta High Court in the case of Alkali & Chemical Corpn. of India Ltd. (supra) has also held that what is ultimately to be computed under Schedule II is the amount of capital and in the computation of the amount of capital the amount of reserve is a necessary item. According to the High Court while taking note of the increase of share capital by issue of bonus shares out of reserve, the corresponding decrease in the amount of reserves cannot be over-looked. It is further observed that it may be possible to take two views of the matter but an alternative view can only be taken by misleading the rules. The High Court has gone to the extent of saying that if in the computation of capital, a mistake has arisen by taking into consideration the capital and the bonus shares, that mistake is an arithmetical mistake and can be rectified.

10. From the foregoing discussion, it is clear that so far as the computation of capital under the Act is concerned, that has been correctly done by the Assessing Officer by not taking into consideration the proportionate capital of Rs. 6,32,876. The available authorities which are relevant to the controversy at hand are the authorities cited by the learned D.R. The other two authorities cited by the learned Counsel for the assessee are under the Super Profit Tax Act, 1963 whose provisions, as demonstrated by the Bombay High Court, were materially different from those of the Act. There is, therefore, no question of adopting a view favourable to the assessee because no such view in the form of a High Court judgment has been brought to our notice.

11. As regards the new plea, the argument of the learned Counsel for the assessee, though attractive, is without any substance. As rightly pointed out by the learned D. R, the entries made in the books of account of the assessee have their importance and relevance and cannot be wished away. As per the entries recorded in the balance-sheet, general reserve as per such balance-sheet came to Rs. 93,09,997. Out of this amount, a sum of Rs. 30 lacs was reduced being utilised for issue of bonus shares, thus leaving a balance of Rs. 63,09,997. This was the position in books as on 15-10-1982. A sum of Rs. 60,73,092 was credited to the reserves account much later on 31-12-1982. So on the face of it, it is not possible to accept the contention of the learned Counsel for the assessee that the withdrawal of an amount of Rs. 30 lacs on account of bonus shares should be attributed to the profit earned during the year. The facts are clear that the amount of Rs. 30 lacs has been utilised for issue of bonus shares out of the brought forward balance of Rs. 93,09,997 in the general reserves account. This argument of the assessee, therefore, fails.

12. Taking into consideration the entire facts and circumstances of the case, we uphold the conclusions of the learned CIT(A).

13. In the result, the appeal is dismissed.

Beaumont, CJ. :—This is a reference made by the Commissioner of Income-tax under section 66(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, XI of 1922. The real question is, whether a certain allotment of shares in the Arvind Mills Co., Ltd., which was made to the assessee as a shareholder in the Raipur Manufacturing Co., Ltd., represented income subject to tax, or represented capital.

The material facts are that in the year 1930, the Raipur Manufacturing Co., Ltd., (which I will refer to as "the Company") had very substantial reserve funds amounting to five times as much as its paid-up capital; and in February 1931, the Company passed a resolution that the capital of the Company be increased to Rs. 30 lakhs by the creation of 25,000 new shares of Rs. 100 each, ranking for dividend and in all other respects pari pasu with the existing shares in the Company. At the same time the articles were altered, in particular by giving power to apply the reserve funds for the issue of bonus shares. On the 23rd of June 1931, the Company passed a resolution capitalising the sum standing to the credit of the reserve funds amounting to Rs. 25 lakhs, and providing that the capitalised funds be distributed amongst the members of the Company in effect as bonus shares by allotting, five new shares in respect of each of the old shares held in the Company. On the 24th of June 1931, that is the next day, the Company resolved to purchase shares in the Arvind Mills Co. Ltd., out of its capitalised reserve. The Madras High Court has pointed out in Commissioner of Income-tax v. K. Srinivasan [1963] 50 ITR 788, to quote the placitum only:

But if rule 3 is read along with rules 1 and 2, the matter becomes clear. What is ultimately to be computed under Schedule II is the amount of capital and in the computation of the amount of capital the amount of reserve is a necessary item. While taking note of the increase of the share capital by issue of bonus shares out of reserves, the corresponding decrease in the amount of reserves cannot be overlooked. It may be possible to take two views of the matter but an alternative view can only be taken by misreading the rules. Heald J.—Up to the 2nd of June 1921 the Indo-Burma Petroleum Company had an authorised capital of one crore of rupees divided into one lakh of Rs. 100 shares of which 93,380 were issued. On the 18th of May 1921 the Company by special resolution resolved to increase its capital to two crores. That special resolution was confirmed on the 2nd of June 1921, so that thenceforward the authorised capital of the Company was two crores, of which nearly one crore was represented by shares already issued. On the 29th of June 1921 the Company by special resolution resolved to add to its Articles of Association a new article authorising a general meeting of the Company on the recommendation of the Directors to direct capitalisation of the whole or any part of the profits or reserve funds of the Company by the distribution of paid-up shares of the Company among the holders of the ordinary shares of the Company in proportion to the number or shares held by them and directing the Directors to apply such portion of the profits or reserve funds as may be required for the purpose of making payment in full at par for the shares of the Company so distributed. That resolution was confirmed on the 19th July 1921 and thereafter the Company had power to capitalize its profits or reserve funds by the distribution of shares among its shareholders. On the same date, the 19th of July 1921, the Company resolved to capitalize the sum of 31½ lakhs of rupees out of its reserve fund and to distribute that sum as a bonus free of income-tax amongst the holders of the ordinary shares in proportion to the ordinary shares held by them, and authorised the Directors to distribute amongst the holders of the ordinary shares 31,500 of the unissued Rs. 100 shares, credited as fully paid in the same proportion in satisfaction of such bonus. On the 10th of October 1921 by an exactly similar resolution the Company resolved to capitalize another 25 lakhs of the reserve fund and to distribute similarly another 25,000 of the unissued shares.

As a result of those resolutions Messrs. Steel Brothers & Company, Limited, received shares in satisfaction of bonus to the amount of Rs. 28¼ lakhs, and the question which we have to decide is whether or not those shares represented "income, profits or gains" within the meaning of those words in the Indian Income-tax Act (XI of 1922).

by section 2(6A)(d) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, took place during the year ending November 30, 1954, and not during the year ending November 30, 1955, and consequently there could be no reduction of the rebate under clause (i)(b) of the second proviso to paragraph D of Part II of the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956, read with Explanation (ii)to paragraph D. Now, clause (i)(b) of the second proviso to paragraph D of Part II of the First Schedule to the Finance Act, 1956, provides for reduction of the rebate allowable under clause (ii) of the preceding proviso by an amount computed at certain slab rates on the amount of dividends "in the case of a company referred to in clause (ii) of the preceding proviso which has distributed to its shareholders during the previous year dividends in excess of 6 per cent. of its paid-up capital not being dividends payable at a fixed rate", and the Explanation (ii) to paragraph D provides that for the purpose of paragraph D "the expression 'dividend' shall be deemed to include any distribution included in the expression 'dividend' as defined in clause (6A) of section 2 of the Indian Income-tax Act". Section 2(6A)(d) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, provides that "dividend" includes "any distribution by a company on the reduction of its capital to the extent to which the company possesses accumulated profits which arose after the end of the previous year ending next before the 1st day of April, 1933, whether such accumulated profits have been capitalised or not..."

Obviously, section 2(6A)(d) contemplates a distribution on reduction of capital under section 55(1)(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, under which subject to confirmation by the court, a limited company, if so authorised by its articles, may by special resolution reduce the share capital in any way, and in particular may "either with or without extinguishing or reducing liability on any of its shares, pay off any paid-up capital which is in excess of the wants of the company", and may, if and so far as is necessary, alter its memorandum by reducing the amount of its share capital and of its shares accordingly. Section 56 of the Act enables the company to apply to the court for an order confirming the reduction, and under section 60 of the Act, the court may make an order confirming the reduction on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. Upon compliance with certain formalities, the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies is required under section 61 of the Act to register the order and a minute approved by the court, and on such registration, and not before, the resolution for reducing share capital as confirmed by the order so registered shall take effect. Under section 62, the minute when registered shall be deemed to be substituted for the corresponding part of the memorandum of the company.

In the instant case, the issued, subscribed and paid-up capital of the company was Rs. 25 lakhs, consisting of 5 lakhs shares of Rs. 5 each. On December 16, 1953, the company passed a special resolution for reducing, its share capital from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 15 lakhs and for payment of Rs. 2 per share to the existing shareholders under section 55(1)(c) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913. On May 10, 1954, the company applied to the court for an order confirming the reduction. On August 6, 1954, the High Court made an order confirming the reduction. On November 4, 1954, the order and the minute approved by the court were duly registered with the Registrar, and on the same date, the Registrar issued a certificate of registration. On November 5, 1954, the notice of registration was duly published. On the same day, the company issued a circular notice to its shareholders stating that the refund of Rs. 2 per share will be made on receiving confirmation of the registration and requesting the shareholders to send their share certificates to the company at an early date for necessary endorsement and refund of share capital and stating that the refund would be made to the shareholders, whose names stood on November 15, 1954, in the books of the company, the share transfer register would remain closed from November 16 to November 30, 1954, and the refunds would be made to the shareholders whose names stood on November 15, 1954, in the books of the company. The balance-sheet for the year ending November 30, 1954, did not show the reduction, and the capital of the company in this balance-sheet was shown to be Rs. 25 lakhs. FACT: During the course of the previous year (on 31-7-1962), the assessee-company issued bonus shares to the amount equivalent to the paid-up capital. According to the revenue under rule 2 of the Second Schedule of the Act, the capitalised part of the reserve as a result of the issue of bonus shares was also to the proportionately added to the paid-up capital.

The Super Profits Tax Officer did not increase the total capital, as according to him the proportionate increase in paid up capital led to proportionate decrease in reserve. The failure on the part of the Super Profit Tax Officer to do so led to payment of more tax for which the assessee-company objected. The AAC dismissed appeal. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that it was incumbent upon the revenue to increase the paid-up capital due to the issue of bonus shares. As such there was proportionate increase in the total capital. The super profits for tax liability were held to decrease.

On reference :

HELD: It is evident as stated under condition (c ) of Rule 2 that the capital computed in accordance with rule 1 and nothing short of it was to be increased. The revenue authorities intended to reduce the reserve to the extent of the amount of bonus share which according to them was the amount added to paid-up share capital. They could not do so under the plain language used in rule 2. It is the "capital computed in accordance with rule 1" which is to be increased and nothing less than that. The capital would necessarily mean the sum total of the paid-up capital as well as the reserve. To this figure shall be added the proportionate increase in the paid-up share capital. From this enhanced capital, ‘standard deduction’ has to be made which is equal to six per cent of the total capital of the company.

The language used in rule 2 is explicit and the capital computed in accordance with rule 1 has to be increased by the proportionate increase in the paid-up share capital. This capital necessarily includes the reserve as it stood on the first day of the previous year. In other words the reserve could not be reduced to the extent of its capitalisation and if the reserve was computed as it was on the fist day of the previous year, the proportionate increase had to be made in the share capital leading to a benefit which according to the revenue authorities is under and which they preferred to submit as ‘double benefit’. The capitalised part of reserve was to be added to the share capital, while reserve was not to be reduced to that extent. By increasing the base capital the percentage of standard deduction was enhanced. This gave relief to the taxpayer. It was, therefore, held that the expression ‘paid-up capital’ occurring in the Act does include therein even such reserve as has been capitalised without corresponding decrease in the reserve as computed with reference to the first day of the previous year.

FACT: The assessee made a profit of Rs. 90,44,677 subject to the provisions for depreciation and taxation. After making provisions for there, balance of Rs. 5,08,637 was carried to the balance sheet. On 28-2-1946, the directors recommended that out of aforesaid sum Rs. 4,92, 426 should be distributed as a dividend and balance should be carried forward to next year's account. The recommendation was accepted by shareholders in their meeting on 3-4-1946 and dividend was distributed. Two contentions were raised on behalf of the assessee before the ITO, the first being whether the aforesaid sum could be called a "reserve" within the meaning of rule 2 (1) of the Rules in Schedule II and it should be included in its reserves while determining the capital on the 1-4-1946; the second that the proportionate profits of the assessee for three months, between the 1-1-1946, and the 1-4-1946, should also be included in the said reserves. The ITO rejected the contentions holding that a 'reserve' represents profits set apart for some specific or general purpose and, therefore, profits which had not been so set apart could not be treated as forming part of reserves for the purpose of inclusion in the capital. This order was confirmed on appeal by the AAC but was set aside by the Tribunal. The High Court, on reference, held that the amount of Rs. 5,08,637 was a part of the 'reserves' of the assessee-company as on 1-4-1946, within the meaning of rule 2 (1) and that the profits of the assessee-company from 1-1-1946 to 1-4-1946, should not be included in the said reserves as on 1-4-1946.

In accordance with the spirit of loyalty, which seems to pervade the office of (he Commissioner of Income-tax, the Assistant Commissioner agreed with the decision of the Income-tax Officer, and the Commissioner agreed with the decision of the Assistant Commissioner; and the question is whether the view of the Income-tax Officer is right. The real question, which arises, is whether these 16 shares in the Arvind Mills Co., are income, profits and gains liable to tax under section 4 of the Indian Income-tax Act, but the question is not raised in that form. The questions raised in effect ask whether the transaction, to which I have referred, was illusory, and whether there was any evidence to support the view of the Income-tax Officer to that effect. I have considerable doubt in understanding what is meant by these transactions being illusory. There is no doubt that the original resolution for the increase of capital was passed; it is net suggested that it was not passed by a requisite majority ; and as soon as it was passed, the capital of the Company was increased. As soon as the resolution was passed capitalising the reserves, such reserves became capital and could not afterwards be dealt with by the Company as income; and subsequently, when the capital was reduced,—which was in the next year,—and part of the proceeds of the capitalised reserves was handed back to the shareholders, that part could only be handed back, in the form in which it existed, namely, capital. The Income-tax-Officer, when he says the whole transaction was illusory, apparently means! that the real motive of the directors in putting forward these various resolutions, and of the shareholders in passing them, was not to increase the capital for any commercial purposes of the Company, but to increase the capital in order that the subsequent distribution among the shareholders of the reserve funds might be in the form of capital and not of income; but this Court cannot go into the question of what was at the back of the mind of the directors or the shareholders. Similar questions have arisen under the English Act in Blott's case 8 Tax Cas. 101, and in Fisher's case 10 Tax Cas. 302,—both recent decisions of the House of Lords—, in which it has been definitely established that the principle originally laid down by the House of Lords in Bouch v. Sproule [1887] 12 App. Cas. 385 applies to revenue cases. That principle is that a company has power to declare and determine as against the whole world, whether accumulated reserves shall be treated as capital or income, and if the company determines that they are capital, then they are capital. At the time when the reference was made, there might possibly have been a question whether the principle of these cases applied in India, but that question has definitely been decided in the affirmative by the Privy Council in Commissioner of Income-tax, Bengal v. Mercantile Bank of India, Limited 10 ITC 39. It seems to be that the case cuts from under the Commissioner the only ground on which he might have taken a stand in this reference.

In my opinion, the question raised must be answered as follows : The first question is :

"Whether there is any legal evidence to support the observations of the Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, in Appeal No. A/193 of 1934-35 that the procedure and the proceedings taken by the Company for increase of capital and for reduction of capital were illusory and were not genuine."

That must be answered in the negative.

The second question is :

"Whether it is competent to the Income-tax authorities to treat as illusory and ungenuine the capitalization of the Reserve Fund and the Machinery Renewal Fund in the share capital of the Company and the reduction of capital determined by appropriate and legal steps taken by the Company."

That must also be answered in the negative.

The third question is :

"Whether in law it is competent to the Income-tax authorities to go behind the order confirming the redaction of capital made by the District Court at Ahmedabad, viz., the Order dated the 24th day of June 1933 and to hold that what was sought to be released and reduced by the Resolution passed by the Company for reduction of its Share Capital was release of profits and not Share Capital?"

That must again be answered in the negative.

The fourth question is :

"Whether in law the 16 shares of the Arvind Mills Limited received by the Petitioner (the assessee) are liable to be included in the petitioner’s (the assessee’s income for the year 1933."

That again must be answered in the negative.
