[1996] 7 SCL 6 (MAG.)

Treatment of Revaluation Reserve : Question of issuing Bonus Shares out of it

DR. T.P. GHOSH

In this article, the author discusses the purpose and method of revaluation of certain fixed assets by various companies and the accounting practices followed in this regard Since the depreciation charge goes up on upward revaluation of the concerned assets, certain companies take a transfer from revaluation reserve to offset the increase in the depreciation charge and thereby inflate their profits. The author is critical of this practice. The main thrust of the article, however, pertains to the question of making a bonus issue out of revaluation reserve which is barred by the existing SEBI guidelines. The author sees no harm in allowing a bonus issue of shares to be made out of the revaluation reserve, as the profit on revaluation is real profit and not fictitious. The lifting of the ban will, obviously, also promote entrepreneurial freedom in decision-making - EDITOR

Purpose of revaluation

1. Accounting data are mostly generated using the historical cost valuation base. In an inflationary environment it is highly likely that the carrying amount of some fixed assets does not reflect their current costs. It is possible that some fixed value of assets has impaired and their current costs fall below the written historical costs. It is also possible that current costs of some fixed assets are much more than the written down historical costs. In both the situations net asset value of equity is not correctly reflected. Therefore, periodic revaluation of fixed assets is considered necessary to reflect the current value of fixed assets.

Presenting fixed assets at historical cost in an inflationary environment is a somewhat obscure practice. The historical cost balance sheet fails to reflect a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the reporting entity. Periodic revaluation of fixed assets to reflect their current value is not prohibited in the company law. In this article, we shall discuss only the issue of upward revaluation of fixed assets and treatment of revaluation profit.

Process of revaluation

2.1 Adjustment of increase in value - Revaluation is commonly done through an appraisal by competent valuers. Sometimes revaluation may be done by using the price index appropriate to the concerned fixed assets. Para 13.3 of Accounting Standard-10 (AS-10) states that the revalued amount of fixed assets is presented in the financial statements by restating the gross book value and accumulated depreciation. It is also recorded by estating the net book value adding therein the net increase on account of revaluation.

However, Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 requires that where sums have been added by writing up the assets, every balance sheet subsequent to such writing up shall show the increased figures with the date of the increase in place of the original cost. Each balance sheet for the first five years subsequent to the date of writing up shall also show the amount of increase made. For every fixed asset it is required to show (i) the original cost, (ii) additions thereto and deductions therefrom during the year, and (iii) depreciation written off or provided for up to the end of the year. Accordingly, as per company law additions to original cost by revaluation should be disclosed. It is not possible to adjust the increase in value with the net book value.

2.2 Selective revaluation - It is not judicious to revalue fixed assets selectively. This process may result in misleading valuation. It is then possible to revalue such assets wherein writing up results, ignoring such other assets where writing down becomes necessary.

Para 27 of AS-10 requires that when a fixed asset is revalued in financial statements, an entire class of assets should be revalued, or the selection of assets for revaluation should be made on a systematic basis.

2.3 Revaluation above the net recoverable amount -The net recoverable amount of a fixed asset indicates the maximum amount which can be fetched by disposal of that particular asset. As a prudential accounting policy it is suggested that upward revaluation should be restricted to the net recoverable amount.

Para 28 of AS-10 requires that the revaluation in financial statements of a class of assets should not result in the net book value of that class being greater than the recoverable amount of that class.

A comparison of revalued figure with the recoverable amount with reference to a class of fixed assets may result in excess revaluation profit (for a valuation above recoverable amount) against an individual asset falling within a class. This possibility should be avoided by requiring comparison of the revalued figure with the recoverable amount for each individually identifiable item of assets separately.

Accumulated depreciation existing at the date of revaluation cannot be adjusted with such revaluation profit (Para 29). Having regard to the aforesaid reasons, deduction was liable to be made for ascertaining accumulated profits.

As regards the issue of levy of capital gains, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held against levy of capital gains without discussing facts and issues involved and without indicating reasons in support of his finding in the impugned order.

The basic issue for the purposes of levy of capital gains is whether reduction of share capital by a company results in extinguishment of rights in shares held by shareholders covered by the expression ‘transfer’ as defined in section 2(47). When a company reduces its share capital by paying off a part of the capital thereby reducing the face value of the shares, the share remains but the right of the shareholder to dividend of his share capital and the right to share is extinguished proportionately to the extent of reduction in capital. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer had no occasion to consider the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45 as a result of reduction of share capital since he came to the conclusion that accumulated profits possessed by the company exceeded the distribution made to the shareholders on reduction of share capital. While reversing the conclusion of the Assessing Officer and deleting the addition on account of dividend under section 2(22)(a) the Commissioner (Appeals) did not apply his mind to the issue of levy of capital gains under section 45, particularly since the distribution made by the company on reduction of share capital had been treated as transfer by the Supreme Court in the various decisions. In the circumstances the issue of levy of capital gains was set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with the direction that the issue of levy of capital gains might be re-examined by him.

When a company prospers and earns profits, it may do one of the two things with the profits; it may either distribute the profits by way of dividend among the shareholders or accumulate them. Ordinarily, these undistributed profits are employed in the business either in acquisition of fixed assets or as working capital and really represent an increase in the capital employed in the business. When these increase to a considerable extent, the issued capital of the company ceases to bear a true relation to the real capital employed in the business. The company may, in such a case, decide to bring its issued capital into a true relationship with the capital actually employed in the business and may for that purpose capitalise its accumulated profits and issue fully paid-up shares or debentures, of a nominal value equal to the amount capitalised to its shareholders. These new shares or debentures are called as bonus shares or bonus debentures. They are not a gift from the company. They are not issued gratuitously. Their nominal value is paid in full from the capitalized profits or reserves of the company, which could otherwise have been distributed to the shareholders. [Para 14]

12. Cognizant liable to pay DDT on its Rs. 19,000 crores buyback: ITAT [Cognizant Technology Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. Asst. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 309 (Chennai - Trib.)]

The assessee (Cognizant Technology) had purchased its own shares from non-resident shareholders in a 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of provisions of Section 391-393 of the Companies Act, 1956.

In accordance with the scheme, the assessee purchased 94,00,534 equity shares from its shareholder at the price of Rs. 20,297 per share and paid a total consideration of Rs. 19,080.26 crores.

The share capital of the assessee company was held by four non-resident shareholders, out of which three shareholders are residents of the USA, and one shareholder is a tax resident of Mauritius. The net effect of the scheme was that post-sanction of the scheme, the only shareholder left was Cognizant Mauritius Ltd.

The AO held that consideration paid by the assessee to its shareholders for the purchase of its own shares was liable to tax as deemed dividend under Section 2(22)(d). Consequently, the assessee was liable to pay Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) under Section 115-O.

On the other hand, the assessee submits that the 'Scheme of Arrangement & Compromise' was sanctioned by the High Court of Madras in terms of Sections 391 to 393 of the Companies Act, 1956. It cannot be considered as a buyback of shares in terms of provisions of Section 77A or a reduction of capital in terms of Sections 100-104/402 of the Companies Act, 1956.

On appeal, the CIT(A) upheld the findings of AO. The matter reached before the tribunal.

The tribunal held as follows:

Two essential prerequisites must be satisfied to come within the ambit of Section 2(22)(d). First, there must be a distribution to the shareholders on the reduction of the capital, and second, it must be to the extent that the company possess accumulated profits. In the present case, it was evident from the audited financial statement that the share capital has been reduced by around Rs. 9.4 crores, which is equivalent to 54.70% of the total paid-up share capital. The Supreme Court, in CIT v. G. Narasihan 236 ITR 327, has clarified that Section 2(22)(d) is automatically attracted once these parameters are satisfied. Further, Clause 7 of the scheme clarifies that the distribution of money will be out of the general reserves and accumulated credit balance in the profit and loss account. Thus, both conditions are satisfied to treat the transaction within Section 2(22)(d).

The assessee also argued that the scheme of purchase of own shares was made through offer and acceptance. This involves an element of quid pro quo, and thus, there was no 'distribution of the purpose of section 2(22)(d). The tribunal held that the definition of 'distribution' does not contain any aspect of quid pro quo or lack thereof. The prerequisites for distribution are that there must be payment, and the disbursal must be made to more than one person. Section 2(22)(d) does not distinguish whether the reduction of share capital is the intended result of the resultant consequence of the scheme.

The assessee's transaction would either fall under Section 391-393 r.w. Section 77 and Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 or Sections 391-393 r.w Section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956. The scheme clearly states that it is not a buyback under Section 77A. Therefore, once the assessee states it is not buyback under section 77A, it should automatically fall back to Section 77 r.w Sections 100-104 of the Companies Act, 1956. If said sections are applied, then said transaction was nothing but the reduction of capital and distribution of accumulated profits.

The assessee also contended that Section 115QA was amended in 2016, and the present transaction would only be taxable per the amended provisions. The assessee's arguments were not accepted for two reasons. Firstly, there is a distinction between the purchase of own shares upon reduction of share capital and buyback. Buyback is a term used only with respect to transactions covered under Section 77A. If all conditions of Section 115-O r.w Section 2(22) are satisfied, the same cannot be impliedly excluded based on the amendment to Section 115QA.

Any interest tax. 1.9-2 Reserves adjustment under Explanation (b)/(i) - One of the adjustments required to be made relates to amounts carried to any reserve by whatever name called. The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

1.9-2a RESERVES ADJUSTMENT UNDER EXPLANATION (i) - Explanation (i) requires reduction of amount withdrawn from any reserve or provision, if it is credited to profit and loss account.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a)of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

Issuing bonus shares out of revaluation reserve 6.1 Existing prohibition - Section M of the SEBI Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection does not allow issue of bonus shares out of the Revaluation reserve. This prohibition is applicable to listed companies. The Department of Company Affairs vide its Circular No. 9/94 (Circular Letter No. 17/32/93 - CL V dated September 6,1994) has also prohibited issue of bonus shares out of revaluation reserve by the existing private/ closely-held and unlisted companies.

The Guidance note on availability of revaluation reserve for issue of bonus shares issued by the ICAI (Published in November 1994 issue of the Chartered Accountant) argues that the excess of the revalued amount over the net book value of fixed assets, which is credited to revaluation reserve, is created as a result of book adjustment only. The revaluation reserve does not result from an arm's length transaction; it represents an expert's perception of value. The revaluation reserve thus does not represent realised gain.

The ICAI Guidance Note also states that share capital represents money or money's worth received from the owners and capitalisation of earned profits or other gains arising out of arm's length transactions. It is a cardinal principle that only such profits as are earned or the relevant capital receipts (e.g. share premium) as are realised, can be capitalised.

6.2 Expert's value perception - So long as the expert's perception of the fair value of a fixed asset is judicious, there is nothing wrong in depending on such valuation, in case the upper limit of revaluation is restricted to the net recoverable amount. Substitution of historical cost becomes necessary when it materially differs from the fair value of the fixed assets. A going concern may not think of disposing of a particular asset, still the increase in value of the asset, although unrealised, cannot be denied. Since the revaluation reserve forms part of the shareholders' funds, it should be treated as a free reserve.

6.3 Arm's length transactions and business income -The concept of arm's length relationship is altogether irrelevant in this context. The reported net profit of an entity is not necessarily the result of arm's length transactions. Also it is not necessary for the purpose of a bonus issue to consider to what extent the accumulated surplus of the entity has resulted from arm's length transactions.

6.4 Unrealised gain - Of course, the revaluation reserve represents unrealised gain. But it represents real gain and cannot be treated as a fictitious gain. Accordingly, the shareholders should not be denied the right to utilise any such real gain in the manner they want. It is not unknown to the shareholders that such a bonus issue, if any, results from unrealised gain.

6.5 Accounting effect of bonus issue - Presently, many companies take a transfer from the revaluation reserve to the extent of additional depreciation. To that extent profit is inflated every year and the revaluation reserve is converted into the so called 'earned profit'. It is just a matter of time to convert revaluation reserve into 'earned profit' and as soon as the conversion is complete there is no bar on utilising such 'earned profit' for issuing bonus shares.

In case the revaluation reserve is utilised for a bonus issue, the company would have no choice but to charge additional depreciation out of profit.

6.6 Corporate freedom - One of the basic tenets of economic liberalisation is reduction/elimination of bureaucratic interference on the activities of private entrepreneurs. Corporate management should be given freedom to adopt a suitable financial management policy. A bonus issue out of the revaluation reserve will not generally be supported by increase in the earning capacity. However, the management will not find difficulty in maintaining the dividend rate in real terms. A decline in post-equity pricewill have no effect in real terms, since this book adjustment has no effect on the earnings of the entity.

1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2) no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

Reduction of share capital offers significant benefits to companies, such as improving financial ratios, returning surplus funds to shareholders, and aligning the company's capital base with its actual requirements. It can also help increase shareholder value by improving earnings per share (EPS).

Future Outlook:

(b) out of money provided by the Central Government or a State Government for the payment of dividend by the company in pursuance of a guarantee given by that Government: Provided that a company may, before the declaration of any dividend in any financial year, transfer such percentage of its profits for that financial year as it may consider appropriate to the reserves of the company:

Provided further that where, owing to inadequacy or absence of profits in any financial year, any company proposes to declare dividend out of the accumulated profits earned by it in previous years and transferred by the company to the reserves, such declaration of dividend shall not be made except in accordance with such rules as may be prescribed in this behalf: Provided also that no dividend shall be declared or paid by a company from its reserves other than free reserves."

As is clearly provided in the Companies Act 2013, regarding issuance of bonus shares and declaration of dividend, only Free Reserves can be utilized. Drawing from the discussion above, the adjustments arising due to transition of assets and liabilities from GAAP to Ind AS cannot be part of first time Ind AS adopted Free Reserves. Hence, this cannot be used for declaration of dividend and issuance of bonus shares.

Conclusion

Summing up the entire discussion above, when a company is moving to Ind AS way of preparing Financial Statements, it may be required to recognize some assets and liabilities on its Balance Sheet and may be required to put other assets and liabilities off balance sheet. Also, some assets and liabilities may be required to be reclassified or re measured. This is brought about by adjusting the Retained Earnings. However, the question is whether such an Ind AS adjusted Retained Earnings be a part of net worth, free reserves and whether it can be used for issuing bonus shares and declaring dividend? The answer is based on the above discussion. Retained Earnings representing the adjustments arising out of restating the assets and liabilities at its fair value due to its first time Ind AS adoption shall be a part of Net Worth as the amount is attributable to the right valuation of assets and liabilities and not revaluation of the same. The adjustments arising out of first time Ind AS adoption reflected in Retained Earnings shall not be a part of Free Reserves as per definition of Companies Act. These adjustments cannot be considered as free reserves as they are unrealized in nature. Hence, it cannot be used for declaration of dividend and issuance of bonus shares. However, upon their subsequent disposal, the positive or negative surplus shall be realized in nature and then shall form part of Free Reserves.

If the liabilities that accrued from year to year had been taken into account year by year and the accumulated profits had been depleted year by year by writing down the accumulated profits and only the balance carried over, the total of the accumulated profits in any given year will be less than in cases where there has been no deduction made for accrued liabilities. Section 2(22)(e) does not in terms provide that what has been deemed as dividend should be deemed to have come from accumulated profits. But in section 2(22)(e) there is an indication that the deemed dividend is not unconnected with the accumulated profits. In fact, there is a clear provision that the deeming provision will attach only to that part of the amount paid which is represented by the accumulated profits of the company. When this provision is read with the language of the section which provides for deduction of tax on such dividend and also read with the statutory restriction of payment of dividend out of the capital assets, it is reasonable to come to the conclusion that a dividend would and should come out of the accumulated profits. The advances in question must, therefore, be taken as having come out of the profits of the previous year and since it has not been contended or established that there had been deductions made from accumulated profits in the past when dividend was issued or loans made the same had to be deducted from the accumulated profits. Even deemed dividend under the Act, cannot be paid out of the capital and once the law is such that certain payments must be deemed to be payments of dividend, for all purposes it has to be treated as dividend and the restriction that the payment of dividend should not be from capital will attach to such payment as well. Therefore, Tribunal was right in directing the advances being the deemed dividends assessed in the hand of the various shareholders in the past assessment years, should be deducted from the surplus while determining the ‘accumulated profits’ in the hands of the company.

As regards the question of capital gains, there is a particular procedure prescribed by the 1956 Act for reduction of capital. If that procedure is gone through, there can be reduction of capital. In reduction of capital, there need not necessarily be a reduction in the number of shares held by the company. In the instant case too, there had been no such reduction in the number of shares. What had happened was only to reduce the face value of the shares. Consequent upon the reduction of the capital, the company deemed it fit to distribute some assets and some money to the shareholder. That naturally happens in all such cases of reduction for it may be found that it was not necessary to keep all the assets of the company and that it can be distributed to the shareholders. There may be other objects also in such reduction of capital. Perhaps it is to minimise the possibility of such distribution of amounts that the deeming provision in section 2(22)(d ) had been introduced by the statute by insisting that on such assets being distributed, tax should be paid deeming such assets as dividends issued by the company. A shareholder can transfer a share. He can also surrender the share to the company and when surrendering the share, there may be relinquishment of the share. There can also be cancellation of the shares. Apart from that, there can be no transactions vis-a-vis the company and the shareholders as regards the shares held by a shareholder. The shares as such are held by the shareholders and the only provision in the Companies Act which would have any representations between the company and the shareholder would be in the circumstances of surrender and cancellation of shares. There had been no surrender or cancellation of shares in the company. It could not be said that there had been any exchange on reduction of the shares or any part of the value of the shares. The shareholder had not transferred anything to the company. Therefore, section 45 was not attracted. All the rights of the shareholder as a shareholder in the company still remained. He continued to hold the same number of shares. Whether, on liquidation, he would get the amount which he would have received had a liquidation taken place at the time of the reduction of capital could not touch the question as to whether by the reduction of capital there had been any extinguishment. It was conceivable that he would receive less in the event of the winding up of the company after reduction of capital in view of the fact that there had been distribution of assets. But on the possibility of the company not prospering and not augmenting its assets, it is not possible to come to any conclusion that there had been any extinguishment of the rights of the shareholder. The shareholder's right to receive the assets of the company, can arise only in the event of winding up of the company and on liquidation taking effect. That event not having taken place, it could not postulate any extinguishment. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in holding that no capital gain was assessable in the hands of the assessee as there was no extinguishments of any right of the assessee and consequently there was no transfer within the meaning of section 2(47) by the assessee of any capital assets for the relevant assessment year.

, looking again at the provisos, there was no justification for coming to the conclusion, which the Tribunal did, in saying that clause (ii) of the proviso applied only to an Indian company but clause (iii) applied only to foreign companies which had not provided for declaration of dividends in Indian and to Indian companies in which public were not substantially interested. Therefore, that the distinction between foreign and Indian companies intended to be drawn by the Tribunal was not justified on a reading of these provisos. Thirdly, proviso (i)( a) makes it clear that the rebate shall be allowed in the case of a company which satisfies the condition that it must have ‘made the prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment within India of the dividends payable out of such profits and for the deduction of the super-tax from the dividends in accordance with section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The words ‘prescribed arrangements’ could only mean arrangements prescribed either by the Act or the rules made thereunder or by the Companies Act or the rules made thereunder or under the articles of the company. Such prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends could not mean notional or deemed dividends such as were contemplated in section 23A section 18(3D) is not also concerned with deemed or notional dividends but with deducting super-tax on the amount of the dividend as increased in accordance with section 16(2). The two parts of proviso (i)(a ) are clearly separate, namely, the part that makes for ‘prescribed arrangements for the declaration and payment of dividends payable out of such profits’ on the one hand and the part ‘for the deduction of super-tax on dividends in accordance with the provision of section 18(3D) of the Income-tax Act’. The first part cannot include deemed or notional dividends at all. As the language clearly says, it means dividend which has been declared and paid by the prescribed arrangements. The second part under section 18(3D) may include consideration of deemed dividend as the section itself provides. In order to succeed, therefore, the revenue had to establish in the instant case that the dividend taken to be dividend in this case was a dividend according to prescribed arrangements within the meaning of proviso (i)(a ) of Paragraph D of the Finance Act. On the facts the revenue could not do this in the instant case. Therefore, the contention of the revenue to come within clause (a) of proviso (i) could not succeed. No doubt, the ITO, had tried to describe as accumulated profit a certain figure, manifestly under a misconception because he tried to include contingency reserve, accumulated balance under the profit and loss account and provision for income-tax which could by no means be considered as accumulated profits of the company. Even profits from the sale of machinery could not be said to be accumulated profits without something more and mere appreciation of the original value of the machinery will not bring it within the expression ‘accumulated profits of the company’. Accumulation of profits is a deliberate act and implies a conscious volition to accumulate the profits. It is well known that reduction of share capital can be effected in company law by various methods, particularly classified as (i) with sanction of the court, and (ii) without such sanction. Forfeiture or surrender of shares of cancellation of unissued shares are examples of reduction of share capital for which sanction of the court is not necessary. In other cases, where the company wants to reduce its share capital, it can do so after obtaining sanction of the court. Section 2(6A) did not expressly mention or even impliedly include the concept of deemed dividend. The express section dealing with deemed dividend, and specially with super-tax on such deemed dividend, is section 23A. Explanation (ii ) of Paragraph D of Part II of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, expressly says that the expression ‘dividend’ shall be deemed to include any distribution included in the expression ‘dividend’ as defined in clause (6A) of section 2. In the instant case, the reduction of share capital had not produced or had not been shown to have produced on any evidence an income by way of ‘dividend’ as contended by the revenue, according to the extended connotation of the word ‘dividend’. Before the Tribunal came to any finding of following rebate on super-tax, it had to be satisfied that the super tax was leviable on the total income of the company under Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, because it was only in that event that the question of rebates on that super tax could arise. This primary condition, had not been satisfied in the instant case and, therefore, the Tribunal was not right in holding that any rebate of super-tax was allowable in the sense that no super-tax itself was leviable on the reduction of share capital which occurred in the facts and circumstances of the case. As the first condition had not been satisfied the consequential question of allowing rebate on super tax really did not arise. Further, this reduction of share capital had not produced an income on which a super-tax could be attached nor was it a dividend within the meaning of the Act or Paragraph D of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. Further there was no evidence to hold that this reduction of share capital in the particular case meant any return of ‘accumulated profits’

How an assessee chose to treat a particular item of profit either as capital or as trading receipt could not obviously conclude the question, and so mere inclusion in the head of the capital profit account with nothing more could not, in the circumstances of this case, be proof of appropriation for any specific purpose. Specific evidence as to the nature of this particular fund shown, as the capital profit account was not furnished except what appeared exfacie the account. A portion of the profits of the company was taken over to the capital profit account only to be available for deferred distribution of dividends to shareholders. If that be the real position of the capital profit account, it would only mean portion of the profits were kept undistributed, and merely because they were included in separated head of account they were not taken out of what was called "amorphous and undistributed profits", profits available for further distribution. In this case distribution was deferred, and that by itself with nothing more could make the amount so set apart a reserve within the meaning of rule 2.

Therefore, the assessee’s claim that whatever was found in the capital profit account, whether that claim was based upon what was credited or upon what was retained as balance at the end of the relevant period, was a reserve within the meaning of rule 2 will have to be negatived.

The nature of the fund included under the head, "excess profits tax post-war refund suspense account", is to be gathered with reference to sections 39 and 40 of the Finance (No.2) Act, of 1945 of the United Kingdom.

Thus the position was that whatever was given as a refund of excess profits tax in the United Kingdom was available only for use for a limited purpose, and the assessee was under a statutory liability to utilise this amount only for those purposes. Therefore, when the amount was refunded, it was shown under a separate head of account as excess profits tax post-war refund suspense account. It meant the amount was held in reserve, but in suspense, to be utilised for the statutory purposes as directed by section 40 of the English Finance Act of 1945. Therefore, the very inclusion of this amount under this head of account would be proof of an appropriation for a specified purpose, the purpose specified being statutory, but none the less a purpose specified. When that purpose specified was further authorized by the shareholders, the fact that they were under statutory liability to do so did not make the authority of the shareholders any the less effective. Thus the requirements were satisfied to constitute the fund a reserve within the meaning of rule 2, and for the assessee to claim abatement with reference to that amount.

The assessee was entitled to claim a relief of abatement with reference to this sum with reference to the third and the fourth chargeable accounting periods, that is 1-4-1947 to 30-6-1947, and 1-7-1947 to 30-6-1948. The rest of the claim which the Tribunal allowed would have to stand disallowed, and the other sums would have to be brought to tax.

The statutory language is clear that amounts specified in clauses (a) to (i) are to be added only if they are debited to the statement of profit and loss. Explanation 1 explicitly states that ''if any amount referred to in clauses (a) to (i) is debited to the statement of profit and loss or if any amount referred to in clause (j) is not credited to the statement of profit and loss, then such amount shall be added or reduced, as the case may be.'' Since the sales tax subsidy was directly credited to the capital reserve and was never debited to the Profit & Loss Account, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making an addition to book profit under section 115JB. 1.10-1 Certain decisions relating to 'depreciation' - Note the following—

The Delhi Tribunal in SAIL v. DCIT (1991) 38 ITD 193, under the provisions of section 115J held that for the purposes of working out permissible adjustment of the lower of depreciation or loss, profits made in the earlier year cannot be ignored. The losses or the depreciation must be set off against earlier years' profits. In Geetanjali Woollens Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT [1994] 50 ITD 558 the Ahmedabad Tribunal took a view that in determining, amount of loss or depreciation, to be set off, the amount already not set off in the past can only be considered.

The Chandigarh Bench of Income-tax Appellate Tribunal in ITO v. Parbhat Forging Pvt. Ltd [1991] 38 ITD 319 held that unprovided depreciation in respect of the past cannot be adjusted. While holding so, it also considered provisions similar to section 205 which were incorporated in section 115J of the Act.

Section 115JA does not have a similar provision. Now, what is permissible is reduction of the lower of brought forward loss or unabsorbed depreciation, as per books of account. This does imply that the loss or the depreciation must have been reflected in the books of account. In case of a company, which was incurring loss, depreciation may not have been provided at all.

Accordingly, in the year of profit, if it also provides for depreciation in respect of earlier years, then in computing the book profit, whether any adjustment can be made in respect of unprovided depreciation of earlier years ?

Having regard to the provisions, under the Explanation below section 115JA(2)no such adjustment can be made.

However, it may be pointed out that, as discussed earlier, a bench of Tribunal has taken a different view. Possibly, the different view could be contested on the ground that the provision for depreciation is a legal requirement, before declaring any dividends, and therefore in terms of the statute, the provision was made and therefore should not be a subject matter of adjustment.

The Cochin Bench of the Tribunal in Apollo Tyres Ltd v. DCIT [1992] 43 ITD 464 was concerned with a case where assessee provided for extra shift depreciation an its accounts, pursuant to insertion of Schedule XIV to the said Act. It was observed by the Tribunal that in view of the statutory amendment, the assessee was legally bound to provide for arrears of such extra shift depreciation. Further, this was in accordance with the provisions of the Schedule. Apart from that there was no earmarked adjustment for the provision. Accordingly, in computing book profit, an adjustment in respect thereof cannot be made.

In Bombay Tyres International Ltd v. DCIT[1994] 51 ITD 339, the company had changed the method of depreciation from straight line to WDV method based on technical or other evaluation and provided for the same in the accounts. The Bombay Tribunal took a view that change was bona fide based on recommendation of financial and technical personnel; it was a valid change and as per legal or accounting requirement as inferred, it was appropriate and not a colourable device. It took a view that the arrears pertained to a provision of an ascertained and known liability and therefore did not constitute reserve. Having regard to decision of Special Bench in Sutlej case (supra), the adjustment made by the department was not permitted.

In Beta Napthol Pvt. Ltd. v. DCIT [1994] 50 TTJ 375, Indore Bench of the Tribunal with reference to change in method of depreciation and section 115J has taken a view that an assessee is entitled to change method of depreciation and also entitled to claim extra depreciation as arrears of past.

Therefore, according to the scheme of the Schedule VI, profit on revaluation of assets is first required to be taken to the profit and loss account and, only thereafter, the question of transfer to reserve comes up and that every material feature, including capital profits or credits on capital account, are required to be reflected in the profit and loss account prepared in accordance with said Schedule VI. [Para 13] In the light of the above, it was found in the instant case that the assessees taking the profit on revaluation of assets directly to the revaluation reserve, without routing the same through the profit and loss account, did indeed unduly lower the book profits. The thrust of section 115J is on ‘book profits’ and, unlike ‘revenue profits’ which are relevant for levy of taxation. Viewed from that perspective, book profits are effected by creation of revaluation reserve directly by debit to the revaluation assets, because profit on revaluation has not been brought to the profit and loss account at all, whereas, according to the scheme of the Schedule VI of the Companies Act, such a profit should have been reflected in the profit and loss account. Whether an amount is not credited to the profit and loss account, which should have been so credited, or the amount is debited to the profit and loss account, it has the same impact and purpose. Therefore, even in case of revaluation of assets, profits on revaluation of assets are first required to be credited to the profit and loss account and the assessee not having done so, book profits of the assessee stood unduly lowered. In that view of the matter also, the interpretation given by the assessee was not acceptable. For that reason also one must confine itself to the plain and unambiguous expressions in the statute. [Para 15]

In the light of that finding also, it was to be held that when the book profit was not increased on account of creation of reserve, the book profit could also not be decreased on account of transfer from a reserve to the profit and loss account. In Capgemini India (P.) Ltd., In re [2016] 67 taxmann.com 1 (Bom.) it was held that the Indian company law, as it stood then, permitted a company to buy-back its shares either without Court approval (by adopting procedure of buy-back regulations) or with the Court's approval. If the law permitted a company to follow one of the two methods, it could not be compelled to follow only that method that results in higher tax liability. The Court held that the purchase of shares under section 391 of the Companies Act, 1956 (now section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013) was not covered by section 115QA.

In view of the above, section 115QA has been amended with effect from 1-6-2016 to provide that

(a)

Buyback will mean purchase by a company of its own shares in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force relating to companies [Explanation (i) to section 115QA(1)].

(b)

Distributed income means the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares as reduced by the amount, which was received by the company for issue of such shares, determined in the manner as may be prescribed [Explanation (ii) to section 115QA(1)].

7.5-1 'Purchase' of shares is a precondition

Even after the amendment in Explanation (i), 'purchase' of shares by a company is a precondition for applicability of section 115QA. If a particular transaction does not result in 'purchase' by the company, then section 115QA is not triggered.

Thus, section 115QA will now apply to buy backs under

(a)

sections 391 to 394 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(b)

section 395 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 235 of the Companies Act, 2013);

(c)

section 402 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 242(2)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013).

7.5-2 Unlisted share is a precondition

Even after the amendment, section 115QA applies only in respect of purchase of unlisted shares. The term 'shares' will include all types of shares including preference shares and convertible preference shares. However, listed shares or convertible debentures are not covered.

7.5-3 Positive distributed income

It appears that the provision envisages positive distributed income. If the consideration paid by the company on buyback of shares is less than the amount received by the company for issue of such shares than the distributed income would be negative and in these circumstances, obviously there will not be any liability under section 115QA.

7.5-4 Reduction of capital

Section 100 of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 66(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013) provides that a company may reduce the share capital and may 'pay off' any paid up share capital which is in excess of the wants of the company. According to one view, purchase of share under section 77A of the Companies Act, 1956 (corresponding to section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013) and reduction of capital under section 100 pursuant to which shares are 'transferred' to the company are two distinct transactions and such reduction cannot be construed as purchase of shares by the company within the meaning of section 115QA. In Goldman Sachs (India) Securities (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [ITA No. 3726 of 2015, decided on 12-2-2016] (Mum. - Trib.), the Tribunal cited observations from SEBI v. Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. [2003] 45 SCL 475 (Bom.) and held that the observations of the Court did not leave any doubt that buyback of shares could not be equated with reduction of capital.

30. The user of the phrase 'by whatever name called' signifies that the nomenclature given to an amount is of no importance or relevance. If the amount set apart represents a reserve within the meaning of the Schedule, it has to be added back to the net profit.

To illustrate, a company may follow a practice of providing doubtful debts on ad hoc basis and it may be named as 'provision for doubtful debts'. In fact, there may not be any doubtful debts. In other words, the sundry debtors may be realisable at the value stated. In such a case, such setting apart does not constitute a provision within the meaning assigned to it by the Schedule; but, in fact constitutes a reserve as defined in the Schedule. Thus, though it is called a provision, it is a reserve. Therefore, irrespective of the nomenclature, the amount so set apart has to be added back to the profits in terms of Explanation defining book profits.

Such reduction can be made in respect of any reserves or provisions created in respect of any year relevant to assessment year 1997-98 and thereafter only when the amount of such reserves or provision was added back under Explanation (b).

Accordingly, if any reserve has been created in any earlier year and if that is credited to profit and loss account, the adjustment, by way of reduction, under, this Explanation can be made.

1.9-2b CREDIT TO CAPITAL RESERVE - The Special bench of the Tribunal (Calcutta) in Sutlej Cotton Mills Ltd. v. ACIT [1993] 45 ITD 22 was concerned with an adjustment not specifically permitted by section 115J of the Act. The company in that case had revalued its fixed assets in earlier years. In the subsequent year, it revalued all its quoted investments at market value. The difference on revaluation of these shares was credited to capital reserve account. In the next year, relevant to assessment year 1988-89, it sold certain shares. The sale proceeds were not credited to profit and loss account; but were adjusted in the asset account and/or capital reserve account. In the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer took a View that the objective of revaluation was to defraud revenue and avoidance of tax under section 115J by changing method of valuation. In the appellate proceedings, the Appellate Authority held that the treatment was not in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) of the Schedule which read as follows:

"Profits or losses on investments showing distinctly the extent of the profits or losses earned or incurred on account of membership of a partnership firm to the extent not adjusted from any previous provision or reserve." [Emphasis supplied]

On the aforesaid facts, the Tribunal held as follows :

◆ The requirement of the Schedule show that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Thus, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in capital structure. Profit on realisation of capital assets will not be an item of income.

◆ Company had followed a consistent practice in relation to revaluation of capital assets. The practice adopted was in accordance with para 3(xii)(a) referred above, as a credit to Profit & Loss Account was required to be taken to the extent not adjusted, as provided therein. The practice followed by the company was a sound accounting practice as the profit was not available for distribution. Accordingly, the profit realised cannot form part of book profit.

◆ As per Explanation below section 115J(1A) providing for adjustments, only the permitted adjustments can be made. Beyond that, book profit cannot be adjusted. For the purpose, even section 145 cannot be applied. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed with computation of book profit as shown in the Profit and Loss Account.

◆ As far as valuation of assets, etc., is concerned, really it cannot be compared with the method of valuation in relation to stock in trade. In any case, section 145 does not apply to revaluation of fixed assets.

◆ The Assessing Officer cannot disturb reserve, which has been adjusted in accordance with requirement of the Schedule and as per the para referred above.

◆ This was not a device for avoidance of tax.

◆ Provisions of section 45, deeming capital gains as income, cannot apply to book profit under section 115J on account of non obstante clause. This is because a deemed income cannot be included as part of book profit.

Prior to the amendment to section 115J by the Finance Act, 1989 with effect from 1-4-1988, the assessee was entitled to reduction of the amount withdrawn from reserve, if such amount was credited to the profit and loss account. [Para 9]

In the instant case it was found that the case of the assessee could not be considered as per the situation (i) stipulated in Circular No. 550 [F.No. 133/513/89 TPL] dated 1-1-1990 for the reason that the revaluation reserve was not made in any assessment years prior to 1988-89, but could be considered only under situation, (ii) which in turn states that the reduction from the book profits for the amount withdrawn from the reserve is permissible only if such reserve was made in the assessment year 1988-89 or thereafter and it has gone to increase the book profits in any year when the provisions of section 115J were applicable. Admittedly, the revaluation reserve was created in the assessment year under consideration, namely, 1990-91 when the assets were revalued. It was clear from the copy of profit and loss account that the said amount at the time of revaluation had not gone to increase the book profits in the said year. When such amount had not increased the book profits of the company at the time of creating reserve, there was no question of reducing the amount transferred from revaluation reserve to the profit and loss appropriation account as per the interpretation of the said clause (i) of Explanation to section 115J(IA). The idea behind the substitution of that clause by the Finance Act, 1989 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1988, as borne out from the above noted circular, is only to curb such practices aimed at lowering the ‘book profits’ of the company for the purposes of section 115J. The balance sheet of the assessee-company as at 31-3-1986 indicated that the fixed assets had been revalued. The assessee had investments in shares and these consisted of both quoted and unquoted shares. These shares were not revalued in the year ended 31-3-1986 along with the other assets. However, in the next year in the balance sheet as at 31-3-1987 the assessee revalued all the quoted shares at the market value. The difference in revaluation of these shares was taken to capital reserve account. The assessee had sold certain quoted shares on 13-5- 1987 and 21-9-1987. In the balance sheet as at 31-3-1987, the value of the remaining quoted investments was recorded at book value which was as revalued in the earlier year. The amount fetched by sale of shares sold was fully invested in units of the Unit Trust of India, and showed as part of investments held by the assessee. Thus, the sale proceeds of investment in shares were not credited to profit and loss account nor the loss was debited to it but was carried to the capital reserve account.

While completing the assessment for the assessment year 1988-89 the Assessing Officer held that the shares had been revalued with the sole intention of defrauding the revenue and avoiding of payment of tax due under the provisions of section 115J, and that the change in the method of valuation of quoted shares was adopted only for one year and not followed consistently thereafter. Following the principles laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of McDowell & Co. Ltd. v. CTO [1985] 154 ITR 148/22 Taxman 11, the ITO computed the book profit for the purpose of section 115J. On appeal the Commissioner (Appeals) held that under clause 3(xii)( a) of Part II to Schedule VI of the Companies Act, the profit on investment had to be shown in the profit and loss account and that would include also the capital profit. It was held that the book profit taxable under section 115J was not just as shown by the assessee but as should be shown in accordance with the provisions of the Companies Act and that the assessee had tailored its accounts in order to escape the mischief of section 115J.

It was argued on the Revenue's side that a conjoint reading of sub-clause (1) and sub-clause (2) of Section 92 of the Act indicates that what is sought to be taxed is the cost incurred in passing on the benefit to the holding company and not the share premium received. It was highlighted that the difference between the ALP and the price charged for the issue of shares was the benefit being passed on to VTSHL. The High Court held thus: "This manner of reading a provision by ignoring/rejecting certain words without any finding that in the absence of so rejecting, the provision would become unworkable, is certainly not the permitted mode of interpretation…This rejecting of words in a statute to achieve a predetermined objective is not permissible."

2.2-4 Applicability of Chapter X to Share Subscription - With respect to applicability of Transfer Pricing provisions to share subscription the High Court observed as under :

"The charge of Income now has to be found in Section 4 of the Act. If it is income chargeable to tax, under the normal provision of the Act, then alone Chapter X of the Act could be invoked ...the amount received on issue of shares is admittedly a capital account transaction not separately brought within the definition of income, except in cases covered under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act. Thus, such a capital account transaction not falling within a statutory exception cannot be brought to tax"

Referring to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bombay Tyres India Ltd. v. Union of India10, it was held that arriving at the value of transaction on the basis of ALP would not convert non-income to income. Tax could be charged only on income and where income would not arise, the point of applying ALP to measure the value of the transaction itself would not arise.

The Hon'ble High Court further observed that the Parliament had consciously not brought to tax amounts received from a non-resident for issue of shares under Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act, as it would discourage capital inflow from abroad. The High Court went on to hold that, although Section 56(1) of the Act would allow, under the head 'income from other sources', all income which is not otherwise excluded, it does not provide for charging to tax capital receipts in respect of issue of shares as it has been specifically provided for in Section 45 or Section 56(2)(viib) of the Act.

It further explained that while income is a flow, capital is a fund. The decision of the Privy Council in CIT v. Shaw Wallace & Co. Ltd.11 was referred to by the High Court to bring out this distinction, wherein it was observed thus:

"…income has been likened pictorially to the fruit of a tree or the crop of a field. It is essentially the produce of something which is often loosely spoken of as capital"

The High Court further rejected the contention that Chapter X was a complete Code by itself. It held thus:

"It is well-settled position, in law, that a charge to tax must be found specifically mentioned in the Act. In the absence of there being a charging Section in Chapter X of the Act, it is not possible to read a charging provision into Chapter X of the Act."

Relying on the Constitutional Bench's Judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in CIT v. Vatika Township (P.) Ltd.12, the High Court held that there was no charge whether express or implied, in letter or in spirit, to tax the issue of shares at a premium. The High Court also referred to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Shetty13 to explain that the difference between charging provisions and computing provisions is qualitative in nature and computation provisions cannot substitute the charging provisions. In B.C. Srinivasa Shetty14, the transaction was not taxed as, even though there was a charging provision, yet the computation provision failed. The High Court concluded that the facts of the instant case were on a higher pedestal as there was no charging provision to tax issue of shares at premium to a non-resident, thus, there could be no occasion to invoke computational provisions.

Conclusion

Corporate Accounting Policies

5.1 Revaluation of land by DCM Ltd. and reversal- During 1990-91 DCM revalued freehold land pertaining to its closed unit, Delhi Cloth Mills, creating a surplus of Rs. 199.25 crores and subsequently, the revaluation was updated by creating an additional surplus of Rs. 74.21 crores. During 1991-92 the company revalued some more land pertaining to its closed unit, Delhi Cloth Mills, creating a surplus of Rs. 6 crores, Revaluation Surpluses were transferred to revaluation reserve.

Thereafter, DCM has converted such land into stock-in-trade and adopted a policy to recognise such lands at their historical costs plus development expenses. It has also reduced the revaluation reserve by necessary adjustments.

The whole accounting process of revaluation of land, recognition of revaluation profit, conversion of land into stock-in-trade and reversing revaluation has made the financial statements non-understandable and unreliable.

Up to the assessment year 1984-85, there was no capital gains tax incidence if any capital asset was converted into stock-in-trade for the difference between market value as on the date of conversion and cost by virtue of the Supreme Court's decision in CIT v. Bai Shirinbai K. Kooka [1962] 46 ITR 86. The tax advantage of converting a capital asset into stock-in-trade has now been eliminated by insertion of section 45(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and notional capital gain arising out of conversion is taxable as capital gains; there was thus no tangible purpose to reverse the revaluation at the time of conversion of land into stock-in-trade.

The prudent concept of valuation of stock-in-trade at the lower of the historical cost and market price is not applicable to real estate AS-2 valuation of inventories is not applicable to real estate.

Through the process of reversal of revaluation, DCM rather undervalued its stock-in-trade and thereby it has generated a set of grossly misleading financial statements in 1992-93 and thereafter. In fact, the choice of accounting policies should be directed to produce relevant and reliable accounting data to aid users' decision-making.

The revaluation in respect of factory and service buildings, plant and machinery and railway siding of the paper Mills Division were updated and similar assets of the Lakshmi Cement Division were revalued as on April 1,1990 based on current replacement cost by the valuers appointed for the purpose. Now the term ‘reserves’ have been further defined elsewhere in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI as including both capital and revenue reserves. Thus, para 35 provides a flexibility in the matter of adjustment of additional price paid either against capital reserves or general reserves including profit and loss account surplus. Normally such difference is very large and it is unlikely that a company would so choose to adjust such difference in the profit and loss account for that would impact the Earning Per Share (EPS) and the market capitalization. Any such company, therefore, would like to prioritize such adjustment against capital reserves such as share premium, etc. But in any case there is nothing that prevents a company to adjust such difference against profit and loss account. And even while it so chooses to make such an adjustment for the purpose of section 115JB, there would be no shift in the manner of treatment since the accounting standard adopted for preparation of profit and loss account in either case would be the same. In other words the treatment meted out in either case would be in accordance with the accounting standard.

Provisioning of deferred tax liability

5. Yet another instance is the provisioning of deferred tax liability when AS-22 so requires such provision for the period prior to the coming into force of standard against the reserves. Para 33 of AS-22 in this regard reads as under :

"33. On the first occasion that the taxes on income are accounted for in accordance with this statement, the enterprise should recognize, in the financial statements, the deferred tax balance that has accumulated prior to the adoption of this Statement as deferred tax asset/liability with a corresponding credit/charge to the revenue reserves, subject to the consideration of prudence in case of deferred tax assets (see paragraphs 15-18). The amount so credited/charged to the revenue reserves should be the same as that which would have resulted if this Statement had been in effect from the beginning."

In that case while the company so chooses to make such provision against general reserves in the balance sheet, yet it can draw a separate profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB after charge to the profit and loss account and take benefit of such deduction. Such an exercise would be well within the ambit of income-tax laws since revenue reserves would always include profit and loss account surplus.

Act of the actual cost of new plant and machinery other than ships and aircraft installed after 1.4.2002 for the manufacture or production of any article or thing as an incentive for expansion of capacities of production and improved quality of the products. 28.4-1a Ascertainment of depreciation provision under Companies Act is different from that under the Income-tax Act - Thus, the ascertainment and computation of depreciation for the same assets under the Companies Act and the Income-tax Act are now distinctly different while the concept of actual cost to the company of acquisition of any depreciable fixed asset on which depreciation is to be calculated is common with one major difference: Finance Act, 1986 brought into force a restricted meaning retrospectively from 1.4.1974 of the ‘actual cost’ different from that adopted almost universally on the basis of mercantile system of account keeping and the decision of Supreme Court in the Challapalli Sugars case, with respect to the interest on the funds borrowed and applied to acquire the depreciable asset being capitalized, that is, the interest includible in the actual cost computation is not in full but only such amount of interest payable on the long term loan moneys borrowed for its acquisition as is relatable to any period till such asset is installed but not for the spill over period for re-payment of the balance in full. In other words, the interest falling due and payable for the period subsequent to the date of installation of such asset on the outstanding balances of the loans does not form part of the ‘actual cost’, and it has to be charged to the revenues year after year, necessitating on account of this timing difference partial decapitalisation of the interest capitalized earlier as the actual cost. This has called for re-calculation of the ‘actual costs’ and the depreciation charged thereon accordingly for purposes of Income Tax for the years prior to 1986, resulting in yearly higher taxable income with the incidence of tax on it particularly the 100% write-off of as depreciation variety of assets. But, no co-extensive amendment to section 205(2)(b) of the Companies Act has been made, and therefore companies have continued to charge depreciation for purposes of Schedule VI as before with no re-calculation of the actual costs and depreciation charges of earlier years that consequently affect the profit or loss after depreciation of each succeeding year. It will not be in accord with sound company practice to utilize the excess amount resulting from the recomputation of depreciation for distribution to members by way of dividend or otherwise. It will also be inappropriate to show the amount so written back under a separate head ‘Reserve not available for distribution’ in the company’s books as well as in its balance sheet, Company News and Notes, 1.7.1963. Even otherwise, it would appear that it might not have fitted into the Schedule VI procedure to increase the profit and the distributable profit under Companies Act, because, if a company proposes for any other good and valid reason to write back the depreciation provided in excess in earlier years, DCA’s view is that—though there is no legal bar against it under the Act—as a sound company practice, it should not be credited to the profit and loss account and made available for distribution as dividend to the shareholders, but should be credited to a separate (capital) reserve, Company News and Notes, July 1, 1963.

28.4-1b Net profit according to Schedule VI and income chargeable of tax under income-tax are different - For these reasons of differential depreciation charges and some other items of debits and credits to the profit and loss account to be deferred or advanced as specified by law variously and in a manner different from the generally accepted accounting rules, in the pursuit of Tax Policy under the Income Tax Act, the computation of and the amount arrived at as income chargeable to tax is different, examples of deviations include the outgo on voluntary retirement schemes, or the substantial amounts of fees paid to the Registrar on increase of authorized capital, or the claim allowable at 125% of the payments (independent of expenditure) made to National Laboratories for Research and Development Projects. Consequently, it has become a necessity to disclose the ‘current and deferred tax’ effect in accordance with AS-22, in recognition of the deferred tax assets and liabilities for the future tax consequences of timing differences, subject to the consideration of prudence, using the current tax rates enacted or substantively enacted by law by the balance sheet date. Accordingly, the difference between Schedule VI or the book and tax depreciation on the fixed assets over the years forms the Deferred Tax liability and the disallowances and partial allowances and long term capital loss carried forward, difference in the bases of valuation of stocks as well as past revenue losses and allowances unabsorbed form the Deferred Tax Assets, the net value of which is disclosed as a Deferred Tax effect in a Schedule to the audited statements of accounts every year.

Revaluation reserve balance in respect of asset disposed off/retired (proposed amendment to Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2))

3. Explanation 1 to section 115JB has been amended with effect from A.Y. 2013-14 to substitute the words "if any amount referred to in clauses (a) to (i) is debited to the profit and loss account, and as reduced by,—" with the words "(j) the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset, if any amount referred to in clauses (a) to (i) is debited to the profit and loss account or if any amount referred to in clause (j) is not credited to the profit and loss account, and as reduced by,—". Para 14.4 of (AS) 10 "Accounting for Fixed Assets" provides that "The amount standing in revaluation reserve following the retirement or disposal of an asset which relates to that asset may be transferred to general reserve". Since (AS) 10 permits companies to transfer "revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset", to general reserve, companies follow this treatment. The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill, 2012 explains that as a result of this treatment permitted by (AS) 10 "the gains attributable to revaluation of the asset is not subject to MAT liability. It is, therefore, proposed to amend section 115JB to provide that the book profit for the purpose of section 115JB shall be increased by the amount standing in the revaluation reserve relating to the revalued asset which has been retired or disposed, if the same is not credited to the profit and loss account."

Thus, the impact of the proposed amendment is that revaluation increase will act be subject to MAT not in the year of revaluation but in the year of disposal/retirement of revalued asset.

Thus, if on disposal or retirement of a revalued asset, if the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset on the retirement or disposal of such asset is not credited to profit and loss account but directly transferred to general reserve or any other reserve without routing it through P&L account or allowed to remain in Revaluation Reserve, the same must be added to net profit to arrive at the book profit. In view of the words "if the amount standing in revaluation reserve relating to revalued asset", the amendment would affect companies who have credited the increase on revaluation to revaluation reserve. It would not affect companies which credit increase on revaluation to capital reserve. Companies could credit revaluation increase to capital reserve only upto financial year 2010-11. With effect from financial year 2011-12, Revised Schedule VI is applicable which requires distinct disclosure of Revaluation Reserve implying that revaluation increase cannot be credited to Capital Reserve.

The above amendment has been made to overcome the decision in ITO v. Galaxy Saws (P.) Ltd. [2011] 13 taxmann.com 179 (Mum.) wherein it was held that no addition could be made to the net profit on account of revaluation reserve directly taken to the balance sheet while computing the book profit (even after revalued asset is sold off and the balance in revaluation reserve represents realized gains). In that case, the assessee, company had sold its premises for Rs. 96 lakhs. Book value of property was Rs. 3,30 lakhs (approx.). Assessee got property revalued and as per report of registered valuer, value of property was Rs. 97.44 lakhs. Gain in book value of property was taken by assessee to balance sheet as revaluation reserve. However, loss arising on sale, i.e., Rs. 1.44 lakhs (Rs. 97.44 lakhs minus Rs. 96 lakhs) was debited by assessee to profit and loss account. Assessing Officer rejected computation of book profit made by assessee based on revalued cost and added gain of Rs. 92.70 lakhs computed on basis of book value of asset originally shown. The ITAT held that since revaluation reserve had been directly taken to balance sheet and not debited to profit and loss account, it could not be added under clause (b) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2).
