The Revised Schedule VI has no Part III as it omits Parts III (definitions of 'reserve', 'provision', 'revenue reserve' and 'capital reserve') and Part IV ('Balance Sheet Abstract of Company's General Business Profile'). Therefore, section 115JB(2) required amendment by omission to 'Part III' of Schedule VI to bring it line with Revised Schedule VI. Further, proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act,1956 permits certain companies, e.g. insurance, banking or electricity company to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions specified in their regulatory Acts. Also, Courts and ITAT have held in a catena of decisions that since profit and loss account for MAT purposes is required by section 115JB(2) to be prepared as per Schedule VI, banks, electricity companies etc. which are exempt from Schedule VI are not liable to MAT. For instance, in Krung Thai Bank PCL v. Jt. DIT (International Taxation) [2011] 16 taxmann.com 239 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that the provisions of section 115JB can only come into play when the assessee is required to prepare its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act. The starting point of computation of MAT under section 115JB is the result shown by such a profit and loss account. In the case of banking companies, however, the provisions of Schedule VI are not applicable in view of exemption set out under proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act. The final accounts of the banking companies are required to be prepared in accordance with the provisions of the Banking Regulation Act. The provisions of section 115JB cannot thus be applied to the case of a banking company. In Kerala State Electricity Board v. Dy. CIT [2010] 8 taxmann.com 118/[2011] 196 Taxman 1 (Ker.), the Kerala High Court held that section 115JB stipulates that the accounting policies, accounting standards, etc., shall be uniform, both for the purpose of income-tax as well as for the information statutorily required to be placed before the annual general meeting conducted, in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956. However, the assessee though was by definition a company under the Income-tax Act and deemed to be a company for the purpose of the Income-tax Act, by virtue of the declaration under section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act, it was not a company for the purpose of the Companies Act. Therefore, it was not obliged either to convene an annual general meeting or place its profit and loss account in such general meeting. As a matter of fact, a general meeting contemplated under section 166 of the Companies Act, 1956 was not possible in the case of the assessee, as there were no shareholders for the assessee-board. On the other hand, under section 69 of the Electricity Supply Act, the assessee was obliged to keep proper accounts, including the profit and loss account, and to prepare an annual statement of accounts, balance sheet, etc., in such form as had been prescribed by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Thus, it could be seen that coming to the maintenance of the accounts, the assessee, though was deemed to be a 'company' - both by virtue of operation of section 80 of the Electricity Supply Act for the purpose of Income-tax Act and by virtue of the definition of the expression 'company' under the Income-tax Act, yet it was required to keep and maintain its accounts in a manner specified by the Central Government, but not in the manner specified in the Companies Act. Therefore, MAT would not apply to electricity companies.

So, to bring section 115JB(2) in line with Companies Act,1956 and to overcome judicial pronouncements as above, the Finance Act, 2012 has substituted section 115JB(2) with effect from A.Y. 2013-14. Section 115JB(2) as substituted provides that companies which are not required under the proviso to section 211(2) of the Companies Act to prepare their profit and loss account in accordance with the Schedule VI of the Companies Act, 1956, profit and loss account prepared in accordance with the provisions of their regulatory Acts shall be taken as a basis for computing the book profit under section 115JB and also omits reference to Part III of Schedule VI. It is submitted that since Revised Schedule VI is applicable from 1-4-2011, the amendment dropping reference to Part III of Schedule VI needs to be given retrospective effect from 1-4-2012(A.Y.2012-13). In using the expression ‘actual cost to the assessee’, the legislature wanted to indicate the sum of money or money’s worth which it cost the assessee to acquire the asset. In special cases however the legislature indicated that the ‘actual cost to the assessee’ might be determined at some other figure. The word ‘actual’ means existing in act or fact, really acted or acting, carried out, real as opposed to potential, possible, virtual, theoretical, ideal, etc." Again it may mean ‘in action of existence at the time, present, current’. ‘Actual cost’ means ‘real cost’ – the cost which the assessee incurred in act or fact. This can only mean the cost at which the assessee acquired the asset, namely, the original cost.

Under section 211 of the Indian Companies Act, balance-sheet of the company has to be prepared in the form prescribed in Schedule VI. The heads of reserve there shown are: ‘(1) capital reserves, (2) capital redemption reserve, (3) share premium account, (4) other reserves specifying the nature of each reserve and the amount in respect thereof, (5) surplus, i.e., balance in profit and loss account after providing for proposed allocations, namely, dividend, bonus or reserves, (6) proposed additions to reserves, and (7) sinking funds.’ Depreciation does not find a place there but in Part III clause 7(1)(b) the expression ‘reserve’ shall not, subject as aforesaid, include any amount written off or retained by way of providing for depreciation, renewals or diminution in value of assets or retained by way of providing for any known liability. It would thus, appear that a provision for depreciation was not to be included in any reserves.

If the company is not obliged to show depreciation in its balance-sheet by way of reserves and indeed ought not to do so under the form prescribed by section 211, depreciation cannot be considered in the context of reserves.

The Assessing Officer treated the sales tax subsidy as revenue receipt and made addition to the total income of the assessee under normal provisions. Additionally, the Assessing Officer made an adjustment to the Book Profit under section 115JB.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) examined the issues raised by the assessee concerning the treatment of sales tax subsidy and its impact on book profit computation under section 115JB and concluded that once a subsidy was accepted as a capital receipt, it should be adjusted against the cost of the asset and thereby depreciation was to be recalculated for the purpose of computing book profit.

■

Regarding the re-computation of book profit under section 115JB, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the Assessing Officer could not arbitrarily add back the subsidy amount, as book profit is to be computed as per net profit disclosed in the Profit & Loss Account. However, since the subsidy affected depreciation, which in turn affected the net profit, the Assessing Officer was directed to recompute depreciation and then revise the book profit accordingly.It held that the accounts of the assessee had not been prepared in accordance with Part II and III of Companies Act, 1956

CIT v. Caminco Binoni Zinc Ltd. [1993] 204 ITR 56 (Cal.), Co-operative Sugars Ltd. v. IAC [1993] 47 ITD 188 (Coch.). In all these cases involving substantial expenditure on replacement of parts of machinery like revamping of an old textile unit for improvement of business operations, which capitalised in books in some cases, it was held that the expenditure is allowable as deduction by way of current repairs. The items of equipment replaced under a modernisation scheme are of two types, the first category being of cases where the replacements do not result in adding to the existing production capacity but only result in increasing the efficiency and improving the profit-earning capacity, either by way of savings in fuel cost or improving the yield of the product, etc., and the other category being of cases where the replacements result in increase in capacity as well as efficiency. The cost of both these categories of items can be capitalised in the accounts in accordance with AS 10, while for tax purposes the expenditure on the former is allowed as deduction as current repair. It may be noted that according to the legal authorities, except in the case of a claim for deduction under section 37, in order to claim any expenditure as deduction under any of the sections 30 to 36 of the Act, it is not necessary that such expenditure should be of revenue nature, as there is no prohibition for allowing as deduction even capital expenditure, if it falls under any of the categories provided in those sections, as in the case under section 37. Examples are provided by the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of India Cements Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 60 ITR 52 and decisions of several High Courts (interest on borrowings utilised for acquisition of an asset not put to use or for setting up a new project not commissioned). There are similar decisions in the case of current repairs - Hanuman Motor Service v. CIT [1967] 66 ITR 88 , 91 (Mys.) and Nathmal Banketlal Parikh & Co. v. CIT [1980] 122 ITR 168 (AP)(FB). In the case of Madras Cements v. CIT [1990] 42 TTJ 175 , the Madras Bench of the Tribunal has held that the cost of replacement of an entire Cement Mill, out of several existing mills, is an allowable deduction as current repair. These two measures if utilised properly would go a long way in not only reducing taxable income to nil but also in providing a hedge against future tax liability, as in such cases there would be substantial loss for tax purposes in spite of there being substantial income in accounts.

Under the Act, their treatment is similar again, varying with facts of each case. Needless to mention that the treatment given in books is of no consequence in this regard. The long-pending issue regarding investment subsidy has been finally settled by the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. P.J. Chemicals Ltd. [1994] 210 ITR 830, holding that it need not be reduced from cost. Subsidy, when given as an incentive to encourage growth of industry, has been considered capital - Sadichha Chitra v. CIT [1991] 189 ITR 774 (Bom.), CIT v. Dusad Industries [1986] 162 ITR 784 (MP) which was followed by the same High Court in CIT v. Plastichem [1988] 174 ITR 546 (MP), Godia Wires v. CIT [1989] 178 ITR 596 (MP) and CIT v. R.C.C. Hume-Pipe & Products [1991] 188 ITR 187 (MP). A far reaching decision in this respect is found in Tamil Nadu Sugar Corpn. Ltd. v. ITO [1994] 48 ITD 345 (Mad.) where it was held that the rebate of excise duty granted under an incentive scheme for establishing new sugar factories is a capital receipt not liable to tax. When subsidy is related to profitable conduct of business, it was held to be revenue in Merinoply & Chemicals Ltd. v. CIT [1994] 209 ITR 508 (Cal.).

Other accounting standards

12. There are no significant conflicts concerning the remaining ac counting standards, viz., disclosure of Accounting Policies (AS 1), Changes in Financial Position (AS 3), Accounting for Investments (AS 13), Accounting for Amalgamations (AS 14) and Accounting for Retirement Benefits in Financial Statements of Employers (AS 15) except for certain specific provisions for disallowance. This short article will be of interest only to companies which are obliged to pay MAT under the provisions of section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The author has pointed out that the accounting treatment to certain items in the accounting standards is made flexible, so as to offer a choice to the companies to make accounting entries in the manner found suitable to the subject, and has in this context explained two illustrative situations - EDITOR

The Supreme Court ruling

1. The Supreme Court in Apollo Tyres Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 255 ITR 273/ 122 Taxman 562 held that the first and the foremost thing in the computation of the book profits is whether the account statements are drawn in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956.

The statutory requirement

2. Upon close reading of sub-section (2) of section 115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 it requires every company assessee to draw its profit and loss account in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI of the Companies Act. The proviso to such sub-section (2) further requires that the accounting policies, the accounting standards and method and rates of depreciation adopted in the preparation of profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB must be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts as laid down before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with section 210 of the Companies Act. Sub-section (2) reads as under :

"(2) Every assessee, being a company, shall, for the purposes of this section, prepare its profit and loss account for the relevant previous year in accordance with the provisions of Parts II and III of Schedule VI to the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided that while preparing the annual accounts including profit and loss account,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall be the same as have been adopted for the purpose of preparing such accounts including profit and loss account and laid before the company at its annual general meeting in accordance with the provisions of section 210 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956) :

Provided further that where the company has adopted or adopts the financial year under the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), which is different from the previous year under this Act,—

(i )the accounting policies;

(ii)the accounting standards adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account;

(iii)the method and rates adopted for calculating the depreciation,

shall correspond to the accounting policies, accounting standards and the method and rates for calculating the depreciation which have been adopted for preparing such accounts including profit and loss account for such financial year or part of such financial year falling within the relevant previous year."

In other words nothing prevents a company to draw a separate profit and loss account for the purposes of section 115JB subject, however, to the fact that the accounting policy, accounting standards and the depreciation formula adopted is identical to the accounts prepared for AGM show. This is more so when the accounting period adopted by a company for the purposes of the Companies Act, is other than the financial year.

Requirements under accounting standards

3. Upon close reading of the accounting standards it can be found that the accounting treatment to certain items is made flexible. In other words companies have a choice to provide accounting entry in the manner found suitable to the subject.

The Pooling of Interests Method

4. Let us take an example of a company who has acquired the business of another company under an amalgamation scheme approved by the Court. Accounting Standard 14 has application in such cases. Under the Pooling of Interests Method the amalgamated company is required to disclose the assets and liabilities of the transferor company at their book values. Para 16/35 of AS-14 further requires the transferee-company to adjust the difference in the book value and the purchase consideration against the reserves. Para 35 reads as under :

"35. The difference between the amount recorded as share capital issued (plus any additional consideration in the form of cash or other assets) and the amount of share capital of the transferor-company should be adjusted in reserves."

Now the term ‘reserves’ have been further defined elsewhere in the Guidance Note issued by the ICAI as including both capital and revenue reserves. Thus, para 35 provides a flexibility in the matter of adjustment of additional price paid either against capital reserves or general reserves including profit and loss account surplus.

Further Discussion on Net Worth Having adopted Ind AS, another pertinent question will be, whether gains/losses sitting in the "Other Comprehensive Income" will be regarded as a part of net worth. Here it may be noted that Ind AS 109 allows reporting entities allow some of the financial instruments to be fair valued through Other Comprehensive Income (OCI). Any changes in the fair value of these instruments are effected through OCI, which is carried to the Balance Sheet as Other Equity.

It may be noted that the definition of net worth allows inclusion of only such profits which flow from the Profit and Loss. Unrealized OCI do not form part of the profits/ losses earned/ incurred by the reporting entity in a particular as the OCI are shown separately in the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss. As per the new format of Statement of Profit and Loss, after the Profit earned by a reporting entity is arrived at, the same is added with the OCI during the year to show the Total Comprehensive Income of the reporting entity.

Therefore, just because the OCI is shown in the Statement of Profit and Loss does not mean that the same must be considered as Profits earned by the reporting entity. Hence, for the purpose of computation of net worth, OCI cannot be considered as a part of the net worth.

However, as per Ind AS 109, once the unrealized profits trapped in the form of OCI gets realized due to sale of financial asset or otherwise, it gets transferred from Equity to Profit and Loss. In such a situation, the same must be considered as a part of net worth.

Should the retained earnings be Considered Free Reserve?

Section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 defines Free Reserves:

"2(43) ?free reserves means such reserves which, as per the latest audited balance sheet of a company, are available for distribution as dividend: Provided that—

(i)

any amount representing unrealized gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets, whether shown as a reserve or otherwise, or

(ii)

any change in carrying amount of an asset or of a liability recognized in equity, including surplus in profit and loss account on measurement of the asset or the liability at fair value, shall not be treated as free reserves."

The definition of Free Reserves says that the reserves should be available for dividend distribution as per latest audited balance sheet. It specifically excludes notional or unrealized gains and gains on revaluation of assets. It also states that change in carrying amount of asset or liability recognized in equity and surplus in profit and loss account due to restatement of asset or liability at fair value shall not be included in free reserves.

The definition does not include the unrealized part of the gains. It also excludes the surplus arising on restatement of asset or liability fair value restatement. Hence, the retained earnings which is adjusted for any differences in fair value measurement of assets and liabilities during first time Ind AS adoption cannot be considered as free as these are not realized in nature. The definition of net worth does not distinguish between realized and unrealized gains but the definition of Free Reserves does. Hence although it is a part of Net Worth as explained above, it cannot be a part of free reserves as it excludes unrealized and notional gains.

Hence the amount transferred to Retained Earnings as adjustments during transition of Financial Statements from GAAP to IND AS cannot be considered as Free Reserves.

That is, even if not actually discharged out of the profits, as where the same stand locked up in an asset/s, the profits have been deemed to have been absorbed to that extent, so as to become the source of its discharge.

Therefore, the revenue is not incorrect in stating that the said set aside of the profits is only an appropriation of profits, and would not amount to a provision, so as to qualify for deduction in the computation of the profit of the assessee-company. The issue, in fact, is not if it is a 'provision' against an ascertained liability or a 'reserve' per se, but whether it could be considered as deductible in computing the profit of the enterprise. On the contrary, as aforestated, the said accounting treatment, i.e., the set aside of profit, ensures capitalization of the profits, so that the debenture funds forming part of the capital structure, the same (capital) is no depleted on the redemption of the liability representing the said source of funds. In short, the liability, for the discharge of which the profits are being set aside, is in the capital field, so that neither the liability (on its assumption) nor the profit set aside (for its discharge) could be considered as a charge against the profits. This is precisely the reason that the same is not either claimed or allowed as deduction in the computation of income under the regular provisions of the Act.

Accordingly, the adjustment made by the assessee in the computation of book profit under section 115JB gets validated. [Para 5]

This FAQ also obviates what would have been an unfair interpretation. Share application that are presented within other equity are capital transactions rather than income. Therefore, mere reclassification of share application money to Other Equity should not be taxed. The above FAQ seems to be excluding the interest cost arising on preference shares which are classified as financial liabilities (for example, redeemable preference shares) from the computation of book profit under MAT. Therefore, such interest cost would not be tax deductible under MAT. The FAQ, however, does not explicitly deal with the treatment from the holders' perspective. By analogy, the interest income should also be excluded from computation of book profit for MAT.

The FAQ also does not deal with the equity component that arises on initial recognition of the redeemable preference shares that is either bearing dividend rate below-market interest or bearing discretionary dividend (and considered as compound instrument). Many Indian companies fund their group companies through preference shares. Inclusion of the initial equity credit that arises on issue of such preference shares is unfair since the issue of shares is not an revenue income, but essentially a capital transaction. The CBDT should reconsider the taxation of such instrument, particularly given that the future dividend/interest on the unwinding of such preference shares would not be tax deductible. Taxing the initial equity arising on such instruments is truly unfair on the taxpayers.

[2003] 131 TAXMAN 169 (ART) DEDUCTION OF DEFERRED TAX IN THE WORKING OF BOOK PROFITS UNDER SECTION 115JB

Gopal Nathani*

In this short article, the author examines the question as to whether deferred tax liability is covered as a permissible adjustment while determining book profits under section 115JB of the Income-tax Act. Analyzing the relevant provisions, as well as the relevant Accounting Standards and judicial views, the author concludes that deferred tax liability is ‘Outside the list of adjustments’ to be made in terms of the Explanation to section 115JB, while determining book profits - EDITOR

Introduction

1. In the determination of book profits under section 115JB, the starting figure is the net profit after tax as per profit and loss account. Such a profit is arrived at after providing for both current year tax and deferred tax liability. The current tax provision requires an adjustment though but whether deferred tax too needs to be added back for the purpose of computation of book profits is a point in issue.

The Supreme Court decision

2. In a recent decision dated 3-5-2002 in the case of Apollo Tyres Ltd. v. CIT [2002] 255 ITR 273/ 122 Taxman 562 , the Supreme Court held that the Assessing Officer has the limited power of making increases and reductions to such net profit as provided for in the Explanation to section 115J. Thus, the Assessing Officer does not have the jurisdiction to go behind the net profits shown in the profit and loss account except to the extent provided in the Explanation.

The permitted adjustments

3. Such Explanation provides for adjustment of the following sums if debited to the profit and loss account :—

(a)The amount of income-tax paid or payable, and the provision therefor; or

(b)The amounts carried to any reserves, by whatever name called other than a reserve specified under section 33AC; or

(c)The amount or amounts set aside to provisions made for meeting liabilities, other than ascertained liabilities; or

(d)The amount by way of provision for losses of subsidiary companies; or

(e)The amount or amounts of dividends paid or proposed; or

(f)The amount or amounts of expenditure relatable to any income to which section 10 or section 10A or section 10B or section 11 or section 12 apply.

Position qua deferred tax liability

4. Clause (a) above essentially refers to current tax liability. Clause (43) of section 2 also defines ‘tax’ meaning income-tax chargeable under the provisions of the Act. Even AS-22 defines such current tax as ‘the amount of income-tax determined to be payable in respect of taxable income for a period’ akin to the language used in such clause (a). Further, such clause has remained in its original form all through in the history of taxation on book profits since 1987. The statutory requirement for provision of deferred tax liability has however come into effect from 1-4-2001 and this certainly cannot assume the same treatment as applicable in the case of current tax or as part of income-tax payable under the Act as provided for in clause (a).

Position qua Accounting Standards (AS)

5. Further, AS-22 read such debit as a charge to the profit and loss account and not by way of amounts withdrawn for reserves requiring any adjustment as per clause (b) above. Also, AS-22 clearly mean that such liability is ascertainable and for this purpose also provide for the manner of determination of tax effect of timing difference (deferred tax), hence, such sum falls outside the purview of adjustment referred to in clause (c) as per supra. The remaining three clauses (d), ( e) and (f) have no application either.

Judicial views

6. Further, the Supreme Court in Harshad Shantilal Mehta v. Custodian [1998] 231 ITR 871/ 99 Taxman 216 held that tax, penalty and interest are different concepts under the Income-tax Act. The definition of ‘tax’ under section 2(43) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, does not include penalty or interest. In CIT v. Fertilisers & Chemicals Travancore Ltd. [2003] 126 Taxman 145, the Kerala High Court in the context of admissibility of deduction of interest on income-tax for the purpose of computation of book profits under section 115J held that the adjustment clause (a) in the Explanation only refers to income-tax paid or payable and that does not include interest.

As regards the preliminary objection to the constitution of Special Bench, no doubt, where there are conflicts between Benches, the proper way of resolving such conflict can only be by constituting a larger Bench. But it does not preclude the President from constituting a Bench of three or more members for a particular case if it appears to him that the case is so complicated or raises a substantial issue that in the interests of providing a certainty with respect to the law which is to be administered all over India it should be decided by a Special Bench.

In the present case, the assessee had applied for stay of collection of taxes which was disposed of by order dated 3-3-1992 in S.P. No. 7 (Cal.) of 1992. While rejecting the application for stay, the Bench had occasion to consider whether the assessee had a prima facie case. The Bench sent in their unanimous recommendation for constituting the Special Bench. Pursuant to this, the President considered that this was a fit case to be heard by a larger Bench because there was no decided case on that issue and the matter had to be decided on first principles. Therefore, it would be appropriate for a Bench consisting of more than two Members to apply their minds to the question. The practice in such cases is to give wider publicity and invite intervention by affected parties. It enables the Bench to have the assistance of a wider section of the Bar in arriving at a considered decision.

In Union of India v. Paras Laminates (P.) Ltd. [1990] 186 ITR 722 (SC), though that case related to a difference of opinion among the CEGAT Benches, the basic power of the President to regulate the functioning of the Benches has been affirmed by the Supreme Court and that principle equally applies to the functioning of the Tribunal. Thus, the power of the President to regulate the functioning of the Benches by constituting the Benches is well-recognised. Since that power is a purely administrative act of allocating the work, the parties to the Litigation can have no say in the matter as otherwise it would amount to granting them the privilege of choosing the Bench which is the exclusive power of the, President. The preliminary objection of the revenue thus had no substance and deserved to be rejected.

As regards the merits of the case, a reference to the requirements of the Companies Act shows that it is concerned with the result of the working of the company. Consequently, it cannot be directly concerned with changes in the capital structure. In particular, the profit and loss account is concerned with items of income and expenditure and, therefore, any profit by realisation of capital asset will not be an item of income. In the instant case, the assessee had consistently followed the practice of crediting sale proceeds. of capital assets to the asset account and shown in the balance sheet directly. The shares having been already revalued in the earlier year and the price fetched on sale being less than that, the shortfall was deducted from the revaluation reserve account. Thus, it was clear that entries made by the assessee in the capital reserve account with reference to the realisation by sale of shares, was correct and was in accordance with the requirements of item (xii) of Part II of Schedule VI of the Companies Act. As a matter of sound accepted accounting practice, the assessee was entitled to treat the accretion to fixed asset when realised as a capital reserve particularly when the realised amount had been reinvested in another asset and was not available for distribution as profit. Therefore, the profit realised by the sale of the shares by the assessee could not form part of the book profit as required to be shown in the profit and loss account under the provisions of the Companies Act.
